name: Ab Wheel Rollout
summary: An anti-extension movement through range rather than a held position, a real mechanical-tension and eccentric-control stimulus.
why_this_exists: An anti-extension movement that moves through a range instead of holding a position, and scales by how far the user rolls out.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, scales by rollout distance.
best_used_when: A real mechanical-tension and eccentric-control stimulus is wanted once planks have stopped delivering one, since moving through a lengthening range under control is a much harder demand than holding a static position.
less_suitable_when: The lower back arches during the rollout, or the range can't yet be controlled — both signal the load has outrun what the trunk can actually brace against.
mirror_effect: More likely than a plank to add visible ab thickness, since it's real mechanical tension through a full range rather than a static hold — tends to show up as a fuller, more developed look across the whole rectus abdominis, not just tighter-looking abs at the same size.
limitations: The skill and control demand is high, and the lower back is the first thing to give out under too much rollout distance too soon, which is a real injury risk if progressed carelessly.
There's a real floor to entry — a lifter with a weak core often can't control any useful range at all when starting out, unlike a plank which scales down more gracefully.
technique_cues: Kneel on a mat with the wheel on the floor under the shoulders, arms straight and hands on the handles.
Brace the abs and tuck the pelvis slightly so the lower back stays neutral to slightly rounded, never arched.
Roll the wheel forward slowly, letting the hips follow, only as far as the lower back stays in that position.
Pull the wheel back toward the knees using the abs, keeping the hips in line, until you're back at the start.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back arch as the wheel rolls out: the spine takes the load the abs are meant to resist.
Rolling out further than the trunk can control: the set ends in a collapse, the injury risk the record warns about.
Hips staying high and pulling the wheel back with the hips first: the movement turns into a hip hinge and the abs do less.
complements: An anti-rotation movement.
video_title: Ab Wheel- How to PROPERLY Use an Ab Wheel | MIND PUMP

name: Adductor Rock-Back
summary: From hands and knees with one leg straight out to the side, rocking the hips back and forward to open the inner thigh.
why_this_exists: Wide lunges and side steps in badminton need comfortable inner-thigh range. The rock-back works that range gradually without standing load.
movement_patterns: quadruped rock-back with one leg out
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; how far the hips rock back sets the depth.
best_used_when: Inner-thigh range is wanted as part of a warm-up before court sessions or leg training.
less_suitable_when: The groin is strained or kneeling is painful.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds inner-thigh range.
limitations: The lower back tends to round at the end of the rock, which ends the useful range.
It builds range only; the Copenhagen plank builds inner-thigh strength.
technique_cues: Start on hands and knees, then straighten one leg out to the side with the foot flat and pointing forward.
Keep a flat back and the chest tall.
Rock the hips back toward the bent-leg heel until the inner thigh of the straight leg stretches.
Rock forward again under control and repeat.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back at the end of the rock.
Turning the straight leg's foot up or out, which changes the stretch.
Rocking fast and bouncing.
programming_notes: A short pause at the back of each rep adds a gentle hold.
complements: The Copenhagen plank for inner-thigh strength.
video_title: Adductor Quadruped Rockback - Hip Mobility Drill

name: 45° Back Extension (Hip-Hinge-Dominant Execution)
summary: A loaded hip-extension pattern executed with bent knees and a neutral lower back, biasing the hamstrings and glutes specifically.
why_this_exists: Trains hip extension with far less setup and systemic cost than a heavy hinge. Bending the knees slightly and driving the movement from the hips — keeping the lower back neutral rather than actively extending it — is what shifts this movement's emphasis onto the hamstrings and glutes specifically. This is the execution this record describes; the back module has the same equipment used with a different execution for a different emphasis.
secondary_targets: spinal erectors (less than the spinal-extension-dominant execution)
resistance_profile: Bodyweight or lightly loaded.
best_used_when: A moderate mechanical-tension hip-extension stimulus specifically for the hamstrings and glutes is wanted, easier to recover from than a heavy hinge, or Romanian deadlifts are grip-limited before the hamstrings are.
less_suitable_when: The spinal erectors need to be biased instead — keeping the legs straighter and allowing controlled lumbar extension, described in the back module's copy of this exercise, does that instead. Back symptoms are a stop-and-assess signal either way, not something to train through.
mirror_effect: Similar visible direction to a Romanian deadlift — hamstring and glute fullness together, viewed from behind — but at a lighter load ceiling, so the effect tends to be more modest unless this is adding volume on top of heavier hinge work rather than replacing it.
limitations: The bent-knee, hip-driven technique this record describes is easy to blur into the straighter-leg, spinal-extension-dominant version without deliberate cueing, muddying which muscles actually get trained.

Loading options are limited on most equipment — a plate held to the chest or a light barbell across the back is usually the ceiling before stability becomes the limiting factor rather than the target muscles.
technique_cues: Set the pad so its top edge sits just below the hip crease, letting the hips bend freely, and hook the heels under the rollers with a slight bend in the knees.
Cross the arms over the chest, or hold a plate there, and set the lower back in a neutral position.
Hinge down from the hips until the hamstrings are stretched, keeping the back neutral rather than rounding it.
Drive the hips into the pad to raise the torso until it's in line with the legs, stopping without arching the lower back past neutral.
common_mistakes: Pad set too high, at the stomach: the hips can't bend, so the lower back does the moving instead of the hips.
Arching the lower back at the top: turns it into the lower-back version and moves work off the hamstrings and glutes.
Rounding the back to get lower: the range comes from the spine rather than the hips.
complements: A leg-curl pattern.
overlaps_with: back-extension-45-spinal-dominant (back module) — same equipment, spinal-extension-dominant execution, erector bias instead.
evidence_notes: Unverified. The claim that bending the knees slightly shifts this movement's emphasis onto the hamstrings and glutes has no direct support: the available studies use different movements and give mixed, indirect evidence. Yamamoto et al. (2015, Japanese Journal of Physical Fitness and Sports Medicine 64(3):289–294; abstract checked), using maximal isometric prone hip extension, found higher hamstring EMG at 15° than at 90° of knee flexion and higher gluteus maximus EMG at 90°. Keerasomboon et al. (2020, Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 19:630–636; full text checked), using a kneeling 45° hip extension, found higher biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus EMG at 45° and 90° than at 0° of knee flexion. Andersen et al. (2021, Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 20:181–187; abstract checked) found high hamstring and gluteus maximus EMG in a 45° Roman-chair back extension but did not report knee position. No study tested a slight knee bend on a 45° back-extension bench.
video_title: 45 Degree Hip Extension - Exercise Tutorial

name: 45° Back Extension (Spinal-Extension-Dominant Execution)
summary: A loaded hip-extension pattern executed with straighter legs and controlled lumbar extension, biasing the spinal erectors specifically.
why_this_exists: A loaded hip-extension and spinal-support pattern that can be trained without the setup and systemic cost of a heavy deadlift. Keeping the legs nearly straight and allowing a small, controlled amount of lumbar extension through the top of the rep — rather than hinging purely from the hip — is what shifts this movement's emphasis onto the spinal erectors specifically. This is the execution this record describes; the hamstrings module has the same equipment used with a different execution for a different emphasis.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight or lightly loaded, adjustable emphasis by execution.
best_used_when: A moderate mechanical-tension stimulus specifically for the spinal erectors is wanted, without the systemic fatigue cost of a heavy hinge.
less_suitable_when: The glutes and hamstrings need to be biased instead — bending the knees more and driving the movement from the hips, described in the hamstrings module's copy of this exercise, does that instead. Back symptoms are a stop-and-assess signal either way, not something to train through.
mirror_effect: Contributes to spinal-erector definition and thickness along either side of the spine — the "Christmas tree" lines visible in a lean lower back — at a lighter load ceiling than a full deadlift, so the effect tends to be more modest unless it's adding volume on top of heavier hinge work.
limitations: The controlled lumbar extension this execution deliberately uses is exactly the technique cue that's easy to overdo, so anyone new to the movement should build up load and range gradually rather than starting aggressively.
Loading options are limited on most equipment — a plate held to the chest or a light barbell across the back is usually the practical ceiling before stability becomes the limiter.
technique_cues: Set the pad at the hips so the legs stay fairly straight, hook the heels under the rollers, and cross the arms over the chest.
Lower the torso by rounding the back one section at a time, starting from the upper back, as far as is comfortable.
Raise the torso by uncurling the spine back to a straight line with the legs.
Start with bodyweight and add load only in small steps, ending the set if any back pain appears.
common_mistakes: Arching hard past a straight line at the top: the lower back is forced into extension under load beyond what the movement needs.
Swinging up quickly from the bottom: momentum replaces the controlled spinal extension the exercise trains.
Adding load too soon: the lower back is the limiting tissue here, and it needs a gradual build-up.
complements: A hinge pattern; see the hamstrings and hips modules for overlap.
overlaps_with: back-extension-45-hip-dominant (hamstrings module) — same equipment, hip-hinge-dominant execution, hamstring/glute bias instead.
video_title: 45 Degree Back Raise

name: Back Squat
summary: The main loadable knee-dominant pattern, the single heaviest mechanical-tension stimulus available for the quads and glutes.
why_this_exists: The main loadable knee-dominant pattern, and the reference point most other quad work is compared against.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile.
best_used_when: The single heaviest, most mechanical-tension-driven quad-and-glute stimulus available is the goal, with strength as a direct byproduct.
less_suitable_when: Recovery is limited, or quad-specific volume is wanted without the whole-body systemic fatigue this movement brings.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as overall mass through the front of the thigh and the glutes together — this is the primary size driver for the whole leg, not a shaping tool for any one part of it.
limitations: Technical demand is high — bar position, depth, and bracing all have to come together, and poor technique carries real injury risk at heavy loads.
Recovery cost is high relative to most other quad movements, since it taxes the whole body and central nervous system, not just the legs.
Ankle, hip, or thoracic mobility limits can cap usable depth or bar position well before the quads reach their true strength limit.
technique_cues: Set the bar on the upper traps (high bar) or across the rear delts (low bar) and pull it into your back with your hands so the upper back stays tight.
Take a big breath into your belly and brace before unracking and before every rep; hold it through the bottom.
Start the descent by bending hips and knees together, letting the knees travel forward in line with the toes.
Squat as deep as you can while keeping a neutral lower back, ideally thighs at least parallel.
Drive up through the whole foot so the chest and hips rise at the same rate.
common_mistakes: Hips shooting up first out of the bottom: the squat turns into a good-morning and load moves off the quads onto the lower back.
Knees caving inward under load: stresses the knee and usually means the weight is too heavy for the current stance and control.
Cutting depth as the weight climbs: the numbers go up while the quads do less work. Keep depth constant from set to set.
Losing the brace at the bottom so the pelvis tucks and the lower back rounds: the spine takes load the legs should carry. Stop just above the depth where this starts.
complements: A single-joint knee-extension movement, or a stable machine pattern.
video_title: How to BACK SQUAT: How to Barbell Back Squat properly - exercise demo with perfect technique

name: Band Shoulder Pass-Through
summary: Holding a band with a wide grip and taking straight arms overhead and behind the back, then returning, to move the shoulders through their full range.
why_this_exists: Overhead strokes need the shoulders to move freely through a big arc. Pass-throughs take both shoulders through that arc under light tension.
resistance_profile: Light band tension; a wider grip makes it easier, a narrower grip harder.
best_used_when: A shoulder warm-up is wanted before overhead training or court sessions.
less_suitable_when: The shoulders are injured or unstable; a narrow grip or forced range can strain them.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds overhead shoulder range.
limitations: A grip that is too narrow forces the shoulders past their range, so the grip needs to be wide enough for smooth reps.
A stick or broomstick works similarly but has no give.
technique_cues: Stand tall and hold a light band in front of the thighs with a wide grip and straight arms.
Keep the ribs down and lift the band overhead in a slow arc.
Continue behind the body as far as is comfortable, keeping the elbows straight.
Return the same way to the front, and widen the grip if any rep feels forced.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows to get the band over: the shoulders are no longer moving through range.
Arching the lower back to get the arms back.
Gripping too narrowly and forcing the reps.
programming_notes: Narrow the grip gradually over weeks as range improves, never within a set.
complements: The doorway pec stretch after training.
video_title: How To Do Band Dislocates / Pass-Throughs (Shoulder Mobility)

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row (Pronated Grip)
summary: The reference free-weight horizontal pull and one of the most heavily loadable back-thickness exercises.
why_this_exists: The reference free-weight horizontal pull, loadable with small increments and useful when a user wants one row that also demands trunk and hip control. The overhand grip is the default most people mean by "barbell row," and it flares the elbows wider than an underhand grip, biasing the upper back and rear delts somewhat more.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, fixed bar path.
best_used_when: A heavily loaded back-thickness stimulus is the goal, with the hinge itself adding a secondary training demand on the spinal erectors.
less_suitable_when: Lower-back fatigue from other work already limits how much can safely be loaded, capping the mechanical-tension ceiling this movement can deliver.
mirror_effect: Same thickness-building visible direction as any row — mass and density through the mid-back viewed from the side — and, as one of the most heavily loadable rows, often a major contributor to that thickness.
limitations: The bent-over hinge position places real demand on the lower back, which can become the limiting factor before the target back muscles are.
Technical demand is high — maintaining a neutral spine under load while pulling takes real practice, and poor form here carries real injury risk.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet about hip width apart, grip the bar overhand just outside the knees, and hinge at the hips with soft knees until the torso is well inclined, with the back flat.
Let the bar hang at arm's length below the shoulders, then brace the trunk before each rep.
Pull the bar toward the lower ribs, driving the elbows back and out, until it touches or nearly touches the body.
Lower under control to straight arms while keeping the torso angle fixed.
common_mistakes: The torso rising with each rep: the row turns into a shrug-and-lean, and the back muscles move less of the weight.
Rounding the lower back under load: the main injury risk on this lift, and the reason the record rates its skill demand high.
Jerking the bar up with the hips: momentum moves the weight instead of the back muscles.
programming_notes: Pendlay row variation: the torso is close to parallel with the floor and each rep starts from the bar resting on the floor, so every rep begins without momentum. It trades some time under tension for a stricter start.
complements: A supported row or vertical pull that does not add further spinal loading.

video_title: How to do the Bent Over Row with a barbell (pronated grip)

name: Barbell / Dumbbell Shrug
summary: Direct upper-trap loading, a mechanical-tension, size-focused stimulus rows and pulls only train indirectly.
why_this_exists: Direct upper-trap loading for users who want that area trained beyond what rows and pulls provide.
resistance_profile: Free weight or cable; the "why choose this" answer is the same across barbell, dumbbell, and cable. A band stood on gets heavier as the shoulders rise, so it is hardest at the top of the shrug.
best_used_when: A mechanical-tension, size-focused stimulus for the upper traps specifically is the goal, since rows and pulls only train them indirectly.
less_suitable_when: Grip gives out well before the traps are meaningfully fatigued, capping how much stimulus the set can deliver — straps or a different grip may be needed to keep training past that point.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as added height and mass at the top of the shoulders and base of the neck — the "trap mountain" look, visible from both the front and back, which changes the line from neck to shoulder more than it changes back width or thickness.
limitations: The range of motion is small by nature, which limits how much mechanical work each rep can do compared to a full joint-range movement.
Grip commonly fails before the traps are meaningfully fatigued at heavier loads, capping the achievable stimulus without straps or a hook grip.
technique_cues: Stand tall with straight arms and let the weight pull the shoulders fully down at the start of each rep.
Shrug straight up toward the ears, not in a forward or backward roll.
Hold the top for about a second with the shoulders as high as they go, then lower under control to the full bottom stretch.
Keep the elbows straight; the arms only hold the weight.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders at the top: adds no trap work and puts the shoulder joint through extra motion under load.
Bending the elbows to help lift: part of the rep becomes a curl or upright row and the traps travel less.
Going so heavy the range shrinks to a short bounce: the traps do far less work per rep than with a lighter, full, paused shrug.
programming_notes: Band version: stand on the middle of a band with the feet about hip width and hold the ends at your sides. A wider stance or a shorter grip on the band adds resistance.
complements: Mid- and lower-trap work such as rows or face pulls.
video_title: Barbell Shrugs - Tutorial

name: Barbell or EZ-Bar Curl
summary: The most straightforward loadable curl, the primary mechanical- tension, strength-building biceps movement.
why_this_exists: The most straightforward loadable curl, with small load steps and an easy progression path.
primary_targets: biceps (both heads, roughly even at a neutral shoulder position)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, fixed bar path.
best_used_when: The primary mechanical-tension, strength-building curl is wanted, to progress load on over time.
less_suitable_when: A straight bar irritates the wrists — an EZ bar or dumbbells deliver the same stimulus without that cost.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as overall biceps mass and peak when the arm is flexed, viewed from the front — the classic "bigger arms" driver most people picture, without emphasizing one part of the biceps over another.
limitations: The fixed bar path doesn't let the wrists find their own natural rotation through the rep, which is part of why a straight bar in particular bothers some lifters' wrists and elbows.
Momentum from the shoulders and lower back is an easy substitute for elbow-flexor tension once the load gets heavy, and it's not always obvious from the outside that this has happened.
technique_cues: Grip the bar about shoulder width with palms up; on an EZ-bar use the angled grip that keeps your wrists comfortable.
Pin the upper arms to your sides and keep them there; only the forearms move.
Curl until the forearms are close to vertical and squeeze, then lower until the elbows are fully straight.
Keep knees soft and glutes tight so the hips and lower back stay still.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso back to start the rep: the hips and lower back move the bar and the biceps skip the hardest part of the range.
Elbows drifting forward at the top: the front delts take over and tension leaves the biceps where the contraction should peak.
Stopping short of straight arms at the bottom: skips the lengthened part of the curl and makes heavier loads look possible.
complements: A curl with a different arm position, or a neutral-grip curl.
video_title: How To EZ Bar Curl With Perfect Form (Grow Your Biceps)

name: Bench Thoracic Extension ("Prayer" Stretch)
summary: Kneeling in front of a bench with the elbows on it and the hands together, sinking the chest toward the floor to extend the upper back and stretch the lats.
why_this_exists: Reaching overhead for high shots needs the upper back to extend and the lats to lengthen. This stretch works both in one position using a bench.
movement_patterns: kneeling upper-back extension on a bench
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; how far the hips sit back sets the depth of the stretch.
best_used_when: Overhead reach and upper-back extension are wanted after training or on a rest day.
less_suitable_when: The shoulders are irritated in a fully overhead position; start with the doorway pec stretch or the cross-body stretch instead.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds overhead reach and upper-back extension.
limitations: The lower back can arch to fake depth, so the ribs need to stay down.
It needs a bench or similar raised surface at about knee to hip height.
technique_cues: Kneel facing a bench with the elbows on its edge, shoulder width apart, and the palms together.
Sit the hips back toward the heels until the arms are overhead relative to the body.
Let the chest sink gently toward the floor while keeping the ribs drawn in.
Bend the elbows so the hands drop behind the head to deepen the stretch, and breathe slowly.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back: the stretch moves out of the upper back.
Elbows flaring wide: the lat stretch is lost.
Forcing the chest down into pain at the front of the shoulder.
programming_notes: Holding a light stick or band between the hands helps keep the elbows narrow.
complements: The kneeling lat stretch for one side at a time.
video_title: How To Do a Thoracic Extension Prayer Stretch

name: Box Jump
summary: A two-foot jump onto a box, landing softly on top, for vertical power with a low landing impact.
why_this_exists: Jumping onto a box trains explosive vertical leg drive, useful for jump smashes and overhead reaches, while the box shortens the fall and softens the landing.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; box height sets the challenge, and stepping down keeps landing impact low.
best_used_when: Vertical jumping power is the goal and a stable box is available.
less_suitable_when: No stable box is available, or the shins and knees need protecting from a missed jump.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds vertical jumping power.
limitations: A missed jump onto a hard box can catch the shins, so box height must stay well within ability.
Height is limited by hip mobility on landing as much as by power, so a higher box is not always a better jump.
technique_cues: Stand about a foot from a stable box with the feet hip width apart.
Dip quickly into a quarter squat while swinging the arms back.
Swing the arms forward and jump up onto the box, landing softly on the whole foot in the same quarter-squat position.
Stand tall on the box, then step down rather than jumping down.
common_mistakes: Choosing a box so high you land in a deep squat: it tests hip mobility, not power, and raises the risk of a missed jump.
Jumping down off the box: adds landing impact the drill is meant to avoid.
Knees caving inward on landing: the main joint risk in two-foot jumping.
programming_notes: Raise the box only when every landing is quiet and in a quarter squat.
complements: A heavy squat pattern for underlying leg strength.
video_title: How to Do Box Jumps

name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Long-Stance, Hip-Dominant Execution)
summary: A long-stance, hip-dominant unilateral pattern biasing the glutes and hamstrings, distinct from the quads module's short-stance version.
why_this_exists: A unilateral pattern that loads the hip through a long range with much less absolute load than a bilateral squat. Setting the front foot further out in front, keeping the torso upright, and letting the hips sink straight down and back — rather than letting the front knee travel forward — is what shifts this movement's emphasis onto the glutes and hamstrings specifically. This is the stance and execution this record describes; the quads module has the same exercise with a shorter stance for a different emphasis.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, long stance. Bodyweight with the rear foot on a bench is the entry version and needs no weights at all.
best_used_when: A strong per-side, stretch-mediated stimulus for the glutes and hamstrings is specifically wanted, or a side-to-side strength gap needs closing through focused per-leg volume.
less_suitable_when: The quads need to be biased instead — a shorter stance with the knee traveling forward, described in the quads module's copy of this exercise, does that instead. Balance limiting the set before the target muscles are fatigued is also a sign to check load or stance before adding more.
mirror_effect: Similar visible direction to a hip thrust or RDL — glute roundness, with some hamstring fullness alongside it — but built and visible one side at a time, which is what makes it useful for closing a visible left-right glute size difference the bilateral versions can't target directly.
limitations: Balance and stability demand is high, which for many lifters becomes the limiting factor before the glutes or hamstrings are meaningfully fatigued.
The rear-foot-elevated setup is genuinely awkward to get into and adjust, adding real setup time and a fall risk that a bilateral movement doesn't have.
Keeping the hip-dominant technique consistent under fatigue is harder than it looks — the knee tends to drift forward late in a set, sliding the emphasis toward the quads.
technique_cues: Take a long stance: step far enough forward from the bench that the front shin can stay close to vertical at the bottom.
Lean the torso forward over the front thigh as you descend, keeping the back flat. This lean is what makes it hip-dominant.
Sink down and back until the front thigh is about parallel and you feel the stretch in the front-leg glute.
Drive up through the front heel and midfoot; the rear foot is only there for balance.
common_mistakes: Front knee sliding forward as the set fatigues: the work shifts to the quads and it becomes the knee-dominant version.
Staying bolt upright: removes the hip bend that loads the glutes and hamstrings in this variation.
Pushing hard off the rear foot: offloads the front leg and wastes the single-leg stimulus.
programming_notes: Start each set with the weaker leg and match its reps on the stronger side, so a side-to-side gap shrinks rather than grows.
Bodyweight version: the same long-stance, forward-leaning split squat with the hands on the hips; add dumbbells once bodyweight reps are easy.
complements: A bilateral squat or hinge.
evidence_notes: No study specific to this movement was located. The "stretch- mediated" framing draws on the general stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning) found training at longer muscle length tends to match or beat training that avoids the stretch, though a later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found the advantage over full ROM is smaller than earlier work suggested. The long-stance execution's hip-flexion depth is what the claim is actually about, not anything unique to this exercise's other properties.
video_title: Bulgarian Split-Squat (Hip Dominant)

name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Short-Stance, Knee-Dominant Execution)
summary: A short-stance, knee-dominant unilateral pattern biasing the quads, distinct from the hips module's long-stance version.
why_this_exists: Loads one leg through a long range with a fraction of the absolute load, which suits limited equipment and reveals side-to-side differences. Setting the front foot closer under the torso and letting the knee travel forward over the toes — rather than sinking the hips straight down and back — is what shifts this movement's emphasis onto the quads specifically. This is the stance and execution this record describes; the hips module has the same exercise with a longer stance for a different emphasis.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, short stance. Bodyweight with the rear foot on a bench is the entry version and needs no weights at all.
best_used_when: A strong per-side, mechanical-tension stimulus for the quads is specifically wanted, or a side-to-side strength gap needs closing.
less_suitable_when: The glutes and hamstrings need to be biased instead — a longer stance with the hips sinking straight down and back, described in the hips module's copy of this exercise, does that instead. Balance limiting the set before the target muscles are fatigued is also a sign to check load or stance before adding more.
mirror_effect: Same front-of-thigh mass direction as a squat, trained and visible one leg at a time — useful for closing a visible left-right thigh-size difference the bilateral versions can't target directly.
limitations: Balance and stability demand is high, and for many lifters this becomes the limiting factor before the quads are meaningfully fatigued.
The rear-foot-elevated setup is awkward to get into and adjust consistently, adding real setup time and a fall risk a bilateral squat doesn't have.
technique_cues: Use a shorter stance than the hip-dominant version so the front knee can travel well forward over the toes at the bottom.
Keep the torso upright and descend straight down until the back knee is just above the floor.
Let the front knee track over the middle toes and keep the whole front foot planted.
Rest the rear foot laces-down on the bench for balance only and drive up through the front leg.
common_mistakes: Stance so short the front heel lifts at the bottom: unstable, and the knee is loaded without control.
Leaning the torso forward: shifts load toward the glutes, away from the quads this variation is for.
Bouncing out of the bottom: skips the deep knee bend where the quads are most stretched.
programming_notes: Start each set with the weaker leg and match its reps on the stronger side, so a side-to-side gap shrinks rather than grows.
Bodyweight version: the same short-stance split squat with the hands on the hips; add dumbbells once bodyweight reps are easy.
complements: A bilateral squat or press.
video_title: Bulgarian Split-Squat (Knee Dominant)

name: Burpee
summary: A squat, kick back to a plank, return and jump, repeated in timed rounds for whole-body conditioning.
why_this_exists: It works the legs, chest, shoulders and trunk together in one movement, making it a whole-body conditioning option with no equipment.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; pace and whether the push-up and jump are included set the intensity.
best_used_when: Whole-body conditioning is wanted with no equipment and little space.
less_suitable_when: Wrists or lower back are sore; the plank and quick floor transitions will aggravate them.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds whole-body endurance.
limitations: Form tends to break down quickly under fatigue, especially the plank position.
The quick floor transitions load the wrists.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet hip width apart, then squat and place the hands on the floor.
Jump or step the feet back into a straight plank.
Jump or step the feet back in toward the hands.
Stand and jump up with the arms overhead, landing softly into the next rep.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag in the plank: the lower back takes strain.
Landing heavily from the jump: increases impact on the knees and ankles.
Rushing reps with sloppy positions: speed should never cost the plank or the landing.
programming_notes: Step back and in instead of jumping to make it easier; add a push-up to make it harder.
complements: Mobility work for the hips and shoulders afterwards.
video_title: How To Do A Burpee | The Right Way | Well+Good

name: Cable or Band External Rotation
summary: Isolates shoulder external rotation for joint durability, not a primary size driver.
why_this_exists: Isolates shoulder external rotation, which is difficult to load meaningfully inside larger pressing and pulling movements.
resistance_profile: Light load either way. A cable keeps the pull steady through the rotation; a band gets heavier as it stretches toward the end of the rotation.
best_used_when: Joint durability and controlled rotation strength are the goal as part of general shoulder training — a health-and-resilience role, not a primary size driver.
less_suitable_when: Loads are heavy enough to lose control of the movement. This is general training work — shoulder pain or symptoms need professional assessment rather than self-treatment.
mirror_effect: No meaningful visible effect — the rotator cuff muscles trained here are small and deep, and this movement's role is joint durability, not anything that changes shoulder appearance.
limitations: Usable load is very light — the external rotators are small and this is not a movement that will ever feel heavy, which some lifters mistake for it being ineffective.
Technique is easy to get subtly wrong (letting the shoulder or trunk compensate for the rotation), and doing so quietly defeats the purpose without feeling obviously incorrect.
technique_cues: Stand side-on to a cable set at elbow height (or a band anchored at that height), holding the handle in the hand farther from the anchor.
Bend the elbow to 90 degrees and keep it pressed against the side, with a small folded towel between the elbow and the body if that helps keep it there.
Rotate the forearm outward, away from the body, as far as the shoulder comfortably allows, keeping the elbow in place.
Return slowly to the start, with the forearm across the stomach, before the next rep.
common_mistakes: The elbow drifting away from the side: the shoulder lifts the arm instead of rotating it, and the rotator cuff does less of the work.
Twisting the torso to move the handle: the trunk does the rotation the shoulder is meant to do.
Using a load heavy enough to need momentum: control is lost, which defeats the purpose of this light, controlled movement.
complements: Pressing and rear-delt work.
video_title: CABLE EXTERNAL ROTATION: Standing Cable Shoulder External Rot. How To - shoulder stability exercise

name: Cable Chest Press
summary: A standing cable press with constant tension through the range, for a pump-oriented mid-chest stimulus with a converging path.
why_this_exists: A standing cable press keeps constant tension through the range, unlike a free-weight press where the load is easiest at lockout, and also allows a converging path free weights and machines don't.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: A metabolic-stress, pump-oriented mid-chest stimulus is wanted rather than raw mechanical tension — constant cable tension keeps the muscle working hardest exactly where a free-weight press goes slack, near the top.
less_suitable_when: The priority is the heaviest possible loading for a strength-driven stimulus, which free weights deliver more of.
mirror_effect: Same mid-chest mass direction as a barbell bench press, at a lighter load ceiling — a supplementary contributor rather than the primary mass driver a heavy press is.
limitations: Absolute load is capped well below what a barbell or heavy dumbbells allow, so this can't substitute for a heavy press's strength-building role.
Requires a cable station with the right pulley setup, which isn't as universally available as a bench and barbell.
technique_cues: Set both pulleys at about chest height, stand in a split stance between them facing away, and hold a handle in each hand beside the chest.
Lean slightly forward with the chest up and the elbows a little below shoulder height.
Press the handles forward until the arms are nearly straight and the hands come close together in front of the chest.
Return under control to the chest, keeping tension on the cables between reps.
common_mistakes: Leaning far forward to push the handles: the body weight helps finish the rep and the chest does less.
Letting the handles pull the arms back fast: the stretched end is uncontrolled and the shoulders take the strain.
Shrugging the shoulders forward at the end of each press: the front delts take over the last part of the movement.
complements: A heavier free-weight or machine press.
evidence_notes: Same mid-chest evidence as flat-barbell-bench-press — see that record's evidence_notes.
video_title: How to Do a Cable Chest Press | Chest Workout

name: Cable Crunch
summary: A trunk-flexion movement with adjustable load, the genuine mechanical-tension growth stimulus for the abs.
why_this_exists: A trunk-flexion movement with adjustable load, so abdominal work can progress the way other lifts do.
resistance_profile: Small load increments via a cable stack.
best_used_when: A genuine mechanical-tension growth stimulus for the abs is wanted, progressing load over time rather than adding reps indefinitely.
less_suitable_when: The hips take over the movement, shifting the stimulus away from the abs and toward hip flexion instead.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as definition across the upper-to-mid "six-pack" blocks, since that's the segment of the rectus abdominis a crunching motion works hardest — visible ab definition is mostly a body-fat question, but this is the loading that gives the muscle underneath something to show once it's lean enough to see.
limitations: The hips readily take over the movement once the load gets challenging, and it isn't always obvious from how the rep feels that this has happened.
Cable-station setup and pulley height add real setup time compared to a bodyweight ab movement, which matters if abs are being trained as a quick add-on.
technique_cues: Kneel facing the stack with the rope held beside your head, hips stacked over the knees.
Curl the spine down, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis and the head toward the knees.
Keep the hips fixed in place; the movement comes from the spine, not from sitting back.
Return until the spine is extended and the abs are stretched before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Sitting the hips back toward the heels: the crunch becomes a hip hinge and bodyweight moves the stack instead of the abs.
Pulling the rope down with the arms: the hands should stay fixed at the head; arm pulling steals tension from the abs.
Short pulses at the bottom only: skips the extended position, so the abs never work through full flexion.
complements: An anti-rotation or anti-extension movement.
video_title: How to PROPERLY Perform A Cable Crunch to Shape Your Abs (Kneeling Cable Abdominal Crunch)

name: Cable Curl
summary: A curl that keeps biceps tension through the whole range, including the top, for a pump-oriented stimulus.
why_this_exists: A cable keeps tension on the biceps through the whole range, including the top, where a dumbbell or barbell curl loses load.
resistance_profile: The cable pulls with the same force through the whole range, so the top stays loaded where a free weight goes slack. A band, standing on it or anchored low, also keeps the top loaded but gets heavier toward the top instead of staying the same.
best_used_when: A pump-oriented curl is wanted that stays hard at the top of the range, a metabolic-stress stimulus a free weight can't deliver there.
less_suitable_when: The heavier loading a barbell allows is wanted for a stronger mechanical-tension stimulus.
mirror_effect: Same overall biceps mass direction as a barbell or dumbbell curl, without a specific peak-or-width bias.
limitations: Absolute load is capped below what a barbell allows, so this isn't a strong option for building maximal biceps strength.

The cable version requires a cable station and the right attachment, which is a real setup dependency a barbell or dumbbells don't have. The band version needs no station, but its resistance is light at the bottom of the curl and hard to load precisely.
technique_cues: Attach a straight or EZ bar to a low pulley, stand a short step back facing the stack, and hold the bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip and straight arms.
Pin the elbows at the sides and curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows.
Finish with the bar near the shoulders, without letting the elbows drift forward.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight, keeping the weight stack off its rest between reps.
common_mistakes: Leaning back to pull the weight up: the torso and momentum do the work instead of the biceps.
Elbows drifting forward at the top: the front of the shoulder takes over and the biceps unload.
Letting the stack touch down between reps: the tension drops off at the bottom, removing the cable's main advantage.
programming_notes: Bayesian variation: stand facing away from a low pulley and curl with the working arm angled behind the body. The biceps start the rep fully stretched and the cable keeps tension there, which a dumbbell incline curl loses at the bottom.

Band version: stand on the middle of a band (or anchor it low) and curl the handles up with the elbows pinned at your sides. It is the home stand-in for a loaded curl; with dumbbells or a cable available, use those.
complements: A free-weight curl with a different resistance profile.
video_creator: Fit Father Project - Fitness For Busy Fathers
video_title: How To Do Cable Bicep Curls - Full Video Tutorial and Step-by-Step Guide

name: Cable Drag Curl
summary: Combines the drag curl's elbows-behind-the-body path with constant cable tension for a pump-oriented, strict biceps stimulus.
why_this_exists: Combines the drag curl's elbows-behind-the-body path with a cable's constant tension, so the set stays hard even at the top of the range instead of losing load the way a barbell drag curl does.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range, elbows-behind-body path.
best_used_when: The drag curl's strict path is wanted with a pump-oriented, constant-tension stimulus instead of a free weight's fading top-range load.
less_suitable_when: The heavier loading a barbell allows is wanted for a stronger mechanical-tension stimulus.
mirror_effect: Same general biceps mass contribution as the free-weight drag curl, with the same lack of a confident shape-specific claim.
limitations: Same shoulder-mobility limitation as the free-weight drag curl — the elbows-behind-body path isn't accessible to everyone without practice.
Requires a cable station positioned appropriately for this path, which is a more specific setup requirement than the barbell version.
technique_cues: Stand facing a low pulley with a straight bar, holding it underhand at shoulder width with the arms straight.
Let the elbows drift back behind the torso as you begin to curl, keeping the bar close to the body.
Drag the bar up the front of the body to about the lower chest, with the elbows travelling back rather than forward.
Lower the bar back down along the body under control until the arms are straight.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows come forward as in a normal curl: the drag path is lost and it becomes a standard cable curl.
Leaning back to move the weight: the torso does the work instead of the biceps.
Forcing the elbows further back than the shoulders allow: the shoulder is strained before the biceps are worked.
complements: A standard cable or free-weight curl.
evidence_notes: Same unresolved head-bias question as the free-weight drag curl — see drag-curl's evidence_notes. The cable's constant tension is a resistance-profile difference, not new evidence on head bias.
video_title: Cable Drag Curl

name: Cable Fly
summary: A cable-based chest adduction option with adjustable pulley height, the only fly variation that can target upper or lower chest directly.
why_this_exists: A cable-based chest adduction option with flexible line-of-pull and lower systemic fatigue than a heavy press for many users.
primary_targets: chest (pulley height changes the bias — low-to-high is commonly cited as upper-biased, high-to-low as lower-biased, mid-height as most even)
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: Constant tension through the whole range is wanted for a metabolic-stress, pump-oriented finisher, or the upper or lower chest needs specific targeting by adjusting pulley height in a way free-weight flies cannot.
less_suitable_when: The single deepest stretch position a dumbbell fly's lower resistance point allows is wanted, or a movement that can be loaded as heavily as a press for raw mechanical tension is needed.
mirror_effect: Same shape-and-separation visible direction as a dumbbell fly, with pulley height shifting where that effect concentrates — higher toward the upper chest, lower toward the lower chest — in a way a fixed-bench fly can't adjust mid-program.
limitations: Requires a cable station with adjustable pulley height and, ideally, two stations facing each other, which not every gym has set up conveniently.
Standing balance and cable-path control add a coordination demand that a bench-supported fly doesn't have.
technique_cues: Set the pulleys for the target: high-to-low for lower chest, low-to-high for upper chest, around shoulder height for mid chest.
Stand in a split stance a step in front of the cables, chest up and shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Keep a slight, fixed bend in the elbows and sweep the hands together in a wide arc.
Bring the hands together in front of the chest and squeeze, then return until you feel a stretch across the chest without the shoulders rolling forward.
common_mistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows during the rep: the fly becomes a press and the triceps take over.
Letting the shoulders roll forward at the end of the stretch: strains the front of the shoulder instead of stretching the chest.
Leaning into the handles and using bodyweight to pull them: the torso does the work and the chest never reaches a full stretch.
programming_notes: Low-to-high variation: set the pulleys low and sweep the hands up and together to about chin height. This line of pull is the version most often used to bias the upper chest; the record covers every angle, so pick the pulley height for the area being trained.
complements: A pressing movement.
evidence_notes: The low-to-high / high-to-low pulley-height bias claim is unresolved — no study was found that directly tests cable-fly pulley height against measured regional pec activation or growth. It's a reasonable inference from the incline/decline press evidence (the cable's line of pull at each height roughly mirrors those bench angles), but it hasn't been tested as a fly specifically. Treat it as a coaching cue, not a settled finding, until direct evidence turns up.
video_title: TUTORIAL: How To Properly Do Cable Flyes

name: Cable Hammer Curl (Rope)
summary: A rope-attachment neutral-grip curl keeping constant tension on the brachialis and brachioradialis, a pump-oriented arm-thickness finisher.
why_this_exists: A rope attachment held in a neutral grip keeps tension on the brachialis and brachioradialis through the whole range, including the top, where a dumbbell hammer curl loses load.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: A pump-oriented arm-thickness finisher is wanted that stays hard at the top of the range, where a dumbbell hammer curl goes slack.
less_suitable_when: The heavier loading dumbbells allow is wanted for a stronger mechanical-tension stimulus.
mirror_effect: Same brachialis-driven, front-view arm-width effect as a dumbbell hammer curl.
limitations: Absolute load is capped below what dumbbells allow, since the rope attachment and cable setup aren't built for very heavy loading.
Requires a cable station and rope attachment, which adds setup time and equipment dependency a simple pair of dumbbells doesn't have.
technique_cues: Attach a rope to a low pulley, stand a short step back, and hold the rope ends with the palms facing each other.
Pin the elbows at the sides and keep the wrists straight.
Curl the rope up by bending only at the elbows until the hands reach the shoulders, keeping the palms facing in.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight, keeping the stack off its rest between reps.
common_mistakes: Leaning back to pull the weight up: the torso does the work instead of the arms.
Elbows drifting forward at the top: the front of the shoulder helps lift and the target muscles unload.
Letting the stack touch down between reps: the tension drops off at the bottom, removing the cable's main advantage.
complements: A supinated curl.
video_title: Rope Hammer Curl - Exercise Tutorial

name: Cable Kickback
summary: A single-joint hip-extension option, a low-fatigue, pump-oriented glute finisher.
why_this_exists: A single-joint hip-extension option that adds glute work without further loading the knees, spine, or trunk.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, unilateral.
best_used_when: A low-fatigue, pump-oriented glute finisher is wanted late in a session, when heavier compound work has already used up most of the available recovery budget.
less_suitable_when: The lower back extends instead of the hip, shifting the stimulus away from the glute and onto the spine.
mirror_effect: A minor, finishing-touch effect at best — some added glute pump and roundness late in a session, but the light, single-joint loading here isn't enough on its own to be a primary driver of visible glute size or shape.
limitations: The single-joint, unilateral setup means load per side is inherently light — this isn't a movement that can substitute for a compound's overall stimulus.
It's very easy to substitute lower-back extension for hip extension, especially as fatigue sets in, which shifts the stimulus away from the target muscle without feeling obviously wrong.
technique_cues: Attach an ankle cuff, face the stack, and hinge slightly forward holding the frame, with the standing knee softly bent.
Drive the working leg back by squeezing the glute, keeping the knee slightly bent and the pelvis square to the stack.
Stop when the hip is fully extended, just behind the body, and hold for a second.
Keep the lower back still; the hip should be the only joint moving.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back to kick higher: the extra range comes from the spine, not the hip, and work moves off the glute.
Rotating the pelvis open as the leg goes back: lets the lower back and hip flexors substitute.
Swinging the leg: with loads this light, momentum quickly does most of the work.
complements: A heavy hip-extension movement.
video_title: How to: Cable Kickback (Glute Max) | Form Tutorial for Bigger Glutes

name: Cable Lateral Raise
summary: A side-delt option whose resistance stays meaningful in the stretched bottom position, unlike a dumbbell raise.
why_this_exists: A side-delt option whose resistance stays meaningful lower in the range than a dumbbell raise, which changes where the movement feels hardest.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range, meaningful even in the stretched bottom position.
best_used_when: A side-delt stimulus is wanted that stays under real tension in the stretched, bottom position — where a dumbbell raise is easiest — for a genuinely different growth emphasis, or to train one side at a time.
less_suitable_when: The simplest possible setup for side-delt work is preferred, or another movement already provides a stretched-position stimulus and the top-loaded dumbbell profile is wanted instead.
mirror_effect: Same shoulder-width visible direction as a dumbbell lateral raise, since it's the same lateral deltoid being trained.
limitations: Requires a low cable pulley and enough station space to stand at the right distance and angle, which is a real setup constraint most gyms can accommodate but not instantly.
The line of pull only stays ideal for part of the range unless the pulley height and standing position are tuned carefully, which takes more setup attention than a dumbbell raise.
technique_cues: Set the pulley at its lowest point, stand side-on, and hold the handle in the far hand so the cable crosses in front of your body.
Lean slightly away from the stack and keep a soft bend in the elbow.
Raise the arm out to the side, leading with the elbow, to about shoulder height.
Lower slowly until the hand crosses your midline. That stretched bottom position is where a cable beats a dumbbell.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulder up as the arm rises: the upper traps take over the lift.
Bending the elbow more as you lift: the raise turns into a row and the side delt does less.
Cutting the bottom short: skips the stretched range that is the reason to use a cable for this.
programming_notes: Lean-away variation: hold an upright with the free hand and lean the torso well away from the stack. This starts the raise from a more stretched shoulder position, so the cable loads the bottom of the movement more; keep the lean fixed for the whole set so the angle doesn't drift from rep to rep.
complements: A vertical press; may be run alongside dumbbell raises only if the routine needs both profiles.
video_title: Two Ways to Do Cable Lateral Raises

name: Cable Overhead Extension (Leaning Forward)
summary: Leaning forward away from the stack while extending overhead keeps constant tension through the triceps long head's stretch.
why_this_exists: Standing away from the stack, facing away from it, and leaning the torso forward while extending overhead keeps constant tension on the triceps through the stretch, unlike a free-weight overhead extension where the load is hardest only partway through the range.
primary_targets: triceps (long-head-biased, strongly supported by hypertrophy research)
movement_patterns: torso leaning forward away from the stack
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range; rope, straight bar, or V-bar attachment is a grip preference, not a separate movement.
best_used_when: The long head's strongest stretch position is wanted combined with pump-oriented constant tension, rather than a free weight's fading top-range load.
less_suitable_when: The heaviest possible loading for a strength-driven stimulus is the priority, which free weights deliver more of.
mirror_effect: Same long-head, horseshoe-and-length visible direction as the free-weight overhead extension, from the same stretched shoulder position.
limitations: Setting up the leaning-forward position away from the stack takes more space and setup time than a standard pushdown or free-weight extension.
Absolute load is capped below what a barbell or EZ-bar overhead extension allows, so this can't fully substitute for that version's mechanical- tension ceiling.
technique_cues: Set the pulley high, face away from the stack, and lean forward in a staggered stance so the cable runs over your head.
Start with elbows bent and hands behind your head, upper arms beside the head and pointing forward.
Extend the elbows fully in front of you without moving the upper arms.
Let the hands travel back until the triceps are deeply stretched before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Upper arms dropping toward the torso as you extend: turns it into a pushdown and loses the overhead stretch on the long head.
Elbows flaring wide: reduces triceps tension and puts more stress on the elbow.
Rocking the torso to move the handle: the lean should stay fixed; body sway replaces elbow extension.
complements: A pressing movement or a pushdown.
evidence_notes: Same long-head evidence as overhead-triceps-extension (Maeo et al., 2023) — the shoulder is flexed here the same way, so the same MRI hypertrophy finding applies. The leaning-forward, constant-tension cable path changes the loading curve, not the shoulder position the evidence is actually about, so it doesn't add new evidence either for or against the bias claim beyond what the free-weight version already has.
video_title: Cable overhead lean away triceps extension, rope

name: Cable Pull-Through
summary: A hip hinge facing away from a low cable, pulling a rope through the legs by driving the hips forward to stand tall.
why_this_exists: The glute hinges in the library load the spine and grip through a bar or dumbbells. The pull-through trains the same hip extension with the cable pulling from behind at the hips, so the glutes can be worked through a hinge with little lower-back load and very little to learn.
resistance_profile: The cable pulls backward through the legs, so the load is greatest when the hips are bent and stays on through the lockout. A band anchored low behind the lifter works the same hinge but gets heavier toward the top instead of staying constant.
best_used_when: A glute hinge is wanted without loading the spine or grip heavily.
Learning the hip hinge before Romanian deadlifts.
less_suitable_when: Heavy, progressively loaded hip extension is the goal — the cable stack and balance limit the load well below a Romanian deadlift or hip thrust.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and alongside heavier glute work, as fuller glutes from the side — a supporting stimulus rather than a main driver.
limitations: The load is limited by the cable stack or band and by how much can be held without being pulled backward.
It's easy to turn into a squat by bending the knees too much, which shifts work to the quads.
technique_cues: Set the cable at the lowest point with a rope, face away from the stack, and hold the rope between the legs with the feet a little wider than hips.
Walk forward until the weight lifts, then push the hips back with soft knees until the torso leans well forward and the rope passes between the thighs.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, squeezing the glutes at the top.
Keep the back flat throughout and let the hips, not the arms, move the rope.
common_mistakes: Squatting down instead of hinging: the knees bend too much and the quads take over from the glutes.
Leaning back at the top: arches the lower back instead of finishing with the hips.
Pulling the rope with the arms: the arms take load the hips are meant to move.
programming_notes: Band version: anchor a band low behind you (around a post or a heavy object), face away, and stand far enough forward that it stays taut at the bottom of the hinge.
complements: Glute work in the shortened position, such as hip thrusts or glute bridges.
video_title: How to Do Cable Pull Throughs

name: Cable Pushdown
summary: A low-cost, pump-oriented triceps finisher with easy load adjustment and a fast setup.
why_this_exists: A low-cost way to add triceps volume without another press, with easy load adjustment and a fast setup.
primary_targets: triceps (all three heads — no evidence of a lateral-head-specific bias; see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Constant tension; straight bar, V-bar, or rope are a grip preference within this record, not a separate movement.
best_used_when: A pump-oriented triceps finisher is wanted late in a session, or after pressing has already accumulated fatigue and a lower-fatigue-cost stimulus is what's left to give.
less_suitable_when: A lengthened-position, stretch-mediated stimulus is the priority instead — an overhead extension delivers that where a pushdown does not.
mirror_effect: Same general triceps mass and horseshoe-shape direction as other triceps work, at a lighter, finishing-touch level rather than a primary size driver.
limitations: Load ceiling is modest relative to a compound press, since a single- joint, elbow-fixed movement can't move the same absolute weight.
It's easy for the elbows to drift away from the torso as the load increases, which brings the shoulders into the movement and dilutes the intended triceps isolation.
technique_cues: Stand tall facing a high pulley with the elbows pinned to your sides.
Push the attachment down until the elbows are fully straight and squeeze the triceps at lockout.
Let the forearms come back up to about horizontal while the upper arms stay still.
With a rope, pull the ends apart at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Elbows drifting forward and up as the load increases: the shoulders and lats join in and the triceps do less.
Leaning over the bar to push it down with bodyweight: the weight moves without the elbows doing the work.
Stopping short of full lockout: skips the end of the range where the triceps are fully contracted.
complements: An overhead extension, which loads a different position.
evidence_notes: Same correction as close-grip-bench-press: the "lateral-head-biased" framing isn't supported by evidence of the same quality as the overhead long-head claim — see that record's evidence_notes for the full reasoning. A pushdown's elbow stays roughly at the torso through the movement, so if anything it puts the long head in a relatively neutral, unstretched position rather than biasing a specific head.
video_title: Cable Triceps Pushdown

name: Cable Rear Delt Builder
summary: A cable row keeping the elbows below the wrists throughout the pull, holding the resistance angle specifically on the rear delt.
why_this_exists: A cable row that keeps the elbows slightly below the wrists all the way through the pull, which holds the resistance angle on the rear delt's specific action instead of letting the traps or rhomboids take over higher in the range.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, constant tension.
best_used_when: A mechanical-tension rear-delt stimulus is wanted with more loadable progression than a fly typically allows, while keeping the resistance angled specifically at the rear delt rather than the traps.
less_suitable_when: The elbows rise above the wrists at the top, which drifts the stimulus toward the traps and rhomboids instead of the rear delts.
mirror_effect: Same rear-delt visible direction as a fly — roundness on the back of the shoulder — with more loadable progression than a fly typically allows.
limitations: Keeping the elbows below the wrists throughout the pull takes real technical attention — it's an easy cue to lose under fatigue, at which point the movement drifts toward a standard row.
Requires a cable station and some trial and error with the angle and height to hold the resistance specifically on the rear delt, more setup than a simple fly.
technique_cues: Set a pulley at about chest height with a rope or handle, step back until the arms are straight, and stand tall.
Pull back with the elbows travelling out to the sides and kept below the wrists throughout.
Pull until the upper arms are level with the shoulders and the hands are in line with or slightly behind the ears.
Return under control until the arms are straight, keeping the elbows below the wrists the whole way.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows rise above the wrists: the movement drifts toward a standard row and the rear-delt angle is lost.
Leaning back to pull the weight: the torso does the work instead of the rear delts.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears: the upper traps take over the pull.
complements: Side-delt and pressing work.
video_title: How To Do Cable Rear Delt Fly | Exercise Demo

name: Cable Reverse Curl
summary: A cable keeps tension on the forearm extensors and brachioradialis through the whole range, for a pump-oriented reverse curl.
why_this_exists: A cable keeps tension on the forearm extensors and brachioradialis through the whole range, including the top, where a barbell or dumbbell reverse curl loses load.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: A pump-oriented reverse curl is wanted that stays hard at the top of the range, a metabolic-stress stimulus a free weight loses there.
less_suitable_when: The heavier loading a barbell allows is wanted for a stronger mechanical-tension stimulus.
mirror_effect: Same visible direction as the free-weight reverse curl — width at the elbow crease on the thumb side from building the brachioradialis — just delivered with constant cable tension instead of free-weight loading.
limitations: Same load ceiling issue as the free-weight reverse curl — the pronated grip is inherently weaker, so even with constant cable tension the absolute stimulus stays modest.
Requires a low pulley and enough cable-station availability, which is a real setup constraint compared to the barbell or dumbbell version.
technique_cues: Attach a straight or EZ bar to a low pulley, stand a short step back, and hold the bar with an overhand grip at shoulder width.
Pin the elbows at the sides and keep the wrists straight, in line with the forearms.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows until the forearms are close to vertical.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight, keeping the stack off its rest between reps.
common_mistakes: Letting the wrists bend back as the bar rises: the wrist extensors lose their position and the grip weakens.
Leaning back to lift the weight: the torso does the work instead of the forearms and upper arms.
Elbows drifting forward at the top: the front of the shoulder helps lift and the target muscles unload.
complements: A supinated curl and direct wrist work.
video_title: Reverse Cable Curl - For Amazing Bicep Gains

name: Cable Shoulder Press
summary: A standing cable press with constant tension through the range, for a pump-oriented front-delt stimulus.
why_this_exists: A standing cable press keeps constant tension through the range, unlike a free-weight press where the load is easiest at lockout, and lets the path converge in front of the body the way free weights and machines don't.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: An overhead press that stays hard at the top of the range is wanted, or a lower-fatigue finisher after a heavier press.
less_suitable_when: The priority is the heaviest possible loading for a strength-driven stimulus, which free weights deliver more of.
mirror_effect: Same front-delt visible direction as a barbell or machine overhead press, just at a lighter load ceiling — a supplementary contributor to front-shoulder size rather than a primary one.
limitations: Absolute load is capped well below what a barbell or heavy dumbbells allow, so this isn't a strength-building substitute for a free-weight press.
Requires dual cable stations or a dedicated cable press setup, which isn't available in every gym the way a barbell or dumbbells are.
technique_cues: Set both pulleys low, stand between them, and hold a handle in each hand at shoulder height with the palms facing forward.
Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes so the lower back stays neutral.
Press the handles up until the arms are nearly straight overhead.
Lower under control to shoulder height, keeping tension on the cables between reps.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back to finish the press: shifts the load onto the lower back and toward the upper chest.
Letting the handles drop fast to the shoulders: the bottom of the press is uncontrolled.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the top: the upper traps take over the end of the press.
complements: A heavier barbell or dumbbell press.
video_title: How To Do Cable Shoulder Press | Exercise Demo

name: Cable Woodchop
summary: Trains trunk rotation through a range with constant tension, a pump-oriented rotational stimulus for the obliques.
why_this_exists: Trains trunk rotation through a range, the opposite job from the anti-rotation work above.
resistance_profile: Constant tension through the whole range.
best_used_when: A pump-oriented, constant-tension rotational stimulus for the obliques is wanted, alongside anti-rotation work rather than instead of it.
less_suitable_when: The movement is driven by the arms rather than the trunk, which shifts the stimulus away from the obliques entirely.
mirror_effect: Same waist-width caveat as heavy oblique work generally: training this hard and heavy tends to add visible thickness to the sides of the waist, which can work against a tapered look even as it adds rotational strength — dial the load to match which outcome is actually wanted.
limitations: It's easy for the arms to do most of the work instead of the trunk, especially as fatigue sets in, which shifts the stimulus away from the obliques without an obvious form breakdown.
Requires a cable station with adjustable pulley height, which limits where this can be done compared to free-weight rotational options.
technique_cues: Set the pulley high, stand side-on with feet wider than the shoulders, and hold the handle with both hands above the near shoulder.
Keep the arms long and fairly still; rotate the trunk to pull the handle diagonally down across your body.
Let the back heel pivot so the hips can turn, but start the movement from the trunk.
Return slowly against the cable, resisting the pull back to the start.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of rotating: the arms tire out and the obliques barely work.
Rushing the return: the controlled return under cable tension is half the stimulus.
Rounding forward into a crunch: the target is rotation, not flexion.
complements: The Pallof press and other anti-rotation work.
video_title: Cable Woodchop | Proper Form Tutorial for Core Rotation

name: Cat-Cow
summary: On hands and knees, slowly rounding the whole spine up and then arching it down, in time with the breath.
why_this_exists: It gently moves the whole spine through bending and arching, which makes it an easy warm-up or a way to loosen the back after play.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; range is set by spinal mobility.
best_used_when: A gentle spine warm-up is wanted, or the back feels stiff after playing or sitting.
less_suitable_when: Kneeling is painful; a standing version with the hands on the thighs works too.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds spine mobility.
limitations: The movement tends to stay in the lower back unless the upper back is deliberately rounded too.
It is gentle, so it warms up but does not challenge end range much.
technique_cues: Start on hands and knees with the hands under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Breathe out and round the whole back up toward the ceiling, tucking the chin and pelvis.
Breathe in and let the belly lower and the chest lift, arching the back gently.
Move slowly and smoothly between the two positions.
common_mistakes: Moving only the neck or only the lower back.
Rushing the reps out of rhythm with the breath.
Sinking into the shoulders instead of pushing the floor away.
programming_notes: Pause for a breath at each end for a slower, more relaxing version.
complements: Thread the needle for upper-back rotation from the same position.
video_title: Cat-Cow Yoga Pose

name: Chest-Supported Row
summary: A horizontal pull where the bench removes lower-back and balance demand, pushing a back-thickness set closer to true failure.
why_this_exists: A horizontal pull where the bench removes most of the lower-back and balance demand, so effort goes into the pull itself.
resistance_profile: Machine or bench-supported free weight; grip/handle choice (pronated, neutral, supinated) is a preference within this record, not a separate movement.
best_used_when: A strong mechanical-tension stimulus for back thickness is wanted while pushing close to failure — removing the trunk-stability demand means the set ends when the back gives out, not the lower back.
less_suitable_when: The hinge's added trunk and hip demand is wanted as part of the stimulus, which a supported row deliberately removes.
mirror_effect: Rows build back thickness, not width — tends to show up as density and a "3D" stacked look viewed from the side, filling out the back between the spine and the shoulder blades, distinct from the under-arm flare vertical pulling builds.
limitations: The chest pad's angle and height often don't fit every torso length well, and a poor fit can cap the row's range of motion regardless of how heavy the load is.
Removing the hinge also removes the trunk-and-hip training stimulus a free-standing row provides, so strength here doesn't fully transfer to unsupported pulling.
technique_cues: Set the seat or bench so the pad sits on the upper chest and your arms hang straight at full stretch.
Keep the chest on the pad for the whole set.
Pull the elbows back past the torso, squeezing the shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower until the arms are straight and the shoulder blades spread forward before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad to finish reps: brings back the lower-back strain and momentum the pad exists to remove.
Stopping with the elbows level with the torso: misses the end range where the mid back squeezes hardest.
Shrugging toward the ears as you pull: the upper traps take over from the mid back.
programming_notes: Seal row variation: lying face down on a raised flat bench and rowing a barbell or dumbbells from a dead hang removes the legs and lower back entirely, the strictest form of the chest-supported row.
complements: A vertical pull; a free-standing row only if it fills a different role.
video_title: Chest-Supported Row Machine

name: Child's Pose with Side Reach
summary: Kneeling and sitting the hips back toward the heels with the arms stretched forward, then walking both hands to one side to stretch the lats and side of the trunk.
why_this_exists: It stretches the lats and the side of the trunk, which reach and twist on every overhead stroke, in a relaxed, supported position.
movement_patterns: kneeling forward reach to the side
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; reaching further to the side deepens the stretch.
best_used_when: The back and sides feel tight after play, or a relaxing cool-down stretch is wanted.
less_suitable_when: Kneeling or deep knee bending is painful.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds lat and side-trunk range.
limitations: Tight knees or ankles can make the base position uncomfortable before the stretch is felt.
It is gentler than the kneeling lat stretch.
technique_cues: Kneel and sit the hips back toward the heels, with the knees slightly apart.
Stretch both arms forward on the floor and let the chest sink down.
Walk both hands toward one side until the opposite side of the back stretches.
Keep the hips sitting back and breathe slowly into the stretched side, then switch.
common_mistakes: Hips lifting off the heels: the stretch is lost.
Reaching with only one arm and twisting the hips.
Holding the breath: the trunk stays tense and the stretch does not ease.
programming_notes: A cushion under the hips or knees makes the base position more comfortable.
complements: Cat-cow beforehand to loosen the spine.
video_title: Child’s pose with side reach

name: Chin-Up (Supinated Grip)
summary: The same bodyweight vertical pull as the pull-up, with an underhand grip that brings the biceps in more directly.
why_this_exists: The same bodyweight vertical pull as the pull-up, but the underhand grip brings the biceps in more directly, which often lets a user complete more reps or add more load at the same relative lat effort.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; progresses via added load, tempo, or assistance.
best_used_when: The same lat-width stimulus as a pull-up is wanted but with more biceps assistance, often making it easier to reach a growth-effective rep range while still building strength.
less_suitable_when: The lats need to be isolated away from the biceps — the biceps taking on more of the load means less of the set's tension lands on the back per rep.
mirror_effect: Same width-building visible direction as the pull-up — the under-arm flare that creates a V-taper from behind — though with more of each rep's tension shared by the biceps, so the lat-specific stimulus per rep is somewhat less isolated.
limitations: The extra biceps involvement means some of each rep's tension lands on the elbow flexors rather than the back, so how hard a set feels overstates how hard the back itself is working.
Same bodyweight-jump problem as the pull-up — there's no fine-grained way to scale load down for a lifter who can't yet do a full rep.
technique_cues: Hang from the bar with an underhand grip about shoulder width apart and the arms fully straight.
Draw the shoulder blades down, then pull the chest toward the bar by driving the elbows down to the sides.
Pull until the chin clears the bar, keeping the legs still beneath you.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Kicking or swinging the legs to get up: momentum does the work the lats and biceps are meant to do.
Stopping short of straight arms at the bottom: cuts off the bottom of the range, so each rep does less work.
Craning the neck to get the chin over the bar: the rep looks complete while the body hasn't actually risen.
complements: A horizontal row selected for a distinct role.
video_title: Chin ups- supinated grip

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
summary: The heaviest, most mechanical-tension-driven triceps stimulus available, under loads single-joint extensions cannot reach.
why_this_exists: Lets the triceps be trained under loads that single-joint extensions cannot reach.
primary_targets: triceps (all three heads — no evidence of a differential lateral/medial bias; see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; a Smith machine removes the spotter requirement, the same trade-off it offers a regular-grip bench press.
