best_used_when: The heaviest, most mechanical-tension-driven triceps stimulus available is the goal, with chest and shoulder work coming along as a secondary benefit.
less_suitable_when: The elbows or wrists dislike the narrow grip, or the routine already has substantial pressing volume competing for the same recovery.
mirror_effect: The triceps make up most of the upper arm's mass, so heavy compound work like this tends to be a major contributor to overall arm size and thickness, visible from the side and back more than dominating the front- facing view a biceps exercise does.
limitations: The narrow grip places real stress on the wrists and elbows, and some lifters simply can't tolerate it even with otherwise good bench-press technique.
A spotter or safety bars are genuinely needed to train close to failure safely, same as a regular-grip bench press.
technique_cues: Grip about shoulder width, just inside the shoulders. Going narrower stresses the wrists without adding triceps work.
Keep the elbows tucked close to the torso as you lower the bar.
Touch the bar to the lower chest, a little lower than on a regular bench press.
Press to full lockout with the wrists stacked over the elbows.
common_mistakes: Hands so close they nearly touch: strains the wrists and elbows with no extra triceps benefit.
Flaring the elbows out: the lift turns back into a regular bench press and the chest and shoulders take over.
Bouncing the bar off the chest: the rebound, not the triceps, gets the bar through the hardest part of the lift.
programming_notes: JM press variation: lowering the bar toward the upper chest by letting the elbows travel forward, partway between a close-grip press and a skull crusher, shifts more of the work to elbow extension. It is an advanced movement; load it conservatively until the path is consistent.
complements: An overhead triceps extension, which loads a position pressing does not.
evidence_notes: The "lateral- and medial-head-biased" claim carried by this record (and by dip-triceps-biased, cable-pushdown, machine-triceps- extension, and triceps-kickback below) is corrected here: it isn't supported by the same kind of evidence as the long-head claim. The long head crosses the shoulder joint, so its length — and therefore its bias — changes with shoulder position, which is what Maeo et al. (2023, see overhead-triceps-extension) actually measured. The lateral and medial heads only cross the elbow, so shoulder position does not change their length the same way, and no equivalent study was found showing these two heads are differentially biased by grip, shoulder-extension, or non-overhead elbow-extension movements specifically. The safest claim these movements support is that they train the triceps as a whole, with the long head under less stretch than an overhead position provides — not a specific lateral/medial split.
video_title: How To: Close-Grip Barbell Bench Press

name: Close-Grip Push-Up
summary: A push-up with the hands close together and the elbows kept tight, shifting the press toward elbow extension so the triceps can be trained with bodyweight alone.
why_this_exists: The close-grip bench press and triceps-biased dip need a barbell and bench or dip bars. Narrowing the hands on a push-up biases the same press toward the triceps with no equipment at all.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; the narrow hand position and tucked elbows put more of each rep on elbow extension than a regular push-up. Hardest at the bottom.
best_used_when: No barbell, dip bars, cable or dumbbells are available and the triceps need direct pressing work.
A triceps-biased press is wanted at the end of a session with little setup or fatigue.
less_suitable_when: Wrist or elbow discomfort appears with the hands close together — a slightly wider grip or a pushdown suits better.
Long overhead triceps work is the goal — this press doesn't take the shoulder overhead, so it isn't long-head emphasis.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time, as fuller triceps at the back and side of the upper arm — modest at bodyweight for a trained lifter, so it works best where no loaded triceps exercise is available.
limitations: Load is capped by bodyweight, so progression needs elevated feet, a weight vest or slower reps rather than small load increments.
It doesn't take the shoulder overhead, so it won't emphasize the triceps long head.
Hands placed too close together strain the wrists before the triceps are challenged.
technique_cues: Place the hands under the shoulders or slightly narrower, with the fingers pointing forward.
Keep the elbows tucked close to the ribs on the way down.
Hold a straight line from head to heels with the glutes and trunk braced.
Lower until the chest is just above the hands, then press until the elbows lock out.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows flare out: the press turns back into a regular push-up and the chest takes over from the triceps.
Placing the hands in a tight diamond under the face: loads the wrists and elbows awkwardly for most people without adding triceps work.
Cutting the lockout short: skips the part of the rep where the triceps finish the elbow extension.
programming_notes: Progress by elevating the feet, then by adding a weight vest; regress with the hands on a bench or the knees down.
complements: Overhead triceps work, which loads the long head in the stretched position this press doesn't reach.
video_title: Close Grip Push-Up | Proper Form Tutorial for Triceps Strength

name: Conventional Deadlift
summary: Loads the whole posterior chain from a dead stop on the floor — the single heaviest mechanical-tension stimulus available for it.
why_this_exists: Loads the entire posterior chain from a dead stop on the floor, which distinguishes it from hinges such as the Romanian deadlift that start from the top and never fully unload.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, floor start, hardest off the floor.
best_used_when: The single heaviest, most mechanical-tension-driven stimulus available for the whole posterior chain is the goal, and the systemic cost that comes with it can be recovered from.
less_suitable_when: Recovery is limited, or what's actually needed is back-thickness or lat-width growth rather than raw whole-body strength — a rack pull or a compound row delivers a more targeted stimulus at far less systemic cost.
mirror_effect: Contributes to overall back thickness and density broadly — traps, upper back, and especially the spinal erectors, which in a lean physique show up as the "Christmas tree" lines running down either side of the spine. It's a whole-posterior-chain effect, not a targeted width or shape tool.
limitations: The technical demand and injury stakes are higher than almost any other lift in this dataset — poor bar path or a rounded back under heavy load carries real risk.
Recovery cost is high relative to most other back exercises, since the whole posterior chain and central nervous system are taxed, not just the back muscles.
Grip is often the first thing to fail at heavy loads, which can end a set before the back and legs reach their true strength limit unless straps or a mixed grip are used.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet about hip width apart and the bar over the middle of the feet, then grip it just outside the legs.
Bend the knees until the shins touch the bar, set a flat back with the chest up, and brace hard.
Push the floor away and stand up, keeping the bar against the legs until the hips and knees lock out together.
Lower the bar by pushing the hips back first, then bending the knees once it passes them, keeping the back flat.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back off the floor: the main injury risk of the lift.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs: the lower back takes far more load and the lift gets harder.
Hips shooting up first: the legs straighten early and the back does the lifting.
complements: A single-joint hamstring or glute movement that adds volume without the same systemic cost.
overlaps_with: romanian-deadlift (hamstrings module) — related but distinct hinge that starts from the top and never fully unloads.
sumo-deadlift (quads module) — same floor pull, wide stance, emphasis shifted toward quads and adductors.
video_title: How to Do A Conventional Deadlift Correctly

name: Copenhagen Plank (Adduction)
summary: A side plank with the top leg on a bench, raising and lowering the body to load the adductors directly with no machine.
why_this_exists: The only other direct adductor exercise in the library needs a hip-adduction machine. The Copenhagen variation loads the adductors hard with bodyweight and a bench, scales from a short lever (knee on the bench) to a long lever (ankle on the bench), and is the exercise behind a trial that reduced groin problems in football players (see evidence_notes).
resistance_profile: Bodyweight lever: the farther the support point is from the hip (knee, then ankle), the heavier the load. Hardest at the top with the body in a straight line.
best_used_when: No adduction machine is available and the adductors need direct work.
Groin resilience matters, for example in sports with sprinting, kicking or quick changes of direction.
less_suitable_when: There's current or recent groin pain — the long-lever version loads the adductors heavily and has to be built up to.
Small, finely adjustable load increases are wanted — the lever steps are large.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, alongside other leg training, as fuller inner thighs from the front — inner-thigh appearance depends heavily on body composition, so treat this as shaping the adductors rather than changing the look on its own.
limitations: Load progresses in large jumps (short lever to long lever), which can be too big a step without an in-between option.
Bench height and body length have to roughly match for a clean straight-line position, and not every bench allows it.
The bottom shoulder carries the body on the forearm, so shoulder discomfort can end a set before the adductors are worked.
technique_cues: Lie on your side propped on the bottom forearm, elbow under the shoulder, with the top leg on the bench: inner knee for the short lever, inner ankle for the long lever.
Press the top leg down into the bench to lift the hips until the body is straight from head to feet.
Bring the bottom leg up to meet the bench underneath, then lower it as you lower the hips back toward the floor.
Keep the hips stacked and the body facing straight ahead; finish all reps, then switch sides.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging or the body rotating toward the floor: the trunk and shoulder hold the position and the adductors do less.
Starting with the long-lever version: loads the groin heavily before the adductors are ready — the trial programme built up through easier levels first.
Bottom shoulder sinking away from the elbow: loads the shoulder joint instead of keeping it stacked and stable.
programming_notes: Progress lever length before anything else: short lever (knee on the bench) until the planned reps are easy, then long lever (ankle on the bench). A few seconds' hold at the top is a middle step between the two.
complements: Hip abduction work, so both sides of the hip are trained directly.
evidence_notes: Harøy J, et al. 'The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial.' Br J Sports Med 2019;53(3):150-157 (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098937). 652 semi-professional players on 35 teams; the intervention was one Copenhagen adduction exercise with three progression levels. Average groin-problem prevalence was 13.5% vs 21.3% in controls (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40-0.86). Evidence quality: one well-designed randomised trial in male footballers, supporting injury-prevention value in that population. It did not measure muscle size, so it says nothing about this record's inner-thigh appearance framing.
video_title: How To Do A COPENHAGEN HIP ADDUCTION | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Cossack Squat
summary: A side-to-side squat that shifts the hips deep over one bent leg while the other stays straight with the toes up.
why_this_exists: It combines inner-thigh and hip range with single-leg control in a wide stance, close to the low side reach of badminton.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; depth and how much support is used set the challenge.
best_used_when: Inner-thigh and hip range in a wide stance is wanted, as a warm-up or mobility drill.
less_suitable_when: The groin is strained or sore; reduce the range or skip it.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds wide-stance hip and inner-thigh range.
limitations: Ankle and hip mobility often stop depth before strength does.
Balance in the bottom position takes practice; holding a support helps at first.
technique_cues: Take a very wide stance with the toes slightly turned out.
Shift the hips over one leg and sit down as deep as you can, keeping that heel flat.
Keep the other leg straight with the toes pointing up and the chest up.
Shift across through the middle to the other side under control.
common_mistakes: The bent-leg heel lifting: the load shifts onto the toes and the knee.
Rounding the back to get lower: depth should come from the hips.
Bouncing at the bottom: the stretch is no longer controlled, which strains the groin.
programming_notes: Hold a post or a counterweight in front at first to stay balanced in the bottom.
complements: A lateral lunge for strength in a similar position.
video_title: How to Cossack Squat Tutorial

name: Couch Stretch (Hip Flexor)
summary: A kneeling stretch with the back foot raised against a wall or bench, stretching the front of the hip and thigh.
why_this_exists: Lunging repeatedly and sitting for long periods both tighten the front of the hip. This stretch targets the hip flexors and quads directly.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight stretch; how upright the torso is and how far the hips push forward set the intensity.
best_used_when: The front of the hips and thighs feels tight, after court sessions or long periods of sitting.
less_suitable_when: Kneeling on the back knee is painful; use a pad or a standing hip-flexor stretch instead.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds range at the front of the hip.
limitations: The back knee takes pressure, so it usually needs a pad.
The stretch is intense for very tight lifters, who need to start more upright and less deep.
technique_cues: Kneel with one knee close to a wall or bench and that foot resting up against it behind you.
Step the other foot forward into a half-kneeling position.
Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg and tuck the pelvis slightly under.
Bring the torso upright until a strong but comfortable stretch is felt at the front of the hip and thigh.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back to get upright: the stretch moves away from the hip flexors into the lower back.
Skipping the glute squeeze and pelvic tuck: most of the hip-flexor stretch is lost.
Going straight to the deepest position: start with the torso leaning forward and progress.
programming_notes: Hold each side for the same time; spend longer on the tighter side if one is clearly worse.
complements: A deep squat hold for overall hip range.
video_title: Couch Stretch: How to

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
summary: A diagonal-path hammer curl variation toward the opposite shoulder, for a different line of pull once straight hammer curls plateau.
why_this_exists: Curling the dumbbell diagonally toward the opposite shoulder changes the line of pull from a straight hammer curl, which shifts the demand and gives a substitute when a neutral grip alone stops feeling challenging.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, diagonal path.
best_used_when: Straight hammer curls are already established and a variation with a different line of pull is wanted to keep progressing the same arm-thickness stimulus.
less_suitable_when: The diagonal path turns into swinging, trading the growth stimulus for momentum.
mirror_effect: Same brachialis-driven, front-view arm-width effect as a straight hammer curl, from a different angle of pull.
limitations: The diagonal path is a coordination demand on top of the curl itself, and it's easy for that path to degrade into swinging once the load or fatigue increases.
It's a variation on an already-established movement rather than a distinct growth driver, so its main value is breaking a plateau, not adding a new stimulus category.
technique_cues: Hold the dumbbells at your sides with palms facing in.
Curl one dumbbell across the body toward the opposite chest, keeping the palm facing in.
Keep the upper arm against your side; only the forearm moves along the diagonal.
Lower to a straight arm, then repeat on the other side.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso to get the weight across: the diagonal path turns into momentum and the elbow flexors lose tension.
Turning the palm up during the curl: it becomes a regular curl and loses the neutral-grip emphasis.
Elbow travelling forward and across with the dumbbell: the shoulder finishes the rep.
complements: A straight hammer curl or a supinated curl.
video_title: How To Do Cross Body Hammer Curl | Exercise Demo

name: Cross-Body Rear Shoulder Stretch
summary: Pulling one straight arm across the chest with the other hand to stretch the back of the shoulder.
why_this_exists: The back of the hitting shoulder works hard to slow the arm down after each stroke and can tighten over time. This is the simplest way to stretch it.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the pulling hand sets the depth of the stretch.
best_used_when: The back of the hitting shoulder feels tight, after play or on rest days.
less_suitable_when: The front of the shoulder pinches when the arm crosses the body; the sleeper stretch or a lower arm height may suit better.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds range at the back of the shoulder.
limitations: The shoulder blade tends to slide forward, which takes the stretch off the back of the shoulder.
It only stretches the back of the shoulder; overhead range needs other stretches.
technique_cues: Stand or sit tall and bring one straight arm across the chest at about shoulder height.
Hold it just above the elbow with the other hand.
Gently pull the arm closer to the chest until a stretch is felt at the back of the shoulder.
Keep the shoulder blade down and back and breathe slowly.
common_mistakes: Pulling on the elbow joint itself instead of just above it.
Letting the shoulder shrug or roll forward: the stretch is lost.
Twisting the trunk toward the arm instead of moving the arm.
programming_notes: Do both sides, with extra attention to the racket arm.
complements: The sleeper stretch for shoulder rotation.
video_title: Cross-Body Stretch

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
summary: A barbell bench press on a decline bench, a heavy press variation with a shorter bar path than a flat press.
why_this_exists: A heavy horizontal-press option alongside the flat and incline versions. Many lifters find the decline angle comfortable on the shoulders, and the bar travels a shorter distance than on a flat bench.
primary_targets: chest (commonly cited as lower-biased; EMG evidence does not confirm this, see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest off the chest and easiest at lockout; the decline shortens the bar path.
best_used_when: A heavy press variation is wanted by a lifter who finds the decline angle more comfortable than a flat or incline press, or as a different press angle within a chest routine.
less_suitable_when: A flat or incline press is available and comfortable: the decline adds setup and a head-down position without a confirmed lower-chest advantage.
mirror_effect: Overall chest mass, like a flat bench press. It's often credited with building the lower edge of the chest, but EMG evidence doesn't confirm a lower-chest emphasis, so expect a general chest effect rather than a targeted one.
limitations: A spotter or safety arms are genuinely needed: unracking and re-racking from a head-down position is awkward, and a missed rep is harder to escape than on a flat bench.
The head-down position is uncomfortable for some lifters, and decline benches with a rack are less common than flat ones.
technique_cues: Hook the feet under the pads, lie back with the eyes under the bar, and pull the shoulder blades together and down.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it, ideally with a spotter, until it is over the lower chest with straight arms.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest with the elbows tucked to roughly 45 degrees from the torso.
Press back up until the arms are straight over the lower chest, then re-rack with control.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest: the rebound skips the hardest part of the lift and risks a hard impact on the sternum.
Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress at the bottom of the press.
Training close to failure without a spotter or safety arms: a missed rep from a head-down position can pin the bar on the chest or neck.
complements: An incline press or a fly variation selected for a distinct role.
evidence_notes: The lower-chest emphasis commonly credited to decline pressing is not confirmed by the EMG evidence checked for this library. Barnett et al. (1995, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 9(4):222–227; abstract checked) found the sternocostal head of pectoralis major less active during a decline bench press than during a horizontal one. Rodríguez-Ridao et al. (2020, PMC7579505; full text checked) found the middle and lower portions most active on a flat (0°) bench but tested no decline. Glass & Armstrong (1997, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 11(3):163), often cited for this claim, could not be accessed and is unverified. The record is listed under both mid and lower chest at the owner's decision; the lower-chest listing is not evidence-backed. Evidence quality: unsupported for a lower-chest bias.
video_title: Barbell Decline Bench Press - HASfit Lower Chest Exercise Demonstration - Decline Press - Pectoral

name: Decline Dumbbell Fly
summary: Angling the bench down shifts a free-weight fly's stretch and tension toward the lower chest.
why_this_exists: Angling the bench down shifts a free-weight fly's stretch and tension toward the lower chest, a region most fly variations don't reach.
movement_patterns: shoulder horizontal adduction on a decline
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest at the bottom stretch.
best_used_when: A stretch-mediated growth stimulus specifically for the lower chest is wanted, as an isolation-style complement to a heavier compound like the dip.
less_suitable_when: Shoulder comfort in the decline position is limiting, or the dip already covers lower-chest work and a distinct role is wanted instead of an overlapping one.
mirror_effect: Same shape-and-separation effect as a flat fly, positioned at the lower chest — defines the line where the lower pec meets the ribs, an area few other chest movements reach.
limitations: The decline bench setup is less common and more awkward to adjust than a flat or incline bench, adding real setup time.
Same shoulder-vulnerability concern as other free-weight flies — the stretched bottom position caps safe loading regardless of decline angle.
technique_cues: Lie on a decline bench with the feet secured, holding the dumbbells above the lower chest with palms facing each other and a slight, fixed bend in the elbows.
Keep the shoulder blades pulled back and down against the bench.
Open the arms out to the sides in a wide arc until a comfortable stretch is felt across the chest.
Bring the dumbbells back up along the same arc without changing the elbow bend, stopping just before they touch.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows more on the way up: the fly turns into a press and the triceps take over.
Lowering past what the shoulders tolerate: the shoulder is loaded at its most stretched and vulnerable point.
Sitting up or getting off the decline bench while holding heavy dumbbells: the weights pull the body awkwardly; bring them to the chest first.
complements: A dip or other lower-chest-biased movement.
evidence_notes: Unsupported. The lower-chest activation claim formerly attributed to two EMG studies is not supported by either of them. Barnett et al. (1995, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 9(4):222–227; abstract checked) found the sternocostal head of pectoralis major less active during a decline bench press than during a horizontal bench press. Rodríguez-Ridao et al. (2020, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(19):7339, PMC7579505; full text checked) tested only flat and incline angles (0–60°) and included no decline condition. Neither study tested a fly. No MRI or ultrasound hypertrophy trial isolating a decline-specific lower-chest effect was located. The specific claim that a decline fly increases lower-chest activation is therefore unsupported. Evidence quality: unsupported.

The "stretch-mediated growth stimulus" framing draws on the same general stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature cited on flat-dumbbell-fly (Schoenfeld & Grgic, 2020; Wolf et al., 2023, 2025) — a general principle, not a fly-specific or decline-specific finding.
video_title: How to Do a Decline Dumbbell Fly

name: Decline Dumbbell Press
summary: A dumbbell press on a decline bench, with independent arms and a shorter range than a flat dumbbell press.
why_this_exists: A decline press option that needs only dumbbells and a decline bench, with independent arms that let each side find its own path. Many lifters find the decline angle comfortable on the shoulders.
primary_targets: chest (commonly cited as lower-biased; EMG evidence does not confirm this, see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; independent arms, with a lower load ceiling than a barbell decline press.
best_used_when: A decline press is wanted with only dumbbells, or with independent arms when a barbell decline press feels awkward on the shoulders.
less_suitable_when: A flat or incline press is available and comfortable: the decline adds setup and a head-down position without a confirmed lower-chest advantage.
mirror_effect: Overall chest mass, like a flat dumbbell press. It's often credited with building the lower edge of the chest, but EMG evidence doesn't confirm a lower-chest emphasis, so expect a general chest effect rather than a targeted one.
limitations: Getting a heavy pair of dumbbells into position on a decline bench is awkward, and at high weights it needs a spotter to hand them over.
Controlling two independent dumbbells caps the achievable load below what a barbell decline press allows.
technique_cues: Sit on the decline bench with the feet hooked under the pads and the dumbbells on the thighs, then lie back, bringing them to the sides of the lower chest.
Pull the shoulder blades together and down against the bench.
Press the dumbbells up over the lower chest until the arms are nearly straight, letting them move slightly toward each other.
Lower under control until the dumbbells are beside the lower chest, as deep as the shoulders comfortably allow.
common_mistakes: Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress at the bottom of the press.
Letting the dumbbells drift apart or wobble at the bottom: control is lost where the press is hardest.
Sitting up from the decline while holding heavy dumbbells: the weights pull the body awkwardly; bring them to the chest and sit up with control, or have a spotter take them.
complements: An incline press or a fly variation selected for a distinct role.
evidence_notes: The lower-chest emphasis commonly credited to decline pressing is not confirmed by the EMG evidence checked for this library. Barnett et al. (1995, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 9(4):222–227; abstract checked) found the sternocostal head of pectoralis major less active during a decline bench press than during a horizontal one. Rodríguez-Ridao et al. (2020, PMC7579505; full text checked) found the middle and lower portions most active on a flat (0°) bench but tested no decline. Glass & Armstrong (1997, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 11(3):163), often cited for this claim, could not be accessed and is unverified. The record is listed under both mid and lower chest at the owner's decision; the lower-chest listing is not evidence-backed. Evidence quality: unsupported for a lower-chest bias.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial: Decline DB Chest Press

name: Deep Squat Hold
summary: Sitting in the bottom of a deep bodyweight squat and holding it, to build comfortable hip, knee and ankle range.
why_this_exists: Low lunges and pick-ups in badminton need comfortable range at the hips and ankles. Holding a deep squat builds that range without equipment.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; holding a support makes it easier, letting go makes it harder.
best_used_when: Hip and ankle range for low positions is wanted, as a warm-up or daily mobility habit.
less_suitable_when: Knee pain appears in deep bending; work in a shallower range or with a raised heel.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds comfortable range in a deep squat.
limitations: Ankle stiffness often limits depth before the hips do, which a heel lift can work around.
It builds range, not strength or power.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet a little wider than the hips and the toes slightly turned out.
Lower into the deepest squat you can hold with the heels down, holding a post or door frame if needed.
Let the elbows gently push the knees out while keeping the chest up.
Breathe slowly and relax into the position for the whole hold.
common_mistakes: Heels lifting off the floor: the stretch moves away from the ankles and the position becomes unstable.
Forcing depth into pain: mobility work should be a clear but comfortable stretch.
Holding the breath: the muscles stay tense and the position does not relax.
programming_notes: A plate or wedge under the heels is a fine starting point; reduce it as ankle range improves.
complements: Knee-to-wall ankle mobility for ankle range specifically.
video_title: How To Do a Deep Squat Mobility Hold

name: Dip (Chest-Biased, Forward Lean)
summary: A bodyweight press that, with a forward torso lean, is one of the few ways to load the lower chest heavily.
why_this_exists: A bodyweight press that, with a forward torso lean, biases the lower chest more than flat or incline pressing does.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled, hardest at the bottom stretch; loading capacity is capped by bodyweight unless added load or assistance is used.
best_used_when: One of the few genuinely heavy, mechanical-tension-driven options for the lower chest is wanted, with a deep stretch at the bottom most pressing angles don't reach.
less_suitable_when: Shoulder range or tolerance limits how deep the dip can go, which caps the stretch that gives this movement its main growth value — a shallow dip loses most of what makes it distinct from a flat press.
mirror_effect: Tends to fill in the lower chest specifically, the area just above where the pec meets the ribs — one of the few ways to add real heavy mass there, an area flat and incline pressing mostly miss.
limitations: Shoulder range and tolerance genuinely limit how deep the dip can go for many lifters, and a shallow dip loses most of what makes this movement distinct.
The forward-lean, deep-stretch bottom position is demanding on the shoulder joint, and going too heavy too soon carries real injury risk.
technique_cues: Use bars about shoulder width or slightly wider and start at the top with straight arms.
Lean the torso forward and let the elbows flare slightly as you descend. The lean is what shifts this toward the chest.
Lower until you feel a stretch across the chest, around upper arms parallel to the floor or as deep as your shoulders tolerate.
Press back up while keeping the forward lean.
common_mistakes: Staying upright: shifts the work to the triceps and loses the lower-chest emphasis.
Dropping fast into the bottom or going deeper than your shoulders tolerate: the stretched bottom is where shoulder injuries happen.
Shoulders shrugging up toward the ears at the bottom: loads the front of the shoulder joint instead of the chest.
programming_notes: Once bodyweight reps go past the planned rep range, add load with a dip belt. If bodyweight is too much, use an assisted dip machine or a band rather than cutting depth.
complements: An incline press, which covers the opposite end of the chest.
overlaps_with: dip-triceps-biased (arms module) — torso angle is what separates the two.
evidence_notes: Same lower-chest evidence tier as decline-dumbbell-fly — see that record's evidence_notes. EMG on dips specifically shows high lower-pec activation with a forward lean, but no MRI or ultrasound hypertrophy trial isolating the dip's lower-chest effect was located, so this stays a moderate-confidence, EMG-only claim rather than the stronger hypertrophy-trial support the upper-chest claim has.
video_title: How To Do Forward Lean Dips | Exercise Demo

name: Dip (Triceps-Biased, Upright Torso)
summary: An upright-torso dip shifting emphasis toward the triceps rather than the lower chest, a heavy bodyweight compound stimulus.
why_this_exists: With the torso kept upright, a dip shifts emphasis toward the triceps rather than the lower chest, letting one piece of equipment serve two different roles depending on execution.
primary_targets: triceps (all three heads — no evidence of a differential lateral/medial bias; see evidence_notes)
movement_patterns: elbow extension within a vertical-to-horizontal press
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; loading capacity capped by bodyweight unless added load or assistance is used.
best_used_when: A heavy, mechanical-tension-driven triceps stimulus is wanted under a real compound movement rather than an isolation exercise.
less_suitable_when: Shoulder tolerance limits a deep dip, or bodyweight alone is too heavy a starting load to complete a useful number of reps.
mirror_effect: Same overall triceps mass direction as close-grip bench press — a heavy compound contributor to arm thickness, visible mostly from the side and back.
limitations: Shoulder tolerance for a deep dip varies a lot between lifters, and forcing depth without adequate mobility raises real injury risk.
Bodyweight alone can be too much load to complete a useful number of reps for a beginner, and adding assistance or reducing range both come with their own setup complexity.
technique_cues: Use narrow bars if available and start at the top with straight arms and the body vertical.
Keep the torso upright and the elbows tucked, pointing straight back. The upright torso is what shifts this toward the triceps.
Lower until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor, or as deep as your shoulders tolerate.
Press up to full elbow lockout.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward as fatigue builds: the dip turns into the chest-biased version.
Elbows flaring out: less triceps work and more shoulder stress.
Half reps near the top: misses most of the elbow range the triceps work through.
programming_notes: Once bodyweight reps go past the planned rep range, add load with a dip belt. If bodyweight is too much, use an assisted dip machine or a band rather than cutting depth.
complements: A pressing movement or a pushdown.
overlaps_with: dip-chest-biased (chest module) — torso angle is what separates the two.
evidence_notes: Same correction as close-grip-bench-press: no evidence found for a differential lateral/medial-head bias here — see that record's evidence_notes for the full reasoning.
video_title: Triceps - (Upright) Dips (Proper Form)

name: Doorway Pec Stretch
summary: Placing a forearm on a door frame and stepping through, stretching the front of the chest and shoulder.
why_this_exists: A lot of hitting, pressing and sitting tightens the chest. This stretch opens the front of the shoulder and chest with nothing more than a door frame.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; how far the body steps through the frame sets the depth.
best_used_when: Chest and front-shoulder tightness is the issue, after training or on rest days.
less_suitable_when: The front of the shoulder feels pinched or unstable in this position; lower the arm or skip it.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds chest and front-shoulder range.
limitations: Elbow height changes which part of the chest is stretched, so the position needs a little experimenting.
Stepping too far through can stress the front of the shoulder joint rather than stretch the muscle.
technique_cues: Stand in a doorway and place one forearm on the frame with the elbow at about shoulder height and bent to 90 degrees.
Step the same-side foot forward through the doorway.
Turn the chest gently away from the arm until a stretch is felt across the chest.
Keep the shoulder down and back, away from the ear, and breathe slowly.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulder up: the stretch moves into the neck and the joint is less protected.
Leaning in hard enough to feel it at the front of the joint rather than the chest muscle.
Arching the lower back to get further through the frame.
programming_notes: Try the elbow slightly below and slightly above shoulder height to stretch different parts of the chest.
complements: Band shoulder pass-throughs to move the shoulder through range afterwards.
video_title: Doorway Stretch

name: Drag Curl
summary: Dragging the bar up along the torso lets the elbows travel behind the body for a stricter, more isolated biceps stimulus.
why_this_exists: Dragging the bar up along the torso lets the elbows travel behind the body instead of staying pinned forward, which removes front-delt involvement and changes the biceps' loading path.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, elbows-behind-body path.
best_used_when: A stricter, more isolated biceps stimulus is wanted that removes the shoulder swing a standard curl can lean on.
less_suitable_when: Shoulder mobility doesn't allow the elbows to travel back comfortably, limiting how strict the path can actually be kept.
mirror_effect: General biceps mass contribution — no confident claim about a specific peak-vs-width shape bias here, since the evidence for this movement's head bias is genuinely unresolved (see evidence_notes). Its real value is the strict path, not a distinct visible shape effect.
limitations: Shoulder mobility genuinely limits how far back the elbows can travel, and forcing the position without that mobility defeats the strict path that's the point of the exercise.
It's a less intuitive movement pattern than a standard curl, and it takes real practice to keep the bar dragging along the torso rather than swinging forward.
technique_cues: Stand holding the bar underhand at shoulder width with the arms straight and the bar against the thighs.
As you curl, let the elbows travel back behind the torso so the bar stays in contact with the body.
Drag the bar up the front of the body to about the lower chest.
Lower the bar back down along the body under control until the arms are straight.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar drift away from the body: the elbows come forward and it becomes a standard curl.
Leaning back to move the weight: the torso does the work instead of the biceps.
Forcing the elbows further back than the shoulders allow: the shoulder is strained before the biceps are worked.
complements: A standard barbell or dumbbell curl.
evidence_notes: The common coaching cue calls this short-head-biased, but that runs against the mechanical argument usually made for incline curls: drawing the elbows behind the torso extends the shoulder, the same direction incline curls use, which is argued to favour the long head, not the short. Neither side is confirmed: the one direct hypertrophy comparison of shoulder positions (Attarieh et al. 2025, see incline-dumbbell-curl) found no regional difference. No study specifically testing drag curls was found to resolve the contradiction. Treat the head-bias claim as unresolved rather than asserting either side; the movement's real, better-supported value is the stricter, swing-free path (see why_this_exists), not a specific head bias.
video_title: How To: Barbell Drag Curl (Increase Bicep Peaks!)

name: Drop Landing
summary: Stepping off a low box and landing on both feet in a quiet, balanced quarter squat.
why_this_exists: Badminton involves constant landing and stopping. Drop landings teach the legs to absorb force in a safe, repeatable position before faster jumping is added.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; box height sets the landing force.
best_used_when: Landing technique needs building before or alongside jumping drills.
less_suitable_when: Knees are currently painful under impact; strength work comes first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds safe landing mechanics.
limitations: Box height must stay low at first; too high a drop increases landing force faster than technique improves.
It trains absorbing force, not producing it.
technique_cues: Stand on a low box with the feet hip width apart.
Step off with one foot, without jumping up first.
Land on both feet at the same time, sinking into a quarter squat with the hips back and the knees over the toes.
Hold the landing for two seconds, quietly and without wobbling.
common_mistakes: Landing stiff-legged: the joints take the force instead of the muscles absorbing it.
Knees caving inward: the main knee-injury risk in landing.
Landing loudly on the heels: shows the force is not being absorbed through the ankles, knees and hips.
programming_notes: Progress box height slowly, then add single-leg landings or a jump straight after the landing.
complements: Box jumps once landings are consistent.
video_title: Box Drop Land

name: Dumbbell Curl
summary: The same standing curl as the barbell version, with independent arms that can rotate through a fuller supination path.
why_this_exists: The same standing curl as the barbell version, but independent arms let each side move and rotate on its own path, which some find kinder on the wrists and elbows.
primary_targets: biceps (both heads, roughly even at a neutral shoulder position)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, independent arms.
best_used_when: A full supination path through the rep is wanted, or side-to-side differences need spotting.
less_suitable_when: The heavier loading and fixed path a barbell allows is wanted for a stronger mechanical-tension stimulus.
mirror_effect: Same overall biceps mass and peak direction as a barbell curl.
limitations: Absolute load is capped somewhat below a barbell's, since each arm has to stabilize its own dumbbell independently rather than sharing a single fixed bar.
Same momentum risk as the barbell version — body swing is an easy way to move more weight without adding real biceps tension.
technique_cues: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight at the sides, palms facing forward or in toward the body.
Keep the upper arms still at the sides and curl the weights up by bending the elbows, turning the palms up as they rise if they started facing in.
Finish with the palms facing the shoulders, without letting the elbows drift forward.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Swinging the body to start the rep: momentum moves the weight instead of the biceps.
Elbows drifting forward at the top: the front of the shoulder takes over and the biceps get a rest at the top.
Stopping short of straight arms at the bottom: cuts off the lower part of the range, so the biceps do less work per rep.
programming_notes: Concentration curl variation: seated, with the back of the upper arm braced against the inner thigh, one arm at a time. Bracing the arm removes swing, which makes it a strict single-arm option rather than a different stimulus.
complements: A curl with a different arm position, or a neutral-grip curl.
video_title: How to Do a Dumbbell Biceps Curl | Arm Workout

name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
summary: The most available direct side-delt option, a mechanical-tension and pump stimulus that peaks near the top of the range.
why_this_exists: The most available direct side-delt option, and the main way to add shoulder width when pressing already covers the front delts.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest near the top of the range (roughly shoulder height), easiest at the bottom.
best_used_when: A side-delt-specific mechanical-tension and pump stimulus is wanted that peaks near the top of the range, the position most people mean when picturing lateral raise work.
less_suitable_when: Momentum takes over the rep — once the swing is doing the work, the growth stimulus on the side delt mostly disappears even though the weight is still moving.
mirror_effect: This is usually the actual answer when someone wants "wider shoulders" — tends to show up as width across the shoulders viewed from the front, since the lateral deltoid is what creates that width independent of waist size, more directly than front- or rear-delt work does.
limitations: The load ceiling is low relative to how heavy it can feel — most lifters plateau on usable weight quickly since the leverage at the top of the range is poor.
Trap and upper-shoulder involvement can creep in and take over the movement, especially under fatigue, without an obvious change in how the rep looks.
technique_cues: Stand tall with a slight forward lean and a soft bend in the elbows.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides, leading with the elbows, until the arms are about parallel to the floor.
Keep the shoulders down, away from the ears.
Lower slowly and don't rest the dumbbells against your legs between reps.
common_mistakes: Using a weight that needs a body swing to get moving: momentum carries the easy bottom range and the delts do less.
Shrugging as the arms rise: the traps take over.
Lifting well above shoulder height with heavy dumbbells: adds trap work rather than side-delt work.
complements: A vertical press and rear-delt work.
video_title: How To: Dumbbell Side Lateral Raise

name: Dumbbell Pullover (Chest-Biased)
summary: A straight-arm overhead arc that loads the chest in a shoulder-extension role no press or fly reaches.
why_this_exists: A straight-to-slightly-bent-arm arc that extends overhead loads the chest in a shoulder-extension role that no press or fly reaches, and is commonly associated with rib-cage and serratus involvement as well.
primary_targets: chest (commonly cited as general/costal-biased in this straighter-arm form)
movement_patterns: shoulder extension through an overhead arc
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest overhead, easing as the weight returns over the chest.
best_used_when: A strong stretch-mediated stimulus is wanted at the top of an overhead arc, a range no press or fly reaches, or a chest movement that also brings the serratus into play.
less_suitable_when: The elbows bend enough that the movement shifts toward a lat-dominant pullover instead — see the back module's version, which uses more elbow bend specifically to bias the lats.
mirror_effect: A subtler, different effect from a press or fly — tends to contribute to fullness that wraps toward the lower, outer ribcage and the serratus beneath the arm, rather than adding to the front-facing shelf a press builds.
limitations: Shoulder mobility limits how far overhead the weight can be lowered safely, which caps the very stretch position that gives this exercise its value for some lifters.
Keeping the elbow position consistently straight through the set takes real attention — under fatigue it's easy to drift toward more elbow bend, blurring the line with the lat-biased version.
technique_cues: Lie with the upper back across a bench and the feet flat on the floor, holding one dumbbell with both hands above the chest and the arms nearly straight.
Keeping the arms nearly straight, lower the dumbbell back in an arc over the head until the upper arms are roughly in line with the torso, or as far as the shoulders comfortably allow.
Keep the ribs down and the hips low so the lower back doesn't arch as the weight goes overhead.
Pull the dumbbell back over the chest along the same arc without bending the elbows.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows bend more as the set gets hard: the movement drifts into the lat-biased pullover and the chest does less.
Arching the lower back to get the weight further overhead: the range comes from the spine, not the shoulders, and the lower back takes strain.
Lowering past what the shoulders tolerate: the deepest overhead position is where shoulder discomfort starts.
complements: A pressing movement.
overlaps_with: dumbbell-pullover-lat-biased (back module) — elbow bend is what separates the two.
evidence_notes: No research was found on the pullover's regional pec bias specifically — the "general/costal-biased" framing is an inference from the movement's shoulder-extension arc, not a tested finding. Left as an open claim rather than asserted with confidence.

Separately, the "strong stretch-mediated stimulus" claim about the overhead-arc range itself draws on the general stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature cited on flat-dumbbell-fly in this same file (Schoenfeld & Grgic, 2020; Wolf et al., 2023, 2025) — a general principle about training a muscle at long length, not a pullover-specific finding.
video_title: How to PROPERLY Dumbbell Pullover for a BIG Chest | Fix Your Dumbbell Pullover Form NOW!

name: Dumbbell Pullover (Lat-Biased)
summary: A free-weight lat-focused option with more elbow bend than the chest-biased version, loading an overhead range no pulldown reaches.
why_this_exists: A free-weight lat-focused option with the elbow mostly fixed; the load is hardest overhead and eases as the weight comes back over the chest, the opposite feel from a cable pulldown.
movement_patterns: shoulder extension through an overhead arc
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest overhead, easing as the weight returns over the chest.
best_used_when: A stretch-mediated lat stimulus at the top of an overhead arc is wanted, a range compound pulling doesn't reach.
less_suitable_when: Tension held through the whole range is wanted, which a cable straight-arm pulldown provides and this movement's resistance profile does not.
mirror_effect: Similar visible direction to the straight-arm pulldown — fullness at the lower, outer lat and the flare near the sides of the torso — from working the same stretched position with a different resistance curve.
limitations: Shoulder mobility limits how far overhead the weight can be lowered safely, which caps the very stretch position that gives this exercise its value for some lifters.
Keeping the elbow bend consistent through the set takes real attention — under fatigue it's easy to drift toward straighter arms, blurring the line with the chest-biased version.
technique_cues: Lie with the upper back across a bench and the feet flat on the floor, holding one dumbbell with both hands above the chest and a clear bend in the elbows.
Keeping that elbow bend fixed, lower the dumbbell back in an arc over the head until the upper arms are roughly in line with the torso, or as far as the shoulders comfortably allow.
Keep the ribs down and the lower back from arching as the weight goes overhead.
Pull the dumbbell back over the chest along the same arc by driving the upper arms down, not by bending and straightening the elbows.
common_mistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows during the rep: it turns into a triceps extension and takes work off the lats.
Arching the lower back to get the weight further overhead: the range comes from the spine, not the shoulders, and the lower back takes strain.
Lowering past what the shoulders tolerate: the deepest overhead position is where shoulder discomfort starts.
complements: A vertical or horizontal pull.
overlaps_with: dumbbell-pullover-chest-biased (chest module) — same arc with straighter arms; elbow bend is what separates the two.
evidence_notes: Same general stretch-mediated hypertrophy grounding as straight-arm-pulldown above — see that record's evidence_notes. No study specific to the lat-biased pullover or lat length at the overhead position was located.
video_title: How to do Dumbbell Pullovers for Massive Lats

name: Dumbbell Squat (Sides)
summary: Dumbbells held at the sides remove the anti-flexion bracing demand a goblet squat adds and allow more total load.
why_this_exists: Holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, rather than one held at the chest, removes the anti-flexion core-bracing demand a goblet squat adds and allows more total load, since two dumbbells split between two hands aren't limited by how much a single implement can be held at the chest.
resistance_profile: Free weight, self-limiting load, higher ceiling than a single front-held dumbbell.
best_used_when: A heavier loadable dumbbell squat is wanted than a goblet squat allows, without the front-loaded core-bracing demand.
less_suitable_when: Grip becomes the limiting factor before the legs are meaningfully fatigued, capping how much of the intended stimulus the set can actually deliver.
mirror_effect: Same front-of-thigh mass direction as a goblet squat, with more mass potential since two dumbbells split between the hands allow a higher total load than one held at the chest.
limitations: Grip strength commonly becomes the limiting factor before the legs do, especially at heavier dumbbell weights, capping the achievable stimulus.
Two heavy dumbbells are awkward to get into position at the start of a set, and this setup cost adds up over multiple sets more than a barbell rack does.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet about shoulder width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides with the arms straight and palms facing in.
Sit down by bending the knees and hips together, keeping the chest up and the dumbbells hanging straight down beside the body.
Lower until the thighs are about parallel to the floor or as deep as the back stays flat, without letting the dumbbells touch the floor.
Drive up through the whole foot to standing, keeping the knees tracking in line with the toes.
common_mistakes: Leaning the torso far forward as the dumbbells pull down: the squat turns into a hinge and the lower back takes more of the load.
Knees caving inward on the way up: shifts the load away from the quads and stresses the knee.
Letting the dumbbells swing or drift forward: the balance shifts onto the toes and the squat loses its path.
complements: A hip-hinge movement such as a Romanian deadlift.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial: Dumbbell Squat

name: Face Pull
summary: Combines a moderate rear-delt stimulus with a shoulder-rotation, joint-health component in one movement.
why_this_exists: Combines rear-delt work with a shoulder-rotation component, so one movement covers a growth role and a joint-health role together when time is short.
resistance_profile: Cable or band, constant tension.
best_used_when: A moderate rear-delt stimulus is wanted alongside rotator-cuff and shoulder-control work in a single movement, rather than programming them separately.
less_suitable_when: Load is heavy enough that the rotation is lost — at that point it functions more like a rear-delt row and loses the control-work half of its value.
mirror_effect: Contributes some roundness to the back of the shoulder, but as a secondary effect — its main role is joint health and rotation control, so it shouldn't be relied on as the primary way to build visible rear-delt size.
limitations: The rotation component that gives this movement its joint-health value is the first thing to break down as load increases, so it stops delivering its full intended benefit exactly when it's loaded hardest.
The rear-delt stimulus on its own is moderate at best — this isn't a substitute for dedicated rear-delt work when hypertrophy is the specific goal.
technique_cues: Set a rope at upper-chest to face height and hold it with palms facing down or thumbs pointing back.
Pull the rope toward your face, separating the ends so the hands finish beside the ears.
Finish with the elbows high and the hands rotated back behind the elbows, like a double-biceps pose.
Return slowly with the shoulders kept down.
common_mistakes: Pulling to the chest with low elbows: it becomes a row and the rotation component disappears.
Going heavy enough to lean back for each rep: the rotation, the main reason to do face pulls, is the first thing lost.
Shrugging during the pull: the upper traps replace the rear delts.
complements: Pressing work.
video_title: How To: Face Pull

name: Farmer's Carry
summary: Trains grip under load for time, matching how grip actually limits rows, pulldowns, and hinges — a function-and-endurance tool, not primarily a hypertrophy driver.
why_this_exists: Trains grip under load for time, which matches how grip actually limits rows, pulldowns, and hinges.
resistance_profile: Free-weight, whole-body fatigue cost.
best_used_when: Grip is what actually ends a set before the target muscle on pulling work does — this builds the strength-and-endurance capacity to remove that limiter, more than it's meant as a hypertrophy tool in its own right.
less_suitable_when: The systemic fatigue this movement produces isn't worth the cost late in a hard session, when a lighter, more isolated forearm movement would deliver a similar training effect for less overall cost.
mirror_effect: Contributes to general forearm and grip girth over time from repeated heavy time-under-tension, but it isn't a shaping tool — any visible effect is closer to overall forearm size and vein prominence from the endurance demand than a specific outline change.
limitations: The whole-body fatigue cost is disproportionate to the forearm-specific stimulus it delivers, so it's an inefficient choice when forearm growth alone is the goal.
Grip and traps usually fatigue well before the rest of the body does, so it doesn't double as meaningful leg or cardiovascular conditioning despite the systemic fatigue it produces.
Space and equipment requirements (a clear walking lane, loaded handles or dumbbells) make it harder to fit into a typical gym session than most forearm work.
technique_cues: Pick up a heavy dumbbell or farmer's handle in each hand with a flat back, as in a deadlift, and stand tall.
Hold the weights at the sides with the shoulders down and back and the grip crushing the handles.
Walk with short, controlled steps, keeping the torso upright and the weights from swinging.
At the end of the distance or time, set the weights down with a flat back rather than dropping them.
common_mistakes: Picking the weights up with a rounded back: the lower back takes the load before the carry even starts.
Letting the shoulders round forward and the traps shrug up: the posture collapses and the grip work becomes a shoulder strain.
Taking long, fast strides: the weights swing and the carry turns into a balance fight rather than a grip hold.
complements: Pulling work and static holds.
video_title: How to Perform the Farmer's Carry

name: Feet-Elevated Push-Up
summary: A push-up with the feet raised on a bench, turning the press into an incline press relative to the torso so it leans toward the upper chest with no equipment beyond something to stand the feet on.
why_this_exists: Every upper-chest press in the library needs a barbell, dumbbells, a cable or a machine. Raising the feet changes the pressing angle the same way an incline bench does, so the upper chest can be trained with bodyweight and a bench, step or box.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; raising the feet both steepens the pressing angle and puts more bodyweight on the hands. Hardest at the bottom, with the chest near the floor.
best_used_when: No barbell, dumbbells, cable or machine is available and the upper chest needs a direct pressing stimulus.
A regular push-up has become easy and a harder bodyweight press is wanted.
less_suitable_when: An incline barbell or dumbbell press is available and heavy, finely adjustable loading is the goal — bodyweight caps the load.
Sets run to very high reps without real difficulty, which signals the stimulus has drifted toward endurance.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time, as more fullness in the upper chest near the collarbone — modest at bodyweight for a trained lifter, so it works best where no loaded incline press is available.
limitations: Load is capped by bodyweight and foot height, so progression comes in steps (higher feet, a weight vest, a deficit) rather than small increments.
Very high foot positions turn it into a shoulder-dominant press, closer to a pike push-up than an upper-chest press.
The lower back sags easily as the feet go higher, which shifts strain away from the chest.
technique_cues: Put the feet on a bench or box and the hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder width.
Hold one straight line from head to heels, with the glutes and trunk braced.
Lower until the chest is just above the floor, keeping the elbows at roughly 45 degrees from the body.
Press the floor away until the arms are straight, without letting the hips drop or pike up.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag: the lower back takes the strain and the press loses its incline angle.
Piking the hips up: the press turns more vertical, shifting the work from the upper chest to the shoulders.
Stopping well short of the floor: skips the stretched bottom of the rep, where the chest works hardest.
programming_notes: Progress by raising the feet a little at a time, then by adding a weight vest or a deficit with the hands on blocks; keep the feet low enough that the hips stay in line.
complements: A flat press or chest fly, which covers the mid and lower chest this angle leans away from.
video_title: Feet Elevated Push-ups (Exercise Library)

name: Figure-Four Glute Stretch
summary: Lying on the back with one ankle crossed over the other knee and pulling the legs in to stretch the outer hip and glute.
why_this_exists: Deep lunges and quick hip turns need comfortable range at the back and outside of the hip. The lying figure-four is an easy, supported way to stretch it; the pigeon stretch is a deeper option.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; pulling the legs closer deepens the stretch.
best_used_when: The hips or glutes feel tight after training or on rest days.
less_suitable_when: The knee of the crossed leg hurts; reduce the depth or try a seated version.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds hip range.
limitations: If the crossed foot is relaxed, the knee can twist, so the foot should stay flexed.
The pigeon version is deeper but puts more load on the front knee.
technique_cues: Lie on the back with both knees bent and feet on the floor.
Cross one ankle over the opposite knee, keeping that foot flexed.
Reach through and hold the back of the lower thigh, then draw the legs toward the chest.
Keep the head and lower back on the floor and breathe slowly.
common_mistakes: Letting the crossed foot go floppy: the knee takes strain.
Lifting the head and shoulders to pull harder.
Pulling into pain instead of a clear stretch.
programming_notes: Progress to the pigeon stretch only if the knees are comfortable.
complements: The 90/90 hip switches for moving hip rotation.
video_title: How To Do Figure 4 Stretch

name: Flat Barbell Bench Press
summary: The reference horizontal chest press and the primary mechanical- tension, strength-building mid-chest stimulus.
why_this_exists: The reference horizontal chest press, loadable with small increments and the most common way to build and track chest pressing strength.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest off the chest, easiest at lockout.
best_used_when: The primary mechanical-tension and strength-building stimulus for the mid chest is the goal — this is the movement most routines build their pressing progression around, and the one where absolute load climbs fastest over time.
less_suitable_when: The routine already has a heavy pressing movement covering mechanical tension, and what's actually missing is a pump-oriented finisher or a stretch-biased stimulus this movement does not provide.
mirror_effect: Over time, this tends to show up as overall chest mass and depth from the side — the chest projects further off the ribcage and the mid-chest, the bulk most people picture when they think "chest," fills in first. It's not a shaping tool; it doesn't carve a line between the pecs or fill in any one spot specifically, it just adds size to the region as a whole.
limitations: A spotter or safety bars are genuinely needed to train close to failure safely, which limits how hard this can be pushed when training alone.
Shoulder or elbow discomfort at a full range is common for some lifters, and grip width or bar path often has to be individually adjusted to manage it.
technique_cues: Lie with your eyes under the bar, feet planted, and shoulder blades squeezed together and down. Keep that position for the whole set.
Grip slightly wider than shoulder width so the forearms are vertical when the bar touches your chest.
Lower under control to the lower chest with the elbows tucked to roughly 45 degrees from the torso, not flared straight out.
Press up and slightly back so the bar finishes over the shoulders.
Drive the feet into the floor and keep the glutes on the bench.
common_mistakes: Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress, a common source of the shoulder discomfort this lift is known for.
Bouncing the bar off the chest: the rebound skips the hardest part of the lift and risks a hard impact on the sternum.
Shoulder blades coming apart during the set: the shoulders roll forward and take load off the chest.
Training close to failure alone without safety bars set just below chest height: a missed rep can pin the bar on the chest or throat.
complements: A fly variation or an incline press selected for a distinct role.
evidence_notes: Weaker claim to make than it sounds, and supported more circumstantially than the upper-chest claim: the sternocostal (mid/lower-most) head is simply the largest portion of the pectoralis major and the one every horizontal press loads by default, rather than a bias any specific technique creates. EMG support: Rodríguez-Ridao et al. (2020, PMC7579505) found the sternocostal head was more active at 0° (flat) than at incline angles. Hypertrophy support: in Chaves et al. (2020, PMC7449336), mid-chest growth was statistically similar across the flat, incline, and combined groups — consistent with flat pressing doing at least as well here as any other angle, though it doesn't isolate a flat- specific advantage the way the incline data isolates one for the upper chest.
video_title: How to PROPERLY Bench Press for Growth (5 Easy Steps)

name: Flat Dumbbell Fly
summary: A free-weight, mid-chest-biased adduction movement with a strong bottom-range stretch stimulus, performed flat.
why_this_exists: A free-weight chest adduction option performed flat, the opposite feel from a cable fly.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest at the bottom stretch, easing off as the arms come together at the top — the opposite curve from a cable fly.
best_used_when: A strong stretch-mediated growth stimulus for the mid chest is the goal — the resistance is hardest exactly where the muscle is most lengthened, which a press does not replicate.
less_suitable_when: Tension held through the top of the range is wanted; a cable fly holds that tension where this movement's resistance profile gives it up as the arms come together.
mirror_effect: Where a press adds bulk, a fly tends to show up as shape and separation — a visible line down the sternum where the two sides meet, and a rounder sweep out to the sides near the armpit, since the stretch position it's chosen for pulls right along that outer edge.
limitations: The shoulder joint is placed in a vulnerable, widely stretched position at the bottom of the range, and going too heavy or too deep raises real injury risk.
Load progression is inherently limited — the stretched bottom position caps how much weight can be handled safely well below what a press allows.
technique_cues: Lie flat on a bench holding the dumbbells above the chest, palms facing each other, with a slight, fixed bend in the elbows.
Keep the shoulder blades pulled back and down against the bench, with the feet planted.
Open the arms out to the sides in a wide arc until the upper arms are about level with the body, or until you feel a comfortable stretch across the chest.
Bring the dumbbells back up along the same arc without changing the elbow bend, stopping just before they touch.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows more on the way up: the fly turns into a press and the triceps take over from the chest.
Lowering past what the shoulders tolerate, especially with heavy dumbbells: the shoulder is loaded at its most stretched and vulnerable point.
Clanking the dumbbells together at the top: momentum carries the top of the rep, where the load is already lightest.
complements: A pressing movement.
evidence_notes: Same mid-chest evidence as flat-barbell-bench-press applies to the mid-bias claim here — see that record's evidence_notes. No study specific to the fly (adduction) pattern rather than a press was located, so this is an extrapolation from press data to a fly, not a direct finding.

Separately, the "strong stretch-mediated growth stimulus" claim draws on the broader stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) found full/longer-ROM training tends to match or beat partial-ROM training that avoids the stretch, and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning, meta-analysis) found full and partial ROM produced broadly similar hypertrophy, with a possible but inconclusive advantage for partials at long muscle lengths. A later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found lengthened partials produced hypertrophy similar to, not clearly greater than, full ROM — so "strong" should be read as a well-supported direction, not a settled magnitude. This is a general principle, not a fly-specific finding.
video_title: How To: Dumbbell Flys On A Flat Bench

name: Flat Dumbbell Press
summary: A general horizontal chest press with independently moving arms, for a mid-chest mechanical-tension stimulus with extra stretch.
why_this_exists: A general horizontal chest press with independently moving arms.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; independent arms allow a deeper bottom-range stretch than a fixed bar, at the cost of a lower load ceiling.
best_used_when: A mechanical-tension stimulus for the mid chest is wanted with a deeper stretch at the bottom than a barbell allows, since each arm can drop past where a fixed bar would stop.
less_suitable_when: The stability demand of controlling two independent dumbbells caps how much weight can be used, limiting the mechanical-tension ceiling for a stronger lifter.
mirror_effect: Same mid-chest mass and depth direction as a barbell bench press, with a bit more of a stretch at the bottom from the independent arms.
limitations: Controlling two independent dumbbells caps the achievable load below what a barbell allows, and getting a heavy pair into the starting position takes real technique and, at high weights, help from a spotter.
The higher stability demand can become the limiting factor before the chest itself is meaningfully fatigued, especially for less experienced lifters.
technique_cues: Sit on the end of a flat bench with the dumbbells on the thighs, then lie back, bringing them to the sides of the chest.
Keep the shoulder blades pulled back and down, the feet planted and the glutes on the bench.
Press the dumbbells up over the chest until the arms are nearly straight, letting them move slightly toward each other.
Lower under control until the dumbbells are beside the chest, as deep as the shoulders comfortably allow.
common_mistakes: Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress at the bottom of the press.
Dropping the dumbbells out to the sides at the end of a set: a sudden, unloaded stretch on the shoulders; bring them back to the thighs or chest instead.
Letting the dumbbells drift apart or wobble at the bottom: control is lost exactly where the stretch is deepest.
complements: A stable press or fly variation selected for a distinct role.
evidence_notes: Same mid-chest evidence as flat-barbell-bench-press — see that record's evidence_notes.
video_title: Flat Bench Dumbbell Press | Proper Form & Chest Exercise Demo

name: Foam Rolling (Calves, Quads, Upper Back)
summary: Slowly rolling the calves, the front of the thighs and the upper back over a foam roller, pausing on tight spots.
why_this_exists: Badminton loads the calves, quads and upper back heavily. Rolling these areas is a common way to ease tightness around training.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight pressure on the roller; shifting weight onto or off the roller changes the pressure.
best_used_when: Muscles feel tight or heavy after play, or as a short start to a warm-up.
less_suitable_when: An area is bruised, swollen or recently strained; do not roll directly over it.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it is used to ease muscle tightness.
limitations: Any change in range of motion is thought to be short-lived, so it does not replace stretching or strength work.
The lower back and the joints themselves should not be rolled directly.
technique_cues: Calves: sit with the roller under one calf, hands behind you, and roll from just above the ankle to just below the knee.
Quads: lie face down with the roller under the front of the thighs and roll between the hip and just above the knee.
Upper back: lie with the roller across the upper back, hands supporting the head, hips down, and roll between the bottom of the shoulder blades and the top of the shoulders.
Roll slowly and pause for a few breaths on tight spots.
common_mistakes: Rolling fast back and forth: slow rolls and pauses work better.
Rolling over the knee, the ankle or the lower back.
Pressing through sharp or tingling pain.
programming_notes: Count the time per area; do each leg separately for calves and quads.
complements: Held stretches for the same areas afterwards.
video_title: Basic Full Body Foam Rolling Routine

name: Four-Corner Shadow Footwork
summary: Moving from the base to each corner of the badminton court and back without a shuttle, rehearsing real footwork patterns.
why_this_exists: Shadow footwork rehearses the exact steps of badminton: split-step, lunge to the net, and recovery to the rear court. It trains movement speed and pattern without needing a partner or shuttle.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; speed, distance covered and how many corners each set includes set the challenge.
best_used_when: Badminton-specific footwork speed and pattern are the goal, on or off court.
less_suitable_when: The basic footwork patterns are not yet learned; slow, walked-through repetitions come first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds badminton footwork speed and pattern.
limitations: Done fast and long it turns into conditioning, which is useful but no longer trains crisp footwork.
It needs a court or a similar marked-out space to be specific.
technique_cues: Start in the middle of the court in a ready stance and split-step as if the shuttle is being hit.
Move to one corner using the footwork you would use in a rally, finishing with a lunge or a jumping reach.
Push back to the base position quickly and split-step again.
Work through the corners in a set or random order, keeping every step low and balanced.
common_mistakes: Skipping the split-step: the first step to each corner gets slower, which is the main point of the drill.
Lunging with the front knee caving inward: loads the knee badly at the moment of highest force.
Drifting back slowly to the base: the recovery step is half of real court movement.
programming_notes: For footwork quality use short sets with full rest; for conditioning see the shadow-badminton intervals record.
complements: Lateral bounds or split-squat jumps for power.
video_title: 4 Corner Footwork - A Step-By-Step Badminton Tutorial!

name: Front Squat
summary: The front-loaded bar position keeps the torso more upright, shifting more mechanical-tension demand onto the quads than a back squat.
why_this_exists: The front-loaded bar position keeps the torso more upright than a back squat, which shifts more of the demand onto the quads and changes the technical and mobility requirements.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, front-rack position.
best_used_when: A heavy, mechanical-tension squat stimulus is wanted with more of the load specifically directed at the quads than a back squat provides.
less_suitable_when: Wrist or shoulder mobility can't support the rack position, capping how much load can actually be used before form breaks down.
mirror_effect: Similar visible direction to a back squat — front-of-thigh and glute mass — but the more upright torso shifts the balance a little more toward quad-specific development relative to the glutes.
limitations: The front-rack position demands real wrist, shoulder, and thoracic mobility, and lifters who lack it often can't hold the position long enough to complete a heavy set.
Load capacity is meaningfully lower than a back squat's, since the front-rack position and upright torso become the limiting factor before the legs' full strength does.
technique_cues: Set the bar across the front of the shoulders, with the fingertips under the bar and the elbows high, or with the arms crossed.
Stand with the feet about shoulder width apart, brace the trunk and keep the elbows up.
Squat down between the heels with the torso upright, as deep as the back stays flat and the elbows stay high.
Drive up through the whole foot to standing, leading with the elbows.
common_mistakes: Elbows dropping as the set gets hard: the torso tips forward and the bar can roll off the shoulders.
Knees caving inward on the way up: shifts the load away from the quads and stresses the knee.
Gripping the bar tightly with the whole hand and forcing the wrists: strains the wrists; let the bar rest on the shoulders with a fingertip grip.
complements: A hinge pattern or a single-joint knee-extension movement.
video_creator: Fit Father Project - Fitness For Busy Fathers
video_title: How To Properly Do A Barbell Front Squat - Full Video Tutorial & Exercise Guide

name: Glute Bridge
summary: A floor-based hip extension that loads the glutes in their shortened position with no equipment, the low-setup counterpart to the hip thrust.
why_this_exists: The hip thrust's shortened-position glute stimulus needs a bench and a padded bar. The bridge trains the same hip extension from the floor with bodyweight, so the glutes can be worked directly with no equipment, almost no setup, and little fatigue.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, hardest at the top with the hips fully extended. A pause at the top, a single-leg version, a dumbbell or plate on the hips, or a barbell across the hips adds difficulty without changing the movement.
best_used_when: No bench, barbell or machine is available and the glutes need direct work.
A low-fatigue glute finisher or warm-up is wanted alongside heavier squats and hinges.
less_suitable_when: A heavy, progressively loaded glute stimulus is the goal and a hip-thrust setup is available — bodyweight stops being challenging quickly.
