mirror_effect: Same shoulder-width visible direction as a dumbbell lateral raise, since it's the same lateral deltoid being trained.
limitations: Machine design varies significantly, and a poor pivot-point match for a given torso size can create an uncomfortable pinch or a line of resistance that never really loads the side delt well.
Availability is a real constraint — this specific machine is less universal in gyms than a cable station or a simple pair of dumbbells.
technique_cues: Adjust the seat so your shoulders line up with the machine's pivot points.
Press against the pads with the outsides of your arms or elbows, not your hands.
Raise the arms out to about shoulder height, then lower slowly.
Keep the shoulders down and your chest against the pad, if there is one.
common_mistakes: Seat height wrong for your torso: the shoulder pinches and the delt never gets a clean line of pull.
Shrugging into the pads: the traps take over.
Letting the stack touch down between reps: tension drops at the bottom.
complements: A vertical press.
video_title: Machine Lateral Raise | Proper Form Tutorial for Shoulder Growth

name: Machine Reverse Fly
summary: A fixed-path rear-delt fly that removes balance demand, well suited to a rear-delt pump pushed to true failure.
why_this_exists: A fixed-path rear-delt fly that removes the balance demand of a dumbbell version, often with a cam that adjusts the resistance through the range.
resistance_profile: Fixed-path, often cam-adjusted through the range.
best_used_when: A rear-delt pump stimulus is wanted that's safe to push to true failure or a drop set, since there's no momentum available to take over the rep.
less_suitable_when: The machine's pivot point or pad position doesn't suit the individual, which can blunt the tension the rear delts actually feel.
mirror_effect: Same rear-delt visible direction as a dumbbell reverse fly — roundness on the back of the shoulder, visible from behind or the side.
limitations: Machine pivot-point and pad fit vary a lot between models, and a poor match can blunt the rear-delt tension regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
Availability is a real constraint — this specific machine isn't as universal in gyms as a cable station or dumbbells.
technique_cues: Sit facing the pad with the chest against it and set the seat so the handles are at shoulder height.
Hold the handles with the arms nearly straight in front of the body and a slight, fixed bend in the elbows.
Sweep the arms out and back in a wide arc, leading with the backs of the hands, until the upper arms are level with the torso.
Return under control to the front before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Squeezing the shoulder blades hard together to finish each rep: the mid-back takes over the end of the movement from the rear delts.
Bending the elbows more as the set gets hard: turns it into a row, and the back muscles take over.
Lifting the chest off the pad to swing the handles back: momentum moves the weight instead of the rear delts.
complements: A vertical press and horizontal pulling.
video_title: How To Properly Target Rear Delts On Reverse Fly Machine

name: Machine Triceps Extension
summary: A fixed-path elbow extension removing cable-height and attachment setup, well suited to a triceps pump pushed to true failure.
why_this_exists: A fixed-path elbow extension that removes the cable-height and attachment setup of a pushdown, often with a cam that adjusts resistance through the range.
primary_targets: triceps (all three heads — no evidence of a lateral-head-specific bias; see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Fixed-path, often cam-adjusted through the range.
best_used_when: A triceps pump stimulus is wanted pushed safely to true failure without bracing against a cable's pull to help stabilize the movement.
less_suitable_when: The machine's seat or handle position doesn't suit the individual, which can blunt the tension felt regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
mirror_effect: Same general triceps mass and horseshoe-shape direction as a cable pushdown.
limitations: Seat and handle position vary between machines, and a poor fit can blunt the tension felt regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
Availability is a real constraint — this specific machine isn't as universal in gyms as a cable station.
technique_cues: Set the seat so the upper arms rest flat on the pad with the elbows lined up with the machine's pivot.
Grip the handles and sit tall with the back against the backrest if there is one.
Straighten the elbows to push the handles down until the arms are fully straight.
Return under control until the elbows are bent to about 90 degrees or a little more.
common_mistakes: Elbows not lined up with the pivot: the arc fights the elbow, causing discomfort and blunting the triceps tension.
Lifting the upper arms off the pad to push: the shoulders help move the weight and the triceps do less.
Letting the stack drop back fast: the return is uncontrolled, losing half of each rep's triceps work.
complements: An overhead extension, which loads a different position.
evidence_notes: Same correction as close-grip-bench-press: no evidence found for a lateral-head-specific bias here — see that record's evidence_notes for the full reasoning.
video_title: How To Do A SEATED MACHINE TRICEPS EXTENSION | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Mountain Climber
summary: Driving the knees toward the chest one at a time from a high plank, in fast timed rounds.
why_this_exists: It builds endurance and quick leg turnover while the trunk holds a plank, with no equipment.
movement_patterns: alternating knee drives from a plank
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; pace sets the intensity.
best_used_when: Conditioning with no equipment and very little space is wanted.
less_suitable_when: Wrists or shoulders are sore; the plank position keeps them loaded throughout.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds endurance and trunk control under fatigue.
limitations: The wrists and shoulders carry bodyweight the whole time.
The hips tend to bounce up and down as fatigue sets in.
technique_cues: Set up in a high plank with the hands under the shoulders and the body in a straight line.
Drive one knee toward the chest, then switch legs quickly.
Keep the hips level and the shoulders over the hands.
Keep a fast, steady rhythm for the whole interval.
common_mistakes: Hips piking up high: shortens the lever and the trunk does less work.
Hips sagging: the lower back takes strain.
Feet only shuffling a few centimetres: the knee drive is the main work.
programming_notes: Slow the tempo to make it more of a trunk exercise, or speed it up for conditioning.
complements: Hip-flexor and hip mobility work afterwards.
video_title: How to do Mountain Climbers Exercise the RIGHT way.

name: Neck Extension
summary: Loads the back of the neck, the region most responsible for visible neck thickness.
why_this_exists: Loads the back of the neck, which is what most neck-size goals are actually about, and which sitting posture rarely trains.
resistance_profile: Harness, plate, or machine.
best_used_when: A genuine mechanical-tension growth stimulus is wanted for the area most responsible for visible neck thickness, once control has already been built through isometric work.
less_suitable_when: Load or range can't yet be controlled — a lighter load with a slower tempo is the better next step, not a heavier one.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as width and thickness across the back and sides of the neck, viewed from behind or the side — this is the region most responsible for the "thick neck" look people are usually picturing when they say a neck looks bigger.
limitations: The neck is a small, structurally sensitive area — load has to increase far more conservatively here than in almost any other muscle group, or symptoms can appear well before a meaningful growth stimulus is reached.
Equipment for loading neck extension directly (a harness or dedicated machine) is uncommon in most gyms, which limits how heavily this can realistically be progressed for many people.
technique_cues: Seated with a harness on the head (or in the machine), lean the torso forward slightly with the hands on the thighs and the back flat.
Start with a very light plate or setting and let the head lower forward to a comfortable position, not as far as it will go.
Lift the head back up to a neutral position by extending the neck, without arching the upper back.
Lower slowly, and increase the load only in small steps, ending the set if any pain or symptoms appear.
common_mistakes: Letting the head drop quickly at the bottom: the neck takes the load at the end of its range without control.
Throwing the head back past neutral at the top: the neck is pushed into extension under load further than the movement needs.
Adding weight quickly: the neck tolerates fast load increases poorly, and symptoms can appear before any real benefit.
complements: Neck flexion work, so the region is not trained in one direction only.
evidence_notes: This is a lower-stakes claim than the region-bias claims elsewhere in this dataset — it's a claim about visible anatomy, not about differential muscle recruitment or growth. The neck extensors and upper trapezius make up the visible bulk of the back and sides of the neck, which is standard anatomical description rather than a contested hypertrophy finding, so it doesn't carry the same evidence-quality caveats as the muscle-head-bias claims in the arms, chest, and calves modules.
video_title: How To: Seated Head Harness Neck Extension

name: Neck Flexion
summary: Loads the front of the neck, which shrugs, rows, and extension work do not cover.
why_this_exists: Loads the front of the neck, which shrugs, rows, and extension work do not cover.
resistance_profile: Plate or band.
best_used_when: Neck extension is already trained and a balanced growth stimulus on both sides of the neck is wanted rather than one direction only.
less_suitable_when: Range or load can't be controlled, or symptoms appear at any point in the range — this is a stop signal, not something to push through for more stimulus.
mirror_effect: Less visually prominent than extension work, since the front-of-neck muscles contribute less to overall neck bulk — the visible effect is more about rounding out the front profile and avoiding a lopsided, extension-only look than adding comparable size.
limitations: Usable load is low relative to the effort involved, since the neck flexors are comparatively weak and the safe range of motion is small.
Plate or band positioning at the forehead is awkward to set up consistently, which makes clean progressive overload harder to track than with most other exercises.
technique_cues: Lie face up on a bench with the head and upper neck off the end, holding a folded towel and a light plate on the forehead with both hands (or a band around the forehead anchored behind you).
Let the head lower back slowly to a comfortable, roughly level position, not as far as it will go.
Tuck the chin and curl the head up toward the chest, then lower it back under control.
Start very light and increase the load in small steps, ending the set if any pain or symptoms appear.
common_mistakes: Letting the head drop quickly into the bottom: the neck takes the load at the end of its range without control.
Lifting the shoulders off the bench to raise the head: the abs and torso do the curling instead of the neck flexors.
Jumping up in plate size too quickly: the neck tolerates fast load increases poorly, and symptoms can appear before any real benefit.
complements: Neck extension work.
video_title: How To: Weight Plate Neck Curl

name: Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown
summary: A parallel or angled pulldown grip that avoids the shoulder's end-range external rotation, often the kindest grip on the joints.
why_this_exists: A parallel or angled grip that avoids the shoulder's end-range external rotation a wide pronated grip asks for, which many find is the kindest grip on the shoulders and elbows.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, small load increments.
best_used_when: Shoulder or elbow discomfort is what actually ends a set before the lats are meaningfully fatigued — the neutral grip removes that limiter and lets more effort go toward a lat-width stimulus.
less_suitable_when: Shoulder and elbow comfort aren't limiting factors, in which case a pronated or supinated grip may deliver a more specific bias without a meaningful downside.
mirror_effect: Same width-building visible direction as any lat pulldown — the grip is a joint-comfort choice, not a change in which muscle or visible outcome is being trained.
limitations: Not every cable station has a neutral-grip attachment available, which limits how consistently this specific grip can be programmed.
The joint-friendlier angle comes at some cost to range of motion on certain machines, depending on where the handle attachment sits relative to the body.
technique_cues: Attach a neutral-grip handle, sit with the thighs under the pads, and hold the handles with the palms facing each other.
Lean back slightly with the chest up and the arms straight.
Pull the handle to the upper chest by driving the elbows down and back toward the ribs.
Let the handle rise under control until the arms are fully straight before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Leaning far back and rocking to pull the weight down: the trunk and momentum do the work instead of the lats.
Stopping short of straight arms at the top: cuts off the stretched part of the pull, so each rep does less work.
Shrugging the shoulders up as the handle rises: the shoulders lose position and the lats stop working at the top.
complements: A rowing pattern.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial - Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
summary: Produces high hamstring tension during the lowering phase with no machine, commonly cited for growth and injury-resilience benefits.
why_this_exists: Produces high hamstring tension during the lowering phase with no machine, and scales through partner support, bands, or range.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, eccentric-emphasis; scales through partner support, bands, or range.
best_used_when: One of the most demanding eccentric-tension stimuli available for the hamstrings is wanted, commonly cited for both growth and injury-resilience benefits.
less_suitable_when: The descent can't yet be controlled at all, or a user is very sore from prior hamstring work — start with a short range and build up rather than loading the full eccentric immediately.
mirror_effect: Consistent training here contributes to overall hamstring density and fullness rather than a specific, localized shape change — its better-documented value is functional (eccentric strength, injury resilience), so don't expect a visibly distinct effect beyond what general hamstring size training already gives.
limitations: The technical and strength floor is high — many lifters cannot control any meaningful range at all without a partner or anchor, making it a poor first hamstring exercise.
Soreness after a hard set is often severe and can linger for days, which makes the movement difficult to program frequently or stack with other hamstring-heavy work.
There's no simple way to add external load once bodyweight control is mastered — progression relies on range, tempo, or band assistance/resistance rather than a barbell-style load increase.
technique_cues: Kneel on a pad with the ankles held down by a partner or a secure anchor, and the body upright from knees to head.
Keep the hips straight so the body stays in one line from knees to shoulders.
Lower the body forward as slowly as possible, resisting with the hamstrings, and catch yourself with the hands when control runs out.
Push lightly off the floor with the hands to return to the start, using the hamstrings as much as you can.
common_mistakes: Bending at the hips as you lower: the body folds and the hamstrings lose their lever, making it easier without training them.
Dropping quickly once the lean gets hard: the slow lowering is the whole point, so the work is lost.
Doing many hard sets too soon: the soreness the record warns about can last days, so build up gradually.
complements: A hinge pattern.
evidence_notes: Worth a correction to the popular framing, not just a citation: the same 2024 trial cited on seated-leg-curl (PMC11419281) directly compared the Nordic curl against lengthened-state training in a hip-flexed position (essentially a loaded seated leg curl) and found the hip-flexed version produced substantially more hamstrings growth (+18% vs. +11% total, +19% vs. +5% biceps femoris long head). The Nordic curl was still an effective hypertrophy stimulus in absolute terms — this isn't a claim that it doesn't work — but "commonly cited for growth" undersells that a simpler, less technically demanding machine exercise outperformed it in this trial. The Nordic curl's real, distinct value shown by this and other research is training the eccentric strength and fascicle adaptations tied to injury resilience, which a leg curl doesn't replicate — not necessarily the largest hypertrophy stimulus available.
video_title: How to Do a Nordic Hamstring Curl

name: Overhead Press
summary: The main loadable vertical press, the primary mechanical-tension stimulus for the front delts and triceps together.
why_this_exists: The main loadable vertical press, useful when a user wants overhead pressing strength rather than only shoulder size.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; barbell allows the heaviest fixed-path load, dumbbells allow independent arms.
best_used_when: The primary mechanical-tension and strength-building stimulus for the front delts is the goal, with the triceps and upper chest sharing a meaningful part of the load.
less_suitable_when: The routine already has a heavy pressing movement covering mechanical tension, and what's missing is a pump-oriented finisher or dedicated side- and rear-delt work.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as roundness and mass on the front of the shoulder, contributing to overall shoulder size from the front — though front delts already get heavy indirect work from chest pressing, so this often isn't the missing piece if the front of the shoulder already looks developed.
limitations: Shoulder mobility limits are common and can cap how heavy or how deep this can safely be loaded, well before the delts and triceps reach their true strength ceiling.
The trunk-bracing and stability demand is high, so a weak core or poor bracing technique can become the limiting factor before the shoulders are.
Load progression is comparatively slow next to other big lifts, since the muscles moving the bar are smaller than a squat or deadlift's.
technique_cues: Start with the bar resting on the front of the shoulders, hands just outside shoulder width and forearms vertical (or dumbbells at shoulder height, palms forward), with the feet about hip width apart.
Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes so the lower back doesn't arch as you press.
Press straight up, moving the head back slightly to let the bar pass the face, then bring the head through once the bar clears it.
Finish with the arms locked overhead and the weight over the middle of the foot, then lower under control to the shoulders.
common_mistakes: Leaning back and arching the lower back to finish the press: shifts the load onto the lower back and turns it into a steep incline press.
Pressing the bar forward around the face instead of straight up: the weight ends up in front of the body, making it heavier on the shoulders and harder to lock out.
Dipping the knees and driving with the legs without meaning to: it becomes a push press, and the shoulders do less of the work.
programming_notes: Arnold press variation (dumbbells): start with the palms facing you at shoulder height and rotate them to face forward as you press. The rotation adds little beyond a standard dumbbell press, so treat it as a preference, not a separate stimulus.

Landmine press variation: pressing the end of an anchored barbell up and forward on one arm gives an angled path that many lifters tolerate when pressing straight overhead is uncomfortable. It needs a landmine and a barbell, and the arc makes it easier at the top.
complements: Side- and rear-delt work, which overhead pressing does not replace.
video_title: How To: Standing Straight-Bar Military / Overhead Press

name: Overhead Triceps Extension
summary: Trains elbow extension with the shoulder flexed, commonly cited as the strongest stretch-mediated stimulus for the triceps long head.
why_this_exists: Trains elbow extension with the shoulder flexed, a position that pressing movements do not load.
primary_targets: triceps (long-head-biased, strongly supported by hypertrophy research)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; barbell or EZ-bar allows the heaviest load on a fixed path, dumbbells allow independent arms. A band anchored under the back foot in a split stance gets heavier as the arms straighten overhead, so it loads the top of the extension more than the stretched bottom.
best_used_when: Triceps work has all been pressing and pushdowns, and what's missing is the long head's strongest stretch-mediated growth stimulus.
less_suitable_when: The overhead position is uncomfortable, capping how much of that stretch can actually be loaded.
mirror_effect: Tends to contribute specifically to the long head, which runs down the back and inner side of the upper arm — this is the part most responsible for the "horseshoe" shape and overall arm length when the arm hangs at the side, viewed from behind.
limitations: The overhead shoulder position demands real mobility, and lifters without it either can't reach the position safely or lose meaningful range trying.
Elbow stress at the bottom of the stretch is real, and load has to be added conservatively compared to a pushdown or a compound press.
technique_cues: Seated or standing, hold an EZ-bar, or one dumbbell in both hands, overhead with straight arms.
Keep the upper arms close to your head and pointing up; only the elbows bend.
Lower the weight behind your head until the triceps are fully stretched, as far as your elbows and shoulders tolerate.
Extend back to straight arms without letting the upper arms drift forward.
common_mistakes: Elbows flaring wide: reduces triceps tension and loads the elbow.
Arching the lower back to get the weight overhead: brace the core, or sit with back support.
Adding load faster than the elbows tolerate: elbow pain usually starts at the bottom of the stretch.
programming_notes: Band version: stand in a split stance with the band under the back foot, hold the ends behind the head and extend overhead. Shorten the band or use a stronger band to add resistance.
complements: A pressing movement or a pushdown.
evidence_notes: Strong evidence, and stronger than the biceps head-bias claims above: Maeo et al. (2023, European Journal of Sport Science) used MRI to measure triceps long-head growth after 12 weeks of overhead extension training vs. a non-overhead (arm-at-side) extension, at matched volume. The overhead group gained roughly 28.5% long-head cross- sectional area at the site closest to the shoulder vs. roughly 19.6% for the non-overhead group, with the gap most pronounced proximally, consistent with the long head being stretched at the shoulder in the overhead position. This is direct MRI-measured hypertrophy data, not just EMG, which is why this claim is stated more confidently than the biceps incline/preacher claims. It only establishes the long head's bias, not any lateral- or medial-head effect — see the notes on close-grip-bench-press, dip-triceps-biased, cable-pushdown, machine-triceps-extension, and triceps-kickback below for why those heads' bias claims are treated differently.

This record's "strongest stretch-mediated growth stimulus" framing is also consistent with the broader stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature — see incline-dumbbell-curl's evidence_notes above for the general citations (Schoenfeld & Grgic, 2020; Wolf et al., 2023, 2025). The Maeo et al. (2023) finding above is the stronger, exercise-specific evidence; this is additional general-principle grounding, not a separate direct finding.
video_title: Overhead Dumbbell Tricep Extension | Proper Form & Triceps Exercise Demo

name: Pallof Press
summary: Loads anti-rotation directly, a control-and-durability tool rather than a primary hypertrophy driver.
why_this_exists: Loads anti-rotation directly, a role that crunches and planks do not cover.
resistance_profile: Band or cable, isometric hold.
best_used_when: Trunk control and stability that transfers to standing, carrying, and single-side loading are the goal — a control-and-durability role more than a primary hypertrophy driver.
less_suitable_when: The hips rotate along with the load, which defeats the anti-rotation demand that's the entire point of the movement.
mirror_effect: A minor, tightening effect on the waist rather than an added-size one — this is control work, and the light loading it uses keeps it unlikely to visibly thicken the obliques the way heavier rotational work can.
limitations: The stimulus is inherently light — this is a control-and-durability tool, not a movement that drives meaningful oblique hypertrophy on its own.
Band or cable resistance is hard to load heavily in a way that keeps adding real challenge over time, unlike a barbell-based progression.
technique_cues: Set a cable or band at chest height and stand side-on, feet about shoulder width, far enough away that there's tension at the start.
Hold the handle at your sternum with both hands, ribs down and glutes tight.
Press the handle straight out from your chest and hold for a few seconds without letting the torso turn toward the anchor.
Bring it back to the chest under control, then finish all reps before switching sides.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso or hips twist toward the anchor: the anti-rotation demand, the whole point of the exercise, disappears.
Standing so close there's little tension: the press feels easy and does little.
Pressing up or out to the side instead of straight forward from the sternum: shortens the lever, so the trunk has less rotation to resist.
programming_notes: Progress by standing farther from the anchor or holding each press longer, rather than only adding stack weight.
complements: Trunk flexion and anti-extension work.
video_title: Cable Pallof Press | Proper Form Tutorial for Core Stability

name: Pike Push-Up
summary: A bodyweight vertical press done from an inverted-V position, the no-equipment way to load the front delts through overhead-style pressing.
why_this_exists: Every loaded vertical press needs a barbell, dumbbells, a cable or a machine. Piking the hips up turns a push-up into a steep, overhead-direction press, so the front delts can be trained directly with no equipment, and progressed by raising the feet toward a handstand push-up.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; the higher the hips and the more the feet are elevated, the larger the share of bodyweight on the hands and the more vertical the press. Hardest at the bottom, with the head near the floor.
best_used_when: No barbell, dumbbells or machine is available and the front delts need a direct pressing stimulus.
A low-fatigue vertical press is wanted in a home or travel session, with a clear progression path (feet elevated, then toward a handstand push-up).
less_suitable_when: A barbell or dumbbells are available and heavy, finely adjustable overhead loading is the goal — bodyweight leverage changes in steps, not small increments.
Wrist extension under load is uncomfortable, since the hands carry the press in a fully extended wrist position.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time, as more roundness on the front of the shoulder — modest at bodyweight for a trained lifter, and front delts already get indirect work from chest pressing, so it is most useful where no loaded press is available.
limitations: Load is capped by bodyweight and body angle, so progression comes in discrete steps (higher hips, elevated feet, deficit) rather than small load increments.
It easily drifts toward an ordinary push-up as the hips drop, which moves the work to the chest without it being obvious.
The hands bear the press with the wrists fully extended, which limits some lifters before the shoulders are challenged.
technique_cues: From a push-up position, walk the feet in and lift the hips until the body forms an inverted V, arms roughly in line with the torso.
Place the hands slightly wider than shoulder width with the fingers spread, and keep the hips high for the whole set.
Lower the top of the head toward a point just in front of the hands, so head and hands form a triangle.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45 degrees from the body rather than flared straight out to the sides.
Press the floor away until the arms are straight, keeping the hips where they started.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drop toward a plank: the press turns horizontal, so the chest takes over and the front delts lose the load.
Lowering the head straight down between the hands: the elbows flare and the shoulders finish in a cramped position instead of a strong pressing line.
Stopping well short of the floor: skips the bottom of the rep, where the press is hardest and the front delts work most.
programming_notes: Progress in this order: feet closer to the hands for a steeper body angle, then feet on a bench or box, then hands on blocks for extra depth, working toward a wall-supported handstand push-up.
complements: Side- and rear-delt work, which vertical pressing does not replace.
video_title: PIKE PUSH UP Tutorial for the Complete Beginner

name: Plank
summary: The lowest-barrier anti-extension option, a stability-and-endurance tool rather than a growth stimulus.
why_this_exists: The lowest-barrier anti-extension option, with no equipment and almost no skill requirement to start.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight isometric hold.
best_used_when: Trunk-bracing control and endurance are the goal rather than a growth stimulus — this is a stability tool first, and a beginner-friendly entry point into anti-extension work.
less_suitable_when: Hold times have grown long enough that the set is mostly endurance — at that point the stimulus has plateaued, and a harder variation or added load delivers more actual growth demand for the same time spent.
mirror_effect: Minimal shaping effect on its own — this builds trunk endurance and bracing control more than muscle size, so any visible ab definition it contributes to is really a body-fat and tightness effect rather than added mass.
limitations: It plateaus quickly for anyone with baseline trunk strength — once a hold can be sustained for a couple of minutes, added hold time stops translating into meaningful further adaptation.
There's no clean way to add load within the exercise itself; progressing past the beginner stage requires switching to a harder variation or a different movement entirely.
technique_cues: Set the forearms on the floor with the elbows under the shoulders, the feet about hip width apart and the toes tucked under.
Lift the hips so the body forms one straight line from head to heels.
Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes, keeping the ribs pulled down toward the hips.
Breathe steadily through the hold, and end the set when the hips start to sag.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging toward the floor: the lower back arches and takes the load the abs are meant to hold.
Hips piked up high: shortens the lever, so the hold gets easier without training the trunk.
Holding the breath: the brace can't be kept for the whole set, and the hold ends early.
complements: A loaded flexion movement and an anti-rotation movement.
video_title: How To: Plank

name: Plank Shoulder Tap
summary: A high plank with alternating hand lifts to touch the opposite shoulder, keeping the hips still against the rotation each lift creates.
why_this_exists: The only anti-rotation exercise in the library, the Pallof press, needs a band or cable. Lifting one hand at a time from a high plank makes the trunk resist rotation with nothing but bodyweight, so anti-rotation control can be trained anywhere.
movement_patterns: alternating hand lifts from a high plank
resistance_profile: Bodyweight. The rotational challenge peaks while one hand is off the floor; a narrower foot stance or a slower tap makes it harder.
best_used_when: Anti-rotation control is wanted with no band or cable available.
A low-fatigue core exercise is wanted as a warm-up or finisher.
less_suitable_when: A loadable anti-rotation exercise is available and progression by load is wanted — bodyweight taps progress only through stance and tempo.
mirror_effect: Minimal shaping effect on its own — this builds trunk control against rotation more than muscle size.
limitations: Progression is limited to a narrower stance, slower taps or longer sets.
The wrists and shoulders carry the bodyweight throughout, which some lifters find uncomfortable.
technique_cues: Set up in a high plank with hands under the shoulders and feet about hip width apart.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes so the body forms a straight line.
Lift one hand to touch the opposite shoulder, keeping the hips level and still.
Return the hand to the floor under control and alternate sides.
common_mistakes: Rocking the hips side to side with each tap: the trunk gives in to the rotation the exercise is meant to resist.
Feet too close together at first: the rotational demand outruns trunk control and the hips swing.
Rushing the taps: momentum hides the rotation instead of the trunk resisting it.
programming_notes: Start with the feet wide; bring them closer together, or slow each tap, once the hips stay still.
complements: An anti-extension hold such as a plank, and a lateral-flexion hold such as a side plank.
video_title: How to Do Plank Shoulder Taps (Core Stability + Control)

name: Pogo Hops
summary: Quick, small, stiff-ankled bounces on the balls of the feet, training springy, reactive ankles.
why_this_exists: Badminton footwork relies on quick, springy steps and split-steps. Short ground-contact hops train the lower legs to absorb and return force quickly.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; ground-contact speed, not height, sets the challenge.
best_used_when: Quick, reactive ankles are wanted as part of a warm-up or before court work.
less_suitable_when: The Achilles or calves are sore; calf raises build tolerance first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds reactive ankle and calf stiffness.
limitations: The repeated impact builds up quickly in the Achilles and calves, so volume has to increase gradually.
It trains small, fast bounces, not maximal jumping height.
technique_cues: Stand tall with the feet about hip width apart and the knees almost straight.
Bounce up and down on the balls of the feet, keeping the heels just off the floor.
Keep each ground contact as short and quiet as possible, letting the ankles do the work.
Stop the set when the bounces lose their rhythm or get loud.
common_mistakes: Bending the knees a lot on each bounce: the knees and hips take over and the ankle stiffness the drill trains is lost.
Letting the heels slam down: removes the springy contact and increases impact on the heel and Achilles.
Doing long sets: once contacts slow down it is no longer the reactive quality being trained.
programming_notes: Progress from two feet to forward, sideways and then single-leg pogos.
complements: A loaded calf raise for strength.
video_title: How To Do Pogo Hops | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Preacher Curl
summary: Fixes the upper arm forward on a pad, removing swing for a strict biceps curl that, with free weights, is hardest with the elbows near straight; the exact curve varies with the pad angle.
why_this_exists: Fixes the upper arm forward on a pad, which removes swing. With a barbell, EZ-bar or dumbbells the curl is hardest with the elbows near straight and gets easier toward the top; the exact curve depends on the pad angle.
primary_targets: biceps (short-head bias proposed, not confirmed by hypertrophy data)
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; barbell, EZ-bar, or dumbbells all work on the same bench — a grip and independent-arm preference, not a different movement.
best_used_when: A strict, swing-free mechanical-tension stimulus is wanted late in a session, when standing curls would start to rely on momentum.
less_suitable_when: The bottom of the range feels uncomfortable under load, which can limit how much of the strict range actually gets used.
mirror_effect: Often credited with favouring the short head and fullness near the base of the biceps, but the one direct hypertrophy comparison of shoulder positions found similar growth across the biceps, so treat any width-versus-peak shape effect as unproven. Its clearer value is a strict curl with the upper arm fixed and swing removed.
limitations: The bottom of the range can feel uncomfortable at the elbow for some lifters, especially near full extension under load, which can limit how much of the strict range gets used.
Requires a preacher bench, which isn't available in every gym or home setup the way a standing curl is.
technique_cues: Sit at the preacher bench with the armpits snug against the top of the pad and the backs of the upper arms flat on it, holding the bar or dumbbells with an underhand grip.
Curl the weight up by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms pressed into the pad.
Stop when the forearms are close to vertical, before the load comes off at the top.
Lower under control until the elbows are almost straight, without letting the weight drop the last part of the way.
common_mistakes: Dropping quickly into the bottom: jolts the elbow at near-full extension, where the load is heaviest and elbow discomfort is most common.
Lifting the elbows or shoulders off the pad to finish the rep: brings back the swing the pad exists to remove.
Sitting too low, so only the forearms rest on the pad: the upper arm isn't fixed and the curl loses its strictness.
programming_notes: Spider curl variation: lying chest-down on an incline bench with the arms hanging straight down gives the same arm-in-front position without a preacher pad. Resistance is lowest with the arms straight and peaks partway up, instead of near straight arms as on the preacher pad.
complements: A lengthened-position curl such as an incline curl.
evidence_notes: Same shoulder-position question as the incline curl's long-head claim, applied in reverse: shoulder flexion (preacher) vs. shoulder extension (incline). The closest direct hypertrophy comparison, Attarieh et al. (2025, European Journal of Sport Science, PMC11906226), trained a preacher cable curl against a Bayesian cable curl and found similar growth at every measured biceps and brachialis site, with no regional difference, so a short-head or base-width bias is not confirmed by hypertrophy data. Evidence quality: low.

Where the free-weight preacher curl is hardest: Oliveira et al. (2009, Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 8(1):24-29, PMC3737788) measured the highest biceps EMG near full extension, falling toward the top. Nunes et al. (2020, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(16):5859, PMC7460162) describe barbell preacher curls as applying greater torque with the elbows extended and cable preacher curls with the elbows flexed (a qualitative description, not a measured torque curve); in their 10-week trial biceps thickness grew similarly in both (8% vs 7%). Neither paper reports the pad angle. Evidence quality: moderate for where the free-weight version is hardest; no support for a growth advantage either way.
video_title: Preacher Curls | How To Perform It Correctly

name: Preacher Curl Machine
summary: A fixed-path preacher curl, well suited to pushing the strict shortened-position stimulus safely to true failure.
why_this_exists: A fixed-path preacher curl that removes the need for a separate bench and free weight, and often adds a cam that adjusts resistance through the range.
primary_targets: biceps (short-head bias proposed, not confirmed by hypertrophy data)
resistance_profile: Fixed-path, often cam-adjusted through the range.
best_used_when: The preacher curl's strict, swing-free stimulus is wanted pushed safely to true failure or a drop set, since the fixed path removes any chance of the bar drifting to help.
less_suitable_when: The machine's pad or handle position doesn't suit the individual, which can blunt the tension felt regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
mirror_effect: Same as the free-weight preacher curl — often credited with fullness near the base of the biceps, but that shape effect is unproven (see preacher-curl's evidence_notes).
limitations: Pad and handle position vary between machines, and a poor fit can blunt the tension felt or create elbow discomfort regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
Availability is a real constraint — this specific machine isn't as universal in gyms as a barbell, dumbbells, or even a preacher bench.
technique_cues: Set the seat so the armpits sit snugly over the top of the pad and the backs of the upper arms lie flat on it.
Grip the handles with the elbows lined up with the machine's pivot.
Curl the handles up by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms pressed into the pad.
Lower under control until the elbows are almost straight, without letting the stack drop.
common_mistakes: Elbows not lined up with the machine's pivot: the arc fights the elbow, causing discomfort and blunting the biceps tension.
Lifting the shoulders or chest off the pad to finish reps: brings back the swing the pad exists to remove.
Letting the stack drop into the bottom: jolts the elbow near full extension, where discomfort is most common.
complements: A lengthened-position curl such as an incline curl.
evidence_notes: Same shoulder-position question as the free-weight preacher curl (the same flexed shoulder position on a fixed path). See preacher-curl's evidence_notes: the one direct hypertrophy comparison found no regional difference. Evidence quality: low.
video_title: Machine Preacher Curl

name: Pronation and Supination Work
summary: Loads forearm rotation directly, a function-and-durability role more than a primary hypertrophy driver.
why_this_exists: Loads forearm rotation directly, which curls and carries only train through part of their range.
resistance_profile: Band, cable, or offset-loaded handle.
best_used_when: Rotational strength is wanted for sport or grip-related goals — this is a function-and-durability role more than a primary hypertrophy driver.
less_suitable_when: Larger movements in the session haven't been covered yet, since this is a low-priority addition rather than a growth-critical one.
mirror_effect: Minimal visible effect on its own — the muscles involved are small and the role here is function and durability, not something that noticeably changes forearm shape or size by itself.
limitations: The rotational range of motion is small and the muscles involved are minor, so the achievable mechanical-tension stimulus is inherently limited regardless of how it's loaded.
It's easy to substitute wrist or shoulder rotation for true forearm pronation/supination if the setup doesn't isolate the movement well, diluting the intended stimulus.
technique_cues: Rest the forearm on a bench or the thigh with the wrist just past the edge, holding the offset handle (or the band or cable handle) with the elbow bent.
Keep the forearm and elbow still on the support so only the forearm rotates.
Rotate the palm slowly down as far as it comfortably goes, then up as far as it comfortably goes.
Use a light load and complete the reps on one side before switching.
common_mistakes: Lifting the elbow or rotating the shoulder to turn the handle: the shoulder does the rotation instead of the forearm.
Letting the handle drop through the range: the rotation is uncontrolled and the small forearm muscles lose the load.
Starting too heavy or too far from the hand on an offset handle: the wrist is strained before the forearm muscles are worked.
complements: Wrist curls, reverse wrist curls, and grip work.
video_title: Forearm Pronation and Supination exercise

name: Pull-Up (Pronated Grip)
summary: A bodyweight vertical pull with an overhand grip, leaning most heavily on the lats and grip with less elbow-flexor assistance than a chin-up.
why_this_exists: A bodyweight vertical pull that requires little equipment and scales through added load, tempo, or assistance. The overhand grip leans on the lats and grip strength more than the chin-up does.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; progresses via added load, tempo, or assistance.
best_used_when: A heavy, bodyweight-scaled mechanical-tension stimulus for lat width is the goal, with grip and upper-back strength building alongside it.
less_suitable_when: Bodyweight is too much load to complete a useful number of reps, capping the growth stimulus until strength improves or assistance is added.
mirror_effect: This is usually the actual answer to "my lats look narrow" — vertical pulling like this is the primary driver of back width, the flare that shows up under the arms and creates the V-taper look from behind. Rows build back thickness, not width; if width specifically is the complaint, this family of movements is where to look first.
limitations: Bodyweight is a large, all-or-nothing jump in load for anyone who can't yet do a full rep, and there's no easy way to fine-tune the resistance down without a band or assisted machine.
Grip strength commonly runs out before the lats do, especially for lifters who haven't built grip capacity separately.
technique_cues: Hang from the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders and the arms fully straight.
Draw the shoulder blades down, then pull the chest toward the bar by driving the elbows down to the sides.
Pull until the chin clears the bar, keeping the legs still beneath you.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Kicking or swinging the legs to get up: momentum does the work the lats are meant to do.
Stopping short of straight arms at the bottom: cuts off the bottom of the range, so each rep does less work.
Craning the neck to get the chin over the bar: the rep looks complete while the body hasn't actually risen.
complements: A horizontal row selected for a distinct role.
video_title: The Perfect Pull Up  - Do it right!

name: Push-Up
summary: An accessible, scalable horizontal press that trains the chest at low equipment cost.
why_this_exists: An accessible horizontal press that scales with leverage, loading, range, and execution.
primary_targets: chest (commonly cited as mid-biased, similar to a flat press)
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled; loading capacity is capped by bodyweight and leverage unless added load (vest, band, or elevated feet) is used.
best_used_when: High-rep, pump-oriented chest volume is wanted, or a technique or warm-up tool, or a genuine mechanical-tension stimulus once loaded with a weight vest or band — bodyweight alone caps how much raw tension it can deliver for a trained lifter.
less_suitable_when: A set can be done for very high reps without real difficulty, which signals the stimulus has dropped closer to muscular endurance than the tension needed to drive further growth.
mirror_effect: Same mid-chest visible direction as a flat bench press, but modest unless loaded with a vest or band — bodyweight alone caps how much of a mass-building effect this delivers for a trained lifter.
limitations: Bodyweight alone caps the achievable load, so this stops being a meaningful mechanical-tension stimulus for a trained lifter without added resistance.
Adding load (a vest, band, or elevated feet) is needed to keep progressing past a beginner level, and not every setting has that equipment available.
technique_cues: Set the hands slightly wider than shoulder width with the fingers pointing forward, and hold the body in one straight line from head to heels by tightening the glutes and abs.
Lower the chest toward the floor with the elbows angled back at roughly 45 degrees from the torso, not flared straight out.
Go down until the chest is just above the floor, or as deep as the shoulders comfortably allow, keeping the hips in line with the shoulders.
Push the floor away to straight arms, moving the body as one piece.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging toward the floor: the lower back arches and takes strain the trunk is meant to hold.
Elbows flared straight out to the sides: raises shoulder stress, as on a flat bench press.
Stopping well short of the floor: shortens the range the chest works through, so the set gets easier without becoming more productive.
programming_notes: Deficit variation: place the hands on blocks, plates or push-up handles so the chest can sink below hand level. The deeper bottom position stretches the chest further; lower only as far as the shoulders stay comfortable.
complements: Loaded press or cable work where available.
evidence_notes: Inferred from flat-barbell-bench-press: see that record's evidence_notes. Those studies tested barbell bench pressing, not push-ups; the push-up is assumed to share the flat press's mid-chest emphasis because it is the same horizontal pressing pattern.
video_title: The Perfect Push Up | Do it right!

name: Push-Up Plus
summary: A low-equipment scapular-protraction drill, a durability and movement-quality tool rather than a primary size driver.
why_this_exists: A low-equipment way to train scapular protraction, which most pressing and pulling does not load directly.
movement_patterns: scapular protraction within a horizontal press
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled.
best_used_when: Scapular control and movement quality are wanted as part of a warm-up or general shoulder health work — a durability role, not a primary size driver.
less_suitable_when: The extra range at the top is skipped, which turns it back into an ordinary push-up and loses the scapular-control value that's the whole point of this variation.
mirror_effect: At the light loading this drill uses, any visible effect is minor — in a lean physique, serratus anterior development shows as diagonal lines along the side of the ribcage near the lat, but this durability drill alone isn't enough volume to be the main driver of that look.
limitations: The added protraction range is small and easy to skip without noticing, at which point it's functionally just a regular push-up.
As a durability and movement-quality drill, it contributes essentially nothing to shoulder size or strength on its own — it isn't a substitute for pressing volume.
technique_cues: Set up in a high push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body in one straight line from head to heels.
Do a normal push-up, lowering the chest toward the floor with the elbows angled back.
At the top, with the arms straight, push the floor further away so the upper back rounds slightly and the shoulder blades spread apart around the ribcage.
Let the shoulder blades settle back to neutral under control before starting the next rep.
common_mistakes: Skipping the extra push at the top: it becomes an ordinary push-up and the serratus work is lost.
Hips sagging or piking during the plus: the trunk changes position instead of the shoulder blades moving.
Letting the shoulder blades snap back together between reps: the return is uncontrolled, so the drill loses the shoulder-blade control it's meant to build.
complements: Overhead pressing and horizontal pulling.
video_title: Push-Up Plus | Push-Up Variation

name: Rack Pull
summary: A partial-range deadlift from an elevated start, overloading the top-of-pull position past what a full deadlift allows.
why_this_exists: Starting the pull from an elevated position removes the hardest, most technical part of a deadlift off the floor, which lets a user load significantly heavier weight and biases the top-of-pull musculature more than a full deadlift does.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, elevated start, partial range of motion.
best_used_when: The top-of-pull position needs overloading with more mechanical tension than a full deadlift allows, specifically training grip and upper-back strength under heavier-than-usual load.
less_suitable_when: The full-range, floor-level strength stimulus a conventional deadlift trains is the goal, since this movement skips that range entirely.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up more in the traps and upper back than the lower-back erector definition a full-range deadlift builds, since the partial range biases the top-of-pull musculature specifically.
limitations: Skipping the floor-level range means it does not build pulling strength or technique off the floor — it should not be mistaken for a full deadlift substitute.

The heavier loads this position allows can tempt lifters into using more back rounding or momentum than they would with a full-range pull, since the working range is shorter and the ego-load temptation is higher.
technique_cues: Set the safety pins or blocks so the bar starts at or just below the knees, then step up with the feet about hip width apart.
Grip the bar just outside the legs, set a flat back, and brace before each rep.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, keeping the bar close to the thighs, and finish with the hips and knees straight.
Lower the bar back to the pins under control with a flat back.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back because the load is heavy: the main injury risk, made worse by the bigger weights this position allows.
Leaning back hard at the top: the lower back is forced into extension instead of the hips finishing the lift.
Bouncing the bar off the pins between reps: momentum replaces the start of each pull.
complements: A Romanian deadlift, which covers the bottom-range hinge work this movement skips.
video_title: How To Do A BARBELL RACK PULL | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Rear-Delt Fly
summary: Direct rear-delt isolation work that pressing-heavy routines commonly leave short.
why_this_exists: Direct rear-delt work, which pressing-heavy routines commonly leave short.
resistance_profile: Free-weight or fixed-path machine, depending on equipment. A band held in front at shoulder height and pulled apart gets heavier as the arms open, so it is hardest at the end of the fly.
best_used_when: An isolated growth stimulus for the rear delts is wanted without adding another heavy pull to the session.
less_suitable_when: The elbows bend enough that the movement turns into a row — the stimulus shifts toward a more mechanical-tension, less isolated rear-delt effect, which may or may not be what was wanted.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as roundness on the back of the shoulder, most visible from behind or the side — this fills out the shoulder's "3D" look rather than adding to front-view width, which is what lateral-delt work does instead.
limitations: Usable load is low since the posterior deltoid is a small muscle, and it's easy to substitute momentum or trap involvement for real range without noticing.
Elbow bend tends to creep in as the weight gets heavier, sliding the exercise toward a row and away from the isolated stimulus that's the point of this record.
technique_cues: Hinge at the hips until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor with a flat back, letting the dumbbells hang under the shoulders with a slight, fixed bend in the elbows.
Raise the arms out to the sides, leading with the backs of the hands, until the upper arms are level with the torso.
Keep the torso and neck still so the movement happens only at the shoulders.
Lower under control until the arms hang straight down again.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows more as the set gets hard: turns it into a row, and the back muscles take over from the rear delts.
Swinging the torso up to start each rep: momentum moves the weight instead of the rear delts.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears: the upper traps take over from the rear delts.
programming_notes: Band version: hold a band in front at shoulder height with straight arms and pull it apart until the hands are level with the shoulders, leading with the backs of the hands. A narrower grip on the band adds resistance.
complements: Horizontal pulling and side-delt work.
video_creator: Fit Father Project - Fitness For Busy Fathers
video_title: How To Do Rear Delt Flys With Dumbbells - Proper Form, Sets & Reps

name: Rear Delt Row
summary: A seated dumbbell row from a dead hang, elbows down and thumbs rotating back and up, driving the rear delts through extension.
why_this_exists: A seated dumbbell row that starts from a dead hang below the hamstrings and pulls back with the elbows staying down and the thumbs rotating slightly back and up, which drives the rear delts through extension rather than only horizontal abduction.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, bent-over seated start position.
best_used_when: A free-weight, mechanical-tension rear-delt stimulus is wanted and a bent-over seated position under light-to-moderate load can be held.
less_suitable_when: The lower back rounds to hold the bent-over position, or the elbows flare up and out instead of staying down and back — both signal the stimulus is drifting away from the rear delts.
mirror_effect: Similar rear-delt visible direction to a fly, plus some contribution to upper-back thickness from the row pattern, so the effect reads as a bit more "connected" to the back than an isolated fly does.
limitations: The bent-over seated position places real demand on the lower back to stay braced, which can become the limiting factor before the rear delts are.
It's easy to let the elbows flare up and out under fatigue, which shifts the stimulus toward the upper back and traps instead of the rear delts.
technique_cues: Sit at the end of a bench and hinge forward with a flat back until the torso is close to the thighs, letting the dumbbells hang straight down.
Row the dumbbells back toward your hips with the elbows staying down, not flaring out to the sides.
As the elbows travel back, rotate the thumbs back and up to finish the movement.
Keep the lower back braced and the torso still throughout.
common_mistakes: Elbows flaring up and out as fatigue sets in: the upper back and traps take over from the rear delts.
Sitting up as the set gets hard: the torso angle changes and the rear delts lose their line of pull.
Shrugging the dumbbells up: the traps do the lifting.
complements: A rear-delt fly or a cable rear delt builder.
video_title: How To Do Dumbbell Rear Delt Row | Exercise Demo

name: Reverse Crunch
summary: A floor crunch from the bottom up, curling the pelvis toward the ribs by lifting the hips, trunk flexion with no equipment.
why_this_exists: The library's loaded trunk-flexion options need a cable, a machine or a pull-up bar. The reverse crunch trains the same rib-to-pelvis flexion lying on the floor, so the abs can be worked through flexion, not only braced, with no equipment.
resistance_profile: Leg and pelvis weight, hardest as the hips leave the floor and the pelvis curls up. Straighter legs increase the lever and the difficulty.
best_used_when: The abs need direct flexion work and no cable, machine or pull-up bar is available.
A low-fatigue ab exercise is wanted alongside bracing work such as planks.
less_suitable_when: Reps have become easy and a loaded crunch is available — bodyweight loading is hard to progress beyond straighter legs and slower tempo.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and at a low enough body-fat level, as more visible ab definition — the same rectus-abdominis stimulus as other crunches, without load.
limitations: The hip flexors can do much of the work if the knees swing toward the chest without the pelvis curling, and that's hard to feel at first.
Progression is limited to leverage and tempo unless a bench or incline is available.
technique_cues: Lie on your back with the hips and knees bent at about 90 degrees and the arms flat by your sides.
Curl the pelvis toward the ribs so the hips lift a few centimetres off the floor, rather than just bringing the knees in.
Pause briefly with the lower back rounded off the floor.
Lower the hips slowly until the lower back touches down, without letting the legs drop.
common_mistakes: Swinging the knees toward the chest without lifting the hips: the hip flexors move the legs and the abs barely work.
Pushing the arms into the floor to lever the hips up: the arms do the lifting instead of the abs.
Dropping the hips quickly: skips the lowering, which is half of each rep's ab work.
programming_notes: Progress by straightening the legs a little, then by slowing the lowering. On a decline bench, gravity adds load once the floor version is easy.
complements: An anti-extension hold such as a plank, and an anti-rotation movement.
video_title: How To Do A Reverse Crunch

name: Reverse Curl
summary: Loads the brachioradialis and forearm extensors through an elbow- flexion pattern, adding arm and forearm work at once.
why_this_exists: Loads the brachioradialis and forearm extensors through an elbow-flexion pattern, so it adds arm and forearm work at once.
resistance_profile: Barbell or EZ-bar allows the heaviest load on a fixed path; dumbbells allow independent arms and let each wrist find its own comfortable angle. A band stood on gets heavier toward the top of the curl.
best_used_when: A forearm-thickness stimulus is wanted that also counts toward elbow-flexion volume, getting two growth roles from one movement.
less_suitable_when: Wrist comfort is limiting with a straight bar — an EZ bar delivers the same stimulus without that cost.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as width right at the elbow crease on the thumb side of the forearm — the brachioradialis is what creates that forearm "peak" when the elbow is bent, and this is a direct way to build it.
limitations: Usable load is capped well below a standard supinated curl's, since the pronated grip is a mechanically weaker position for elbow flexion.
Wrist discomfort with a straight bar is common at this grip angle, which is part of why an EZ-bar or dumbbell version often has to substitute in for it.
technique_cues: Hold the bar or dumbbells with an overhand grip, palms down, hands about shoulder width.
Keep the wrists straight, in line with the forearms; don't let them bend back.
Curl with the elbows fixed at your sides, then lower all the way down.
Switch to an EZ-bar or dumbbells if a straight bar bothers your wrists.
common_mistakes: Wrists bending back under the load: stresses the wrist and takes tension off the forearm muscles.
Loading it like a regular curl: the overhand grip is weaker, so too much weight turns into swinging.
Elbows drifting forward: the shoulders help lift the weight.
programming_notes: Band version: stand on the middle of a band and curl the ends with an overhand grip, elbows pinned at the sides. A wider stance adds resistance.
complements: A supinated curl and direct wrist work.
video_title: Dumbbell Reverse Curl

name: Reverse-Grip (Underhand) Barbell Row
summary: The same heavy free-weight row with an underhand grip, shifting emphasis more toward the lats and biceps.
why_this_exists: The same free-weight row with the grip flipped underhand, which pulls the elbows in closer and brings the lats and biceps into the pull more, the same relationship a chin-up has to a pull-up.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, fixed bar path.
best_used_when: The same heavy, mechanical-tension-driven row as the overhand version is wanted, shifted more toward the lats and biceps.
less_suitable_when: Wrist or elbow comfort favors a pronated or neutral grip, or lower-back fatigue already caps how heavy this can safely be loaded.
mirror_effect: Similar thickness-building direction to a standard row, but the underhand grip pulls the lats in more directly, so this leans a little toward contributing to width as well as thickness rather than thickness alone.
limitations: Same lower-back and technical demands as the overhand version — the hinge position doesn't get any easier or safer just because the grip changed.
The underhand grip can aggravate elbow or bicep-tendon sensitivity in some lifters at heavier loads.
technique_cues: Grip the bar underhand at about shoulder width and hinge at the hips with soft knees until the torso is well inclined, with the back flat.
Let the bar hang at arm's length, then brace the trunk before each rep.
Pull the bar toward the lower stomach, driving the elbows back close to the sides.
Lower under control to straight arms while keeping the torso angle fixed.
common_mistakes: The torso rising with each rep: the row turns into a shrug-and-lean, and the back muscles move less of the weight.
Rounding the lower back under load: the main injury risk on this lift.
Curling the bar up with the wrists and forearms: the biceps take over, and the elbow strain the record warns about increases.
complements: A supported row or vertical pull that does not add further spinal loading.
video_title: Reverse-grip Bent-over Barbell Row Tutorial

name: Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldown
summary: A supinated, closer-than-wide pulldown grip that brings the biceps into the pull more, with adjustable cable load.
why_this_exists: A supinated, closer-than-wide grip that brings the biceps into the pull more, similar to how a chin-up relates to a pull-up, while keeping the adjustable load of a cable stack.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, small load increments.
best_used_when: The pulldown's precise, progressive loading is wanted with more biceps assistance, often making it easier to push a set closer to failure than the wide pronated version.
less_suitable_when: The lats need to be isolated with minimal biceps fatigue — the wide pronated version does that more directly.
mirror_effect: Similar width-building direction to the wide pronated pulldown, with more biceps assistance diluting how isolated the lat-specific tension is per rep.
limitations: Same lean-back and momentum risk as the wide pronated version — the seated position makes it easy to recruit the trunk once the load is heavy.
The closer grip and increased biceps involvement mean less of the pull's tension is specifically isolated to the back muscles.
technique_cues: Sit with the thighs under the pads and grip the bar underhand at about shoulder width.
Lean back slightly with the chest up and the arms straight.
Pull the bar to the upper chest by driving the elbows down and back toward the ribs.
Let the bar rise under control until the arms are fully straight before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Leaning far back and rocking to pull the weight down: the trunk and momentum do the work instead of the lats.
Stopping short of straight arms at the top: cuts off the stretched part of the pull, so each rep does less work.
Pulling with the hands and wrists curled: the biceps and forearms take over more of the pull than the back.
complements: A rowing pattern.
video_title: How To Do A Reverse Grip Lat Pulldown

name: Reverse Lunge
summary: Stepping backward keeps the front knee from traveling far past the toes, often kinder on the knee than a forward-stepping lunge.
why_this_exists: Stepping backward into the lunge, rather than forward, keeps the front knee from traveling far past the toes, which many find kinder on the front knee than a forward-stepping lunge.
resistance_profile: A barbell on the back allows the heaviest load on a fixed path; dumbbells at the sides are a lighter, more accessible setup with independent arms; a shouldered sandbag adds a shifting, unstable load that raises the trunk-bracing demand beyond either.
best_used_when: A lunge pattern is wanted that's easier on the front knee, or an easier entry point into lunging than a walking lunge's continuous balance demand.
less_suitable_when: The continuous, higher-coordination stimulus a walking lunge provides is wanted instead.
mirror_effect: Same per-leg quad mass direction as other lunge variations, generally more comfortable on the front knee, which doesn't change the visible target.
limitations: The step-back motion demands a level of balance and hip control that can be a genuine barrier for less-coordinated or deconditioned lifters starting out.
It's easy to let the step-back distance vary between reps, which changes the knee angle and muddies consistent progressive overload.
technique_cues: Stand tall with the feet about hip width apart, holding the load: dumbbells at the sides, a barbell on the upper back, or a sandbag on one shoulder.
Take a long step straight back with one foot, landing on the ball of that foot, and lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Keep most of the weight on the front foot, with the torso upright and the front knee tracking in line with the toes.
Push through the whole front foot to bring the back foot forward to standing, then repeat on the same side or alternate.
common_mistakes: Stepping straight behind the front foot, as if on a tightrope: the stance gets unstable and the hips twist.
Pushing off mainly with the back leg to stand up: the work shifts away from the front leg's quads.
Changing the step length from rep to rep: the knee angle keeps changing, so progress is hard to compare.
complements: A bilateral squat or press.
video_title: Dumbbell Reverse Lunge Tutorial

name: Reverse Nordic Curl
summary: Loads knee extension with the hip extended, so the rectus femoris works in a lengthened position — a strong stretch-mediated stimulus.
why_this_exists: Loads knee extension with the hip extended, so the rectus femoris works in a lengthened position, and it needs almost no equipment.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, scales by range controlled.
best_used_when: A strong stretch-mediated stimulus is wanted specifically for the rectus femoris, in a position no common machine or squat variation reaches.
less_suitable_when: Knee tolerance is limiting, or the range can't yet be controlled — this movement should be scaled gradually rather than loaded aggressively from the start.
mirror_effect: Tends to contribute to fullness down the center of the front thigh specifically, since the rectus femoris this targets runs down that central line — adds to the quad's central sweep rather than the outer teardrop shape a leg extension emphasizes.
limitations: The knee experiences real end-range stress in this position, and lifters with existing knee sensitivity may not tolerate it well even at a controlled pace.
There's a real skill floor — many lifters can't control any meaningful range at all when starting out, and loading it too aggressively before building control raises injury risk.
There's no simple way to add external load once bodyweight control is mastered, unlike a barbell-based leg exercise.
technique_cues: Kneel on a padded surface with knees hip width and the body straight from knees to head.
Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips straight and lean the whole body back as one line.
Lower only as far as you can control, then pull back up with the quads.
Build range gradually; use a band or hand support for assistance at first.
common_mistakes: Bending at the hips as you lean back: loses the stretch on the front of the thigh, the reason to do this exercise.
Dropping into the bottom uncontrolled: loads the knee at end range without the muscles controlling it.
Increasing range faster than your knees tolerate: the knee is under real end-range stress here, and soreness that lingers past the next day means you progressed too fast.
programming_notes: Progress range of motion before anything else. Once a range is controlled, slowing the lowering phase makes the same range harder without needing extra load.
complements: A loadable squat or press pattern.
evidence_notes: No study using this specific exercise was located, but the underlying principle — that training the quads at a longer muscle length (deep hip/knee flexion) drives more growth than training at a shorter length — has direct support from squat-depth research. Bloomquist et al. (2013) ran a 12-week controlled trial comparing shallow squats (~60° knee flexion) against deep squats (~120° knee flexion): the deep-squat group gained quadriceps cross-sectional area across the entire thigh, while the shallow-squat group only grew measurably in the upper thigh. This is a squat-depth finding, not a reverse-Nordic-curl finding, but it's the same underlying variable — how lengthened the quads get under load — that this record's rectus-femoris claim rests on. It's also consistent with the broader stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning) found training at longer muscle length tends to match or beat training that avoids the stretch, though a later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found the advantage over full ROM is smaller than earlier work suggested.
video_title: How To Do Reverse Nordic Curls For Quad Strength

name: Reverse Wrist Curl
summary: Trains the wrist extensors, which little else in a normal routine loads directly.
why_this_exists: Trains the wrist extensors, which little else in a normal routine loads directly.
resistance_profile: Barbell, dumbbells, or a cable all work the same way a wrist curl's equipment choice does. A band anchored under the foot is lightest at the bottom and heaviest as the wrist extends.
best_used_when: Plenty of gripping work exists and nothing trains the back of the forearm — this fills a growth and balance gap most routines leave open.
less_suitable_when: Elbow-region symptoms are present — pain is a stop-and-assess signal, not something to load through.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fullness on the back-of-hand side of the forearm, which is the side that's actually visible when the arm hangs relaxed at the side — this fills out the top of the forearm rather than the palm-facing side a wrist curl builds.
limitations: The wrist extensors are considerably weaker than the flexors, so usable load is low even for a lifter who is otherwise strong — the exercise can feel trivial in weight compared to everything else in a session.
This is a common site for elbow-tendon irritation (a lateral-elbow, "tennis elbow"-type strain) if volume or load increases too quickly.
technique_cues: Sit with your forearms on your thighs or a bench, palms down and wrists just past the edge.
Let the hands lower slowly, then raise the backs of the hands as high as they go.
Move only at the wrist; keep the forearms flat on the support.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight: the forearms or elbows lift to help and the wrist extensors do little.
Raising load or volume quickly: a common route to irritation on the outside of the elbow (tennis-elbow type).
Bouncing at the bottom: momentum replaces the controlled lowering.
programming_notes: Band version: sit with the forearm on the thigh, palm down, and the band anchored under the foot. Shorten the band to add resistance.
complements: Wrist curls and grip work.
video_title: How to Do Dumbbell Reverse Wrist Curls

name: Romanian Deadlift
summary: The main loadable hinge, and the most direct way to train the hamstrings and glutes together in a lengthened position under heavy load.
why_this_exists: The main loadable hinge, and the most direct way to train the hamstrings in a lengthened position under heavy load.
resistance_profile: A barbell allows the heaviest fixed-path load; dumbbells allow independent arms and are often the easier entry point for learning the hinge; a Smith machine variant exists (see hips module) for beginners still learning to control the bar path.
best_used_when: Heavy hinge work is wanted that trains the hamstrings and glutes together at a long muscle length.
less_suitable_when: Lower-back fatigue is already high, capping how much of the lengthened-position load can safely be used.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as overall thickness through the back of the thigh and glutes together, viewed from behind — this builds hamstring and glute mass as one connected unit rather than shaping either specifically, since the movement trains them together by design.
limitations: Technical demand is real — hips-back, spine-neutral, bar-close-to-the- legs all have to happen together, and it takes real practice to load heavily without the lower back rounding.
Grip often fails before the hamstrings do at heavier loads, capping the set short of the target muscles' true limit unless straps or a mixed/hook grip are used.
Hamstring flexibility limits how deep the hinge can go while keeping the back neutral, so a stiff lifter may not reach a meaningful stretch even with good technique.
technique_cues: Start standing with the bar at your hips, feet hip width, knees softly bent.
Push the hips straight back, keeping the bar against or close to your thighs as it travels down.
Keep the back flat and the knee bend roughly the same all the way down. This is a hip hinge, not a squat.
Lower until you feel a strong hamstring stretch or your back starts to round, often around mid-shin, then drive the hips forward to stand.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach lower: depth should stop where a flat back stops.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs: increases the load on the lower back.
Bending the knees more as you descend: it turns into a deadlift and the hamstring stretch shrinks.
Letting grip end the set before the hamstrings: use straps at heavier loads.
programming_notes: Unlike the 45-degree back extension or Bulgarian split squat, an RDL doesn't have a clean discrete technique switch that biases glutes vs. hamstrings — the moderate knee bend trains both together by design throughout the whole movement. For a more hamstring-isolated stimulus, see stiff-leg-deadlift below. For a more glute-isolated, shortened-position stimulus, see hip-thrust in the hips module.

Good morning variation: the same hip hinge with the bar on the upper back instead of in the hands, so grip never limits the set. The load sits further from the hips, so far less weight is used, and the lower back has to hold position under a longer lever.
complements: A leg-curl pattern, since a hinge alone leaves knee flexion untrained.
overlaps_with: conventional-deadlift (back module) — related but distinct hinge that starts from the floor.
evidence_notes: Draws on the general stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning) both found training at longer muscle length tends to match or beat training that avoids the stretch; a later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found the advantage over full ROM is smaller than earlier work suggested. No study specific to the RDL was located — see seated-leg-curl's evidence_notes below for the closest direct hamstring-length hypertrophy trial found, which used a hip-flexed knee-flexion position rather than a hinge.
video_title: Barbell Romanian Deadlift - Proper Form & Technique [4K]

name: Rowing Machine Intervals
summary: Hard rowing intervals on an indoor rowing machine, driving with the legs and finishing with the arms.
why_this_exists: Rowing works the legs, back and arms together with low impact, so it builds whole-body endurance without the joint load of running and jumping.
resistance_profile: Machine; stroke power and stroke rate set the intensity.
best_used_when: Whole-body conditioning with low impact on the knees and ankles is wanted.
