less_suitable_when: The lower back is sore; poor rowing form loads it heavily.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds whole-body endurance.
limitations: It needs a rowing machine.
Poor technique shifts the work onto the arms and lower back.
technique_cues: Strap the feet in, sit tall and hold the handle with straight arms, shins near vertical.
Drive with the legs first, keeping the arms straight.
As the legs straighten, lean back slightly and pull the handle to the lower ribs.
Return in reverse: arms out, lean forward, then bend the knees.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms before the legs drive: the arms tire and the legs do little.
Bending the knees before the hands pass them on the way back: the handle has to travel over the knees.
Rounding the back at the front of the stroke: loads the lower back.
programming_notes: Track distance or average pace per interval to see progress.
complements: Lower-body mobility work afterwards.
video_creator: Chris Liddle: Fitness, Growth, and Skills
video_title: How to Use a Rowing Machine | Proper Rowing Technique for Beginners

name: Russian Twist
summary: A free-weight rotation option loaded hardest at the ends of the range, the opposite feel from a cable woodchop's constant tension.
why_this_exists: A free-weight rotation option; the load is hardest at the ends of the range and eases through the middle, the opposite feel from a cable woodchop's constant tension.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, hardest at the ends of the range.
best_used_when: A rotational stimulus loaded like a free weight is wanted, hardest at the ends of the range rather than held constant like a cable.
less_suitable_when: The movement turns into fast, uncontrolled swinging rather than a controlled rotation, trading the growth stimulus for momentum.
mirror_effect: Same consideration as the cable woodchop — real oblique loading here can visibly thicken the waist over time if pushed heavy, so the load and frequency used should match whether the goal is a fuller midsection or a tapered one.
limitations: Momentum is an easy substitute for controlled rotation once the load or pace increases, which trades the growth stimulus for speed without feeling like a technique failure.
The seated, often feet-elevated setup can aggravate lower-back or hip-flexor sensitivity in some lifters, independent of the rotational work itself.
technique_cues: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and heels down, holding the weight in both hands close to the chest.
Lean the torso back to about 45 degrees with a straight back, bracing the abs to hold that position.
Rotate the torso to one side, turning the shoulders and the weight together until the weight is beside the hip, then rotate through to the other side.
Keep the pace slow enough to stop and reverse at each end, and lift the feet off the floor only once that's easy.
common_mistakes: Swinging the weight with the arms while the torso stays still: the arms move the load and the obliques barely rotate the trunk.
Rounding the lower back as the lean gets tiring: the back takes the strain of holding the position instead of the abs.
Rushing from side to side: momentum carries the weight through the ends of the range, where the rotation is hardest.
complements: The Pallof press and other anti-rotation work.
video_title: How to Do a Russian Twist | Ab Workout

name: Seated Band Row
summary: A horizontal pull sitting on the floor with a band looped around the feet, the no-anchor way to train back thickness with only a band.
why_this_exists: Every row in the library needs a cable, machine, barbell or dumbbells and a bench. Sitting with legs extended and a band around the feet gives a horizontal pull with nothing to anchor to, so back thickness can be trained with only a band.
resistance_profile: The band gets heavier as it stretches, so the row is hardest at the end of the pull with the elbows back and lightest with the arms extended.
best_used_when: Back thickness needs direct work and only a band is available.
A low-fatigue row is wanted for extra back volume at home or while travelling.
less_suitable_when: A heavy, progressively loaded row is available — band tension is light at the start of each rep and hard to increase in small steps.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and alongside heavier rowing, as more density through the mid-back viewed from the side — a supporting stimulus at band loads.
limitations: Tension is lowest at the start of the pull, where the band is slack, so the stretched position is barely loaded.
Progression comes in band-sized jumps or by shortening the band, which is less precise than adding plates.
technique_cues: Sit on the floor with legs extended and knees slightly bent, and loop the middle of the band around the soles of both feet.
Hold the ends with arms straight, sitting tall with the chest up.
Pull the hands toward the lower ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Return slowly until the arms are straight without letting the torso fold forward.
common_mistakes: Leaning back to finish the pull: the torso does the work and the mid-back barely shortens.
Shrugging the shoulders up as you pull: the upper traps take over from the mid-back.
Letting the band snap the arms forward: loses the controlled return, which is half of each rep's work.
programming_notes: Shorten the band by wrapping it once more around the feet, or switch to a heavier band, once the top of the rep range is easy.
complements: A vertical pull such as a chin-up or a band straight-arm pulldown.
video_title: How To: Resistance Band Seated Row

name: Seated Cable Row
summary: A horizontal pull with the trunk supported by the seated position, for back-thickness work without the hinge's stability demand.
why_this_exists: A horizontal pull with the trunk supported by the seated position, so effort goes into the pull rather than into holding a hinge.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, small load increments; attachment width/grip (wide bar, close V-handle, rope) is a preference within this record, not a separate movement.
best_used_when: A back-thickness stimulus is wanted without the hinge's spinal-stability demand competing for effort, letting a set be pushed closer to failure.
less_suitable_when: The hinge's added trunk and hip demand is wanted as part of the stimulus, which a seated row deliberately removes.
mirror_effect: Same thickness-building visible direction as a free-standing row — density through the mid-back viewed from the side.
limitations: The seated, foot-braced setup removes the hip-and-trunk training stimulus a free-standing row provides, so it builds pulling strength somewhat in isolation from that context.
It's easy to round the lower back or lean too far forward and back to add fake range, which can look like more range of motion without adding real back-muscle tension.
technique_cues: Sit with your feet on the platform, knees slightly bent and torso upright.
Pull the handle toward your lower ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Let the arms straighten and the shoulder blades move forward at the end of each rep while the torso stays upright.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso back and forth: looks like more range but the back muscles do less.
Rounding the lower back at the front of the rep: the spine takes the load instead of the back muscles stretching.
Shrugging at the end of the pull: the upper traps take over from the mid back.
complements: A vertical pull and a free-standing row selected for a distinct role.
video_title: How To: Seated Low Row (LF Cable)

name: Seated Calf Raise
summary: The bent knee takes the gastrocnemius mostly out of play, so the soleus carries the load — a soleus-specific stimulus.
why_this_exists: The bent knee takes the gastrocnemius mostly out of play, so the soleus — the muscle that adds fullness and thickness lower on the leg — carries the load instead.
resistance_profile: Fixed-path machine. Seated on a bench with dumbbells resting on the lower thighs is the free-weight equivalent — the same bent-knee position, with the load capped by what can be balanced on the knees.
best_used_when: A soleus-specific stimulus is wanted that a standing raise mostly misses, or a higher-rep, pump-oriented finisher — the soleus is commonly cited to tolerate and respond well to higher rep ranges and shorter rest than the gastrocnemius.
less_suitable_when: Overall calf size is the goal and the gastrocnemius-dominant position hasn't yet been covered in the same session.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fullness lower on the leg, closer to the ankle, rather than the upper bulge a standing raise builds — it fills out the lower half of the calf's profile from the side, which is often the part that stays thin even when the upper calf has already grown.
limitations: How cleanly the gastrocnemius gets excluded depends on the machine's pad and knee-angle design — a poorly built machine lets it creep back into the movement.
The seated position removes bodyweight as a loading option, so the achievable stimulus is capped entirely by the machine's available load.
technique_cues: Set the knee pad snug on your lower thighs with the balls of your feet on the platform edge.
Lower the heels as far as possible and pause briefly in the stretch.
Push up onto your toes as high as you can and squeeze at the top.
Keep each rep slow; don't bounce out of the bottom.
common_mistakes: Bouncing out of the stretch: the Achilles tendon's rebound does the work instead of the soleus.
Half reps in the middle of the range: skips both the stretch and the top squeeze.
Pushing the pad up with your hands or hips: the calves skip the start of each rep, which is the hardest part.
programming_notes: Dumbbell version: sit on the end of a bench with a dumbbell on each lower thigh, just above the knee. Putting the balls of the feet on a plate or step is optional and adds range at the bottom. A towel under the dumbbells makes heavier loads more comfortable.
complements: A straight-knee raise.
evidence_notes: The rep-range claim has a real anatomical basis: the soleus is consistently measured at roughly 70-90% slow-twitch (type I) fiber composition, well above most skeletal muscle, which is the standard justification for training it with higher reps and shorter rest. Caveat worth stating plainly: newer hypertrophy research (load- range comparison trials) has found that muscles — including slow-twitch-dominant ones — can grow similarly across a wide range of loads and rep ranges as long as sets are taken close to failure, so the higher-rep prescription is a reasonable bias grounded in fiber type, not a strict requirement for soleus growth. Evidence quality: moderate — solid anatomical basis, softer causal link to the specific training prescription.
video_title: How to Do Seated Calf Raises

name: Seated Leg Curl
summary: Trains knee flexion with the hip bent, a stretch-biased mechanical- tension stimulus a hinge alone doesn't provide.
why_this_exists: Trains knee flexion with the hip bent, so the hamstrings are longer during the curl than in a lying version.
resistance_profile: Fixed-path machine.
best_used_when: A stretch-biased, mechanical-tension knee-flexion stimulus is wanted that a hinge alone doesn't provide, pushed safely close to failure on a fixed path.
less_suitable_when: The hips lift off the pad during the set, which shortens the hamstrings and trades away the stretch position that gives this movement its distinct value.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fullness through the upper-to-mid hamstring, the part of the back of the thigh that's stretched hardest in this hip-flexed position — a rounder look through that region rather than added mass at the knee end of the muscle.
limitations: Machine availability and design vary a lot — a poorly fitted thigh pad or pivot point lets the hips creep up during the set, quietly trading away the stretch position that makes this exercise distinct.
The fixed pad position doesn't accommodate every body size well, which can create uncomfortable pressure points before the hamstrings are meaningfully fatigued.
technique_cues: Set the back pad so your knees line up with the pivot and lock the thigh pad down firmly just above the knees.
Sit tall or lean slightly forward to increase the hamstring stretch.
Curl the heels down and back as far as possible, then return slowly to nearly straight legs.
common_mistakes: Thigh pad left loose: the hips rise and the stretched, hip-bent position that makes this exercise distinct is lost.
Letting the stack slam between reps: tension drops at the stretched end.
Short reps that never return to the stretched position: drops the lengthened range this machine is chosen for.
programming_notes: This hip-flexed knee-flexion position is close to what a 2024 direct trial (see evidence_notes) found to be a particularly effective lengthened-position stimulus for the hamstrings — more effective, by that trial's numbers, than the Nordic hamstring curl. See nordic-hamstring-curl below for the comparison.
complements: A hinge pattern.
evidence_notes: Direct hypertrophy trial evidence, not just the general ROM literature. A 2024 study (PMC11419281, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise) compared the Nordic hamstring curl against "lengthened state eccentric training" (LSET) — isoinertial weight-stack resistance trained in an accentuated hip-flexed position, essentially this record's hip-flexed knee-flexion setup. LSET produced substantially greater total hamstrings growth (+18% vs. +11%) and biceps femoris long-head growth (+19% vs. +5%) than the Nordic curl over the training period. This directly supports the seated leg curl's hip-flexed, lengthened-position value — see nordic-hamstring-curl's evidence_notes for the fuller comparison and what it means for that more popular exercise.

This finding sits within the broader stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning) both found training at longer muscle length tends to match or beat training that avoids the stretch, though a later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found the advantage over full ROM is smaller than earlier work suggested.
video_title: Seated Leg Curl

name: Seated Machine Shoulder Press
summary: A stable vertical press well suited to pushing a front-delt set to true failure without managing balance or bar path.
why_this_exists: A stable vertical press that lets the user push closer to failure without managing balance or bar path.
resistance_profile: Fixed-path, often cam-adjusted through the range.
best_used_when: A front-delt set is wanted pushed to true failure, or into a drop set — removing the balance demand means the last hard reps come from the delts giving out, not a stabilizer losing control of the bar.
less_suitable_when: The machine path or handle position doesn't match a user's shoulder mechanics, which can blunt the tension the delts actually feel regardless of how heavy the stack is loaded.
mirror_effect: Same front-delt visible direction as a free-weight overhead press — mass and roundness on the front of the shoulder.
limitations: Machine handle position and pressing angle vary a lot between models, and a poor fit can put more stress on the shoulder joint than the muscle.
Removing the balance and bracing demand also removes the stabilizer training a free-weight press provides, so the carryover to unassisted pressing is only partial.
technique_cues: Set the seat height so the handles start at about shoulder level, then sit with the back flat against the pad and the feet planted.
Grip the handles just outside shoulder width with the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Press the handles up until the arms are nearly straight, without shrugging the shoulders toward the ears.
Lower under control until the handles are back at about shoulder level before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Seat set too low or too high: the press starts from an awkward shoulder position, putting more stress on the joint than on the delts.
Arching the lower back off the pad to finish reps: turns it into an incline press and shifts work onto the upper chest.
Cutting the range short at the bottom: misses the lower part of the press, so each rep does less work for the delts.
complements: Side- and rear-delt work.
video_title: Machine Shoulder Press

name: Shadow Badminton Intervals
summary: Continuous shadow footwork and swings around the court in timed rounds, as badminton-specific conditioning.
why_this_exists: Moving around the court with racket swings in rally-length bursts builds endurance in the exact movements of a match.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight (a racket is optional); speed and interval length set the intensity.
best_used_when: Badminton-specific endurance is wanted, on or off court.
less_suitable_when: The footwork patterns are not yet learned; four-corner shadow footwork at a slower pace comes first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds badminton-specific endurance.
limitations: As fatigue builds, footwork quality drops, so interval length must match current fitness.
It needs a court or similar space to be specific.
technique_cues: Start each round at the base position in a ready stance.
Move to corners in a random or set order, adding a shadow swing at each one.
Recover to the base and split-step before every movement.
Keep the pace hard but repeatable for the whole interval.
common_mistakes: Letting the footwork get sloppy to keep the pace: rehearses bad movement under fatigue.
Skipping the split-step: removes the most badminton-specific part of the drill.
Making rounds much longer than real rallies: it turns into steady cardio rather than rally-style conditioning.
programming_notes: Match the work interval to typical rally length and keep rests short to build match endurance.
complements: Lower-body mobility work afterwards.
video_title: Badminton Footwork Drills ANYWHERE [What is Shadow Footwork?]

name: Shuttle Run
summary: Running back and forth between two markers in timed intervals, with fast turns at each end.
why_this_exists: Repeated sprints with sharp turns build the endurance to keep moving at speed through long rallies, with only open space needed.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; distance between markers and number of turns set the intensity.
best_used_when: Repeated-sprint endurance is wanted and there is open space of 10 to 20 metres.
less_suitable_when: Hamstrings are tight or recently strained; sprinting can aggravate them.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds repeated-sprint endurance.
limitations: Sprinting and sharp turns carry a hamstring and ankle strain risk without a thorough warm-up.
It needs open, non-slip space.
technique_cues: Set two markers 10 to 20 metres apart and start in a ready stance behind one.
Run hard to the far marker, staying low as you approach it.
Plant the outside foot, touch the line, and push back the other way.
Keep each interval at a pace you can repeat for every round.
common_mistakes: Skipping the warm-up: cold sprinting is the main cause of hamstring strains in this drill.
Turning upright with straight legs: slows the turn and loads the knees.
Starting the first round flat out: later rounds collapse and the session loses its endurance value.
programming_notes: Shorter distances mean more turns and more change-of-direction work; longer distances mean more running speed.
complements: Mobility work for the hips and hamstrings afterwards.
video_title: The 300 Yard Shuttle Conditioning Drill

name: Side-Lying Hip Abduction
summary: A floor-based hip abduction lying on one side, the no-equipment way to train the gluteus medius and minimus directly.
why_this_exists: The hip-abduction machine and band versions need equipment. Lying on the side and lifting the top leg trains the same hip abduction against gravity, so the side glutes can be worked anywhere.
resistance_profile: Leg weight against gravity, hardest at the top of the lift. An ankle weight or a band around the knees or ankles adds resistance without changing the movement.
best_used_when: No machine or band is available and the side glutes need direct work.
A low-fatigue glute-medius exercise is wanted as a warm-up or finisher alongside squats and hinges.
less_suitable_when: High reps have become easy with leg weight alone and no ankle weight or band is available — the stimulus becomes mostly endurance.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time, as slightly more fullness at the upper side of the hips — modest unloaded, and only visible alongside heavier glute work and a low enough body-fat level.
limitations: Leg weight alone is light, so it needs an ankle weight or a band to keep progressing.
It is easy to roll the hips backward and turn the lift into a hip-flexor movement without noticing.
Each side is trained separately, which doubles the time per set.
technique_cues: Lie on one side with the hips stacked vertically, the bottom knee bent for balance and the top leg straight.
Turn the top toes slightly down so the heel leads, keeping the leg in line with the body or slightly behind it.
Lift the top leg toward the ceiling until the side of the hip works hard, without letting the hips roll back.
Lower slowly under control, without resting the leg between reps.
common_mistakes: Rolling the top hip backward: the leg swings forward and the hip flexors take over from the gluteus medius.
Lifting the leg as high as it will go: past a moderate height the trunk tilts and the side-bend replaces hip abduction.
Dropping the leg quickly: skips the lowering, which is half of each rep's glute-medius work.
programming_notes: Work to high reps first, then add an ankle weight or a band. A machine or cable abduction is the loaded progression once one is available.
complements: Heavier hip extension such as hip thrusts or squats, which train the gluteus maximus this movement leaves out.
evidence_notes: Distefano et al. (2009, Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy 39(7):532-540, PMID 19574661) measured surface EMG in 21 healthy, active subjects across 12 exercises: gluteus medius activity was highest in side-lying hip abduction (81% ± 42% MVIC), significantly greater than both hip clams, lunges and hops. EMG amplitude shows activation, not hypertrophy, and the wide spread shows how much individuals vary.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial: Side Lying Hip Abduction

name: Side Plank
summary: A bodyweight side-lying hold that trains the obliques by resisting sideways bending, the no-equipment counterpart to the suitcase carry.
why_this_exists: Every other obliques exercise in the library needs a cable, band, dumbbell or kettlebell. The side plank trains the same lateral-flexion resistance as a suitcase carry with bodyweight alone, at low fatigue, so the obliques can be worked directly anywhere.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight isometric hold, one side at a time. Difficulty rises with the lever — knees down is easiest, feet stacked is harder, and elevating the feet or holding a weight on the hip adds more.
best_used_when: No cable, band, dumbbell or kettlebell is available and the obliques need direct work.
A low-fatigue lateral-trunk exercise is wanted alongside heavier training, or as the bodyweight alternative to a suitcase carry.
less_suitable_when: Holds already last well over a minute per side — the stimulus has drifted toward endurance, and a harder lever or a loaded carry gives the obliques more to work against.
Shoulder pain limits weight-bearing on the bottom forearm.
mirror_effect: Modest shaping effect on its own — as an isometric hold it builds lateral-trunk strength and endurance more than oblique size, so any sharper definition at the sides of the waist depends mostly on body-fat level.
limitations: As an isometric hold, it plateaus once long holds become easy; progressing needs a longer lever, elevated feet or added load rather than more time.
The bottom shoulder carries much of the body's weight, which can limit the set before the obliques do.
Each side is trained separately, so a full set takes twice as long as a bilateral hold.
technique_cues: Lie on one side with the elbow directly under the shoulder and the forearm flat on the floor.
Stack the feet, or stagger them for a wider base, and keep the body in one straight line from head to heels.
Lift the hips until there is no sag at the waist, and hold them high for the whole set.
Brace the trunk and keep breathing steadily rather than holding the breath.
Hold for time, then switch sides and match the hold on the other side.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor: the trunk bends sideways instead of resisting it, which takes the load off the obliques.
Rolling the top hip forward or back: the body twists out of line and the hold turns into a partial front plank.
Shrugging into the bottom shoulder instead of pushing the floor away: the shoulder ends up taking the strain before the trunk is challenged.
programming_notes: Progress in this order: knees down, then feet staggered, then feet stacked, then feet elevated or a weight held on the hip. Once a long hold is easy, move to a harder lever or a loaded carry rather than holding longer.
complements: Rotation or anti-rotation work, such as a woodchop or Pallof press, which loads the obliques in a different direction.
video_title: How to do a Side Plank | Proper Form & Technique | NASM

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
summary: A unilateral horizontal pull that lets each side work through its own range and exposes side-to-side differences.
why_this_exists: A unilateral horizontal pull that lets each side work through its own range and exposes side-to-side differences.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile; free arm and slight trunk rotation allow more range and stretch than a bilateral row.
best_used_when: A strong mechanical-tension stimulus per side is wanted, with the free arm and slight trunk rotation allowing a bit more range and stretch than a bilateral row, or a lagging side needs to be brought level with the other.
less_suitable_when: The extra per-side volume needed to match a bilateral row's total work makes this a less efficient way to accumulate back-thickness volume when session time or fatigue budget is tight.
mirror_effect: Same thickness-building visible direction as a bilateral row, trained and visible one side at a time — useful for closing a visible left-right back-thickness difference the bilateral versions can't target directly.
limitations: Per-side volume needs to roughly double to match a bilateral row's total work, which makes this a slower way to accumulate back-thickness volume when time is limited.
The free hand and knee typically brace on a bench, and a wobbly or poorly positioned base can cap how much weight can be handled safely before the target muscles are the limiter.
technique_cues: Place one hand and the same-side knee on a flat bench, with the other foot on the floor and the back flat and roughly parallel to the floor.
Let the dumbbell hang straight below the shoulder, with a slight stretch through the side of the back.
Pull the dumbbell toward the hip by driving the elbow back close to the body, until the elbow passes the torso.
Lower under control until the arm is straight again, then finish all reps before switching sides.
common_mistakes: Twisting the torso open to lift the weight: momentum and trunk rotation move the dumbbell instead of the back.
Pulling the dumbbell toward the chest with the elbow flared: shifts the work toward the upper back and rear delt and away from the lats.
Shrugging the shoulder toward the ear at the top: the upper traps take over the end of the pull.
complements: A bilateral row or vertical pull.
video_title: How To: Dumbbell Bent-Over Row (Single-Arm)

name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
summary: A one-arm cable pulldown that trains each lat on its own and exposes side-to-side differences.
why_this_exists: Working one side at a time lets each lat be trained and compared on its own, and lets the elbow travel down along the side of the body without a bar fixing the hand position.
resistance_profile: Cable stack, one arm at a time, small load increments.
best_used_when: One side's lat lags or a two-arm pulldown feels uneven, or a pulldown is wanted with the elbow free to travel down the side of the body.
less_suitable_when: Session time is tight and a two-arm pulldown covers the same work in half the sets.
mirror_effect: Same width-building direction as other pulldowns, the under-arm flare viewed from behind, and it can help even out a visibly uneven side.
limitations: Each side is trained separately, which doubles the time per set compared with a two-arm pulldown.
It's easy to twist or lean the torso toward the working side to finish the pull, which shortens the lat's range without feeling like a technique breakdown.
technique_cues: Attach a single handle to a high pulley, sit (or kneel) facing the stack, and hold the handle with the arm straight overhead.
Let the shoulder rise slightly at the top so the lat stretches, keeping the torso tall.
Pull the elbow down and in toward the hip until the hand is beside the shoulder.
Let the arm rise under control until it is fully straight, then finish all reps before switching sides.
common_mistakes: Twisting the torso toward the working side: the trunk rotation does part of the pull and the lat works through less range.
Pulling with the hand and wrist instead of driving the elbow down: the biceps and forearm take over.
Stopping short of a straight arm at the top: misses the stretched part of the pull.
programming_notes: Start each set with the weaker side and match its reps on the stronger side.
complements: A rowing pattern.
video_title: How To Do Single Lat Pulldowns

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
summary: Bodyweight on one leg is often load enough, and training one side at a time closes side-to-side gaps a bilateral raise can hide.
why_this_exists: Bodyweight on one leg is often load enough on its own, and training one side at a time exposes and closes side-to-side gaps a bilateral raise can hide.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight-scaled.
best_used_when: A deep-stretch, slow-eccentric stimulus is wanted that bodyweight alone can deliver, or a lagging side needs to be brought level with the other through focused per-side volume.
less_suitable_when: Balance becomes the limiting factor before the calf is meaningfully fatigued, capping how much stimulus the set can actually deliver.
mirror_effect: Same general shape effect as a standing raise — the diamond bulge and width, viewed from behind or the side — but trained and visible one leg at a time, which is what makes it useful for closing a visible side-to-side size difference a bilateral raise can hide.
limitations: Bodyweight alone stops being an adequate stimulus for a well-trained lifter well before the calf is genuinely challenged, and there's no easy way to add load beyond holding a dumbbell.
Balance demand can become the limiting factor before the calf itself is meaningfully fatigued, especially for beginners.
technique_cues: Stand on one foot on a step with the heel hanging off the edge, holding something lightly for balance.
Keep the working knee straight.
Lower the heel as far as possible and pause in the stretch.
Rise as high as you can onto the ball of the foot.
common_mistakes: Bouncing at the bottom: tendon rebound replaces calf work.
Gripping the support hard enough to pull yourself up: the arms take load off the calf, so the set looks harder than the calf work it delivers.
Rolling onto the outside edge of the foot at the top: the ankle wobbles and the calf finishes the rep through a shorter, less stable range.
complements: A seated raise for the soleus.
video_title: Single Leg Body Weight Calf Raise

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
summary: A hip thrust on one leg with the upper back on a bench, the bodyweight progression that keeps the glute bridge's shortened-position stimulus challenging once two legs become easy.
why_this_exists: The glute bridge stops being challenging quickly, and the loaded hip thrust needs a barbell and a padded setup. Working one leg at a time puts roughly twice the load on each glute with nothing but a bench, so home and low-setup lifters can keep progressing direct glute work.
movement_patterns: single leg, upper back on a bench
resistance_profile: Bodyweight on one leg, hardest at the top with the hip fully extended. The range is longer than the floor bridge's because the upper back is raised on a bench, so the hip starts from more bend.
best_used_when: The two-leg glute bridge has become easy and no barbell or hip-thrust setup is available.
A low-fatigue glute finisher is wanted that also shows up left-right differences.
less_suitable_when: A heavy, progressively loaded glute stimulus is the goal and a barbell hip thrust is available.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and alongside other glute work, as fuller glutes from the side — the same shortened-position stimulus as the hip thrust, at bodyweight loads.
limitations: Loading beyond bodyweight is awkward on one leg; once bodyweight reps are easy, a loaded two-leg hip thrust is the next step.
Balance and keeping the pelvis level limit the set before the glute does for some lifters, especially early on.
Each side is trained separately, which doubles the time per set.
technique_cues: Sit with the lower edge of your shoulder blades on the bench, the working foot flat and roughly under the knee, and the other leg lifted.
Keep the ribs down and the chin tucked so the hip moves rather than the lower back.
Drive through the heel of the working leg until hip, knee and shoulder line up, and hold the top for a second.
Keep the pelvis level from side to side throughout the rep, then lower under control until the hip is just above the floor.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top: the spine extends instead of the hip, and the glute does less of the work.
Letting the free-leg side of the pelvis drop: the rep turns into a twist and the working glute unloads.
Working foot too far forward: the hamstrings take over, often cramping before the glute has done much.
programming_notes: Progress from the two-leg glute bridge: add a pause at the top, then move to this, then add a load on the working hip or switch to a barbell hip thrust when one is available. Start each set with the weaker side and match its reps on the stronger side.
complements: Glute work in the lengthened, hip-bent position, such as Romanian deadlifts or single-leg Romanian deadlifts.
video_title: Single leg hip thrust: shoulders on bench

name: Single-Leg Hop and Stick
summary: A small hop forward or sideways on one leg, landing and holding the landing still on the same leg.
why_this_exists: Badminton often ends a movement on one leg. Hopping and sticking the landing trains single-leg landing control and ankle and knee stability.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; hop distance and direction set the challenge.
best_used_when: Single-leg landing control and ankle stability are the goal, as part of a warm-up or power block.
less_suitable_when: Single-leg balance on a flat floor is not yet steady; balance work comes first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds single-leg landing control.
limitations: It needs good single-leg balance first, and the landing loads one ankle and knee at a time.
Distance has to stay small until every landing is stuck.
technique_cues: Stand on one leg with a soft knee and the hips slightly back.
Hop a short distance forward or sideways.
Land on the same leg with a soft knee, the knee over the toes, and the hips back.
Hold the landing still for two to three seconds before the next hop.
common_mistakes: The knee caving inward on landing: the main knee-injury risk the drill is meant to train against.
Hopping too far to stick it: wobbling landings mean the distance is ahead of the control.
Landing on the heel with a straight knee: the joints take the impact instead of the muscles.
programming_notes: Start with small forward hops, then add sideways and diagonal directions.
complements: Single-leg calf raises for ankle strength.
video_title: Single-Leg Forward Hop & Stick

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
summary: A one-leg hip hinge with a dumbbell, loading the hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position while the standing hip controls balance and rotation.
why_this_exists: Every other hinge in the library is bilateral. Training one leg at a time exposes and evens out side-to-side differences, needs only a single dumbbell, and reaches a strong hamstring and glute stretch with far less load on the spine than a barbell RDL.
resistance_profile: One free weight, usually held opposite the standing leg; hardest at the bottom stretch. A kettlebell works the same way. A band stood on under the standing foot gets heavier as the hips straighten, so it loads the top of the hinge more than the stretched bottom.
best_used_when: A hinge is wanted with only a single dumbbell, or with much less spinal load than a barbell RDL.
One side's hamstrings or glutes lag behind, or the hips feel uneven under two-leg hinging.
less_suitable_when: Balance on one leg is still unreliable — sets end on balance, not on the hamstrings.
Maximal hamstring loading is the goal; a two-leg RDL moves far more weight.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fuller hamstrings and lower glutes from the side and back, and can help even out a visibly uneven side — as a lighter, balance-limited hinge its effect is usually smaller than a heavy two-leg hinge's.
limitations: Balance usually gives out before the hamstrings are fatigued, especially early on, which limits how hard a set can be pushed.
Load is limited to what one hand can hold and one leg can balance, so it can't match a two-leg hinge's loading ceiling.
The free leg's hip tends to rotate open toward the ceiling, which changes the movement without obviously feeling wrong.
technique_cues: Stand on one leg with a soft knee and hold the dumbbell in the opposite hand.
Hinge forward from the hip, letting the free leg travel straight back so the torso and back leg move as one line.
Keep both hips square to the floor, with the back foot's toes pointing down.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in the standing leg's hamstring with a flat back, then drive the hip forward to stand.
Keep the dumbbell close to the standing leg throughout.
common_mistakes: Hip opening so the back leg and pelvis rotate toward the ceiling: the hinge becomes a twist and the standing-leg hamstring loses its stretch.
Bending the standing knee more on the way down: it turns into a single-leg squat and the hamstring stretch shrinks.
Rounding the back to reach lower: depth should stop where a flat back stops.
Rushing reps to stay balanced: speed replaces control and cuts short the lowering phase, where most of the hamstring work happens.
programming_notes: Lightly hold a fixed support (a rack or wall) with the free hand until balance stops ending sets, so the hamstrings rather than balance set the limit. Start each set with the weaker side.
Band version: stand on the middle of a band with the working foot and hold both ends, then hinge on that leg. A shorter grip on the band adds resistance.
complements: Knee-flexion hamstring work such as seated or lying leg curls, which load the hamstrings at the knee rather than the hip.
overlaps_with: bulgarian-split-squat-hip-dominant (hips module) — also single-leg and glute/hamstring-biased, but a split squat with much more knee bend rather than a hinge.
video_title: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift (1 Dumbbell) | Exercise Technique Library

name: Sissy Squat
summary: A bodyweight knee-dominant squat where the heels rise, the knees travel far forward and the body leans back in one line from knee to shoulder.
why_this_exists: Most bodyweight quad options in the library are lunges and split squats. The sissy squat loads the quads through deep knee bend with the hips kept straight, giving a hard quad stimulus with nothing but bodyweight and something to hold for balance.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, hardest at the bottom with the knees fully bent and the body leaning furthest back. Holding a weight to the chest adds load once bodyweight is easy.
best_used_when: The quads need direct work and no weights or leg extension machine are available.
A deep-knee-bend quad exercise is wanted alongside squats or lunges.
less_suitable_when: Deep knee bend under load aggravates the knees — a leg extension through a comfortable range is gentler.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and alongside other quad work, as fuller quads above the knee — a supporting contribution at bodyweight loads.
limitations: It puts high load on the front of the knee in deep flexion, which some knees don't tolerate.
Balance and confidence limit the first sessions more than the quads do, so holding a support is usually needed at first.
Loading beyond bodyweight is limited to a weight held at the chest.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet hip width apart and hold a rack, door frame or post with one hand for balance.
Rise onto the balls of the feet and push the knees forward while leaning back, keeping knees, hips and shoulders in one straight line.
Lower as far as the knees comfortably allow without bending at the hips.
Drive the knees back to return to standing, keeping the hips straight all the way up.
common_mistakes: Bending at the hips on the way down: turns it into a partial squat and takes the stretch off the quads.
Going deeper than the knees tolerate on the first sessions: the knee load is high and needs building up gradually.
Pulling on the support to stand up: the arms do the work the quads are meant to do.
programming_notes: Start with a partial range while holding a support, deepen over sessions, and only add a weight at the chest once the full range is controlled.
complements: A hip-dominant movement such as a Romanian deadlift or hip thrust.
video_title: How to Do the Sissy Squat (Complete Beginner Tutorial)

name: Sleeper Stretch (Shoulder Rotation)
summary: Lying on one side with the bottom arm bent to 90 degrees in front, gently pressing the forearm toward the floor to stretch shoulder rotation.
why_this_exists: Overhead hitting can stiffen the shoulder's inward rotation over time, especially on the racket arm. This stretch targets that rotation directly.
primary_targets: back of the shoulder (internal rotation range)
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the top hand sets the depth.
best_used_when: Inward rotation of the racket shoulder feels limited, after play or on rest days.
less_suitable_when: The front of the shoulder pinches or the shoulder is already injured; a towel stretch behind the back or professional advice may suit better.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds shoulder rotation range.
limitations: Pressing too hard can irritate the front of the shoulder, so it should stay gentle.
Rolling too far onto the shoulder blade takes the stretch away.
technique_cues: Lie on the side of the shoulder being stretched, with the head supported.
Bend that elbow to 90 degrees with the upper arm straight out in front at shoulder height.
Use the top hand to gently press the forearm toward the floor.
Stop at a mild stretch at the back of the shoulder and breathe slowly.
common_mistakes: Pressing hard into pain at the front of the shoulder.
Lifting the elbow off the floor or moving the upper arm.
Rolling backwards off the shoulder.
programming_notes: A towel held behind the back, pulled upward by the top hand, is a standing alternative.
complements: The cross-body stretch for the back of the shoulder.
video_title: The Sleeper Stretch - Walkthrough

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
summary: A barbell on a fixed vertical rail, removing the spotter requirement and most of the balance demand of a free barbell bench press.
why_this_exists: A barbell constrained to a fixed vertical or near-vertical rail, which removes the need for a spotter and most of the balance demand of a free barbell bench press while still allowing a fixed-bar loading path.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical/near-vertical rail path; free-weight-like load curve.
best_used_when: A mid-chest press is wanted pushed past what could be handled unspotted with a free barbell, training closer to true failure or running rest-pause sets on a heavy, barbell-style press.
less_suitable_when: The fixed rail's path doesn't match a user's natural press arc, which can shift stress onto the shoulder joint rather than the chest.
mirror_effect: Same mid-chest mass and depth direction as a free-weight flat bench press, since the fixed rail changes balance demand, not which muscle carries the load.
limitations: The fixed rail path doesn't match every lifter's natural press arc, and a mismatch can shift stress onto the shoulder joint rather than the chest.
Removing free-weight balance demand also removes the stabilizer training a barbell version provides, so strength here transfers only partially back to a free bench press.
technique_cues: Set a flat bench under the bar so it comes down to the lower chest, and lie back with the shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it by rotating it off the hooks.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest with the elbows tucked to roughly 45 degrees.
Press back up until the arms are nearly straight, with the safety stops set just above the chest.
common_mistakes: Bench positioned so the bar lands on the neck or upper chest: the fixed path forces an awkward press line.
Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress at the bottom of the press.
Bouncing the bar off the chest: the rebound skips the hardest part of the rep.
complements: A fly variation or an incline press selected for a distinct role.
evidence_notes: Same mid-chest evidence as flat-barbell-bench-press — see that record's evidence_notes.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial: Smith Machine Bench Press

name: Smith Machine Bulgarian Split Squat
summary: Fixing the bar to a vertical rail removes most of the balance demand that limits the free-weight version, letting the stimulus reach the muscles rather than being capped by wobble.
why_this_exists: Fixing the bar to a vertical rail removes most of the balance demand that otherwise limits a free-weight Bulgarian split squat, directly addressing the stability issue that makes the free version hard for many users.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical rail path.
best_used_when: Balance, not leg strength, is what's limiting the free-weight version — fixing the bar path lets the actual growth stimulus reach the quads and glutes instead of being capped by wobble.
less_suitable_when: The fixed rail's path doesn't match a user's natural lunge arc, which can feel awkward and shift stress away from the target muscles.
mirror_effect: Same per-leg quad visible direction as the free-weight version, with the fixed rail reducing how much balance limits the load before the quads do.
limitations: The fixed rail path doesn't always match a lifter's natural lunge arc, and a mismatch can feel awkward or shift stress away from the target muscles.
Removing the balance demand also removes some of the stabilizer and coordination training the free-weight version provides.
technique_cues: Set the bar on the upper back, place the back foot on a bench behind you, and step the front foot forward so it's a little in front of the bar.
Unrack the bar and keep most of the weight on the front foot.
Lower straight down until the back knee nearly touches the floor, with the front knee tracking in line with the toes.
Drive up through the whole front foot, finish all reps, then switch legs.
common_mistakes: Front foot too close to the bench: the knee travels far forward and the heel lifts.
Pushing up off the back foot: the work shifts away from the front leg.
Not setting the safety stops: a failed rep has nowhere to go on the fixed rail.
complements: A bilateral squat or press.
video_title: SMITH MACHINE BULGARIAN SPLIT SQUAT TUTORIAL

name: Smith Machine Incline Press
summary: A barbell on a fixed vertical rail, removing the spotter requirement and most of the balance demand of a free barbell incline press.
why_this_exists: A barbell constrained to a fixed vertical or near-vertical rail, which removes the need for a spotter and most of the balance demand of a free barbell incline press while still allowing a fixed-bar loading path.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical/near-vertical rail path; free-weight-like load curve.
best_used_when: An upper-chest set is wanted pushed past what could safely be handled unspotted with a free barbell, training closer to true failure on a heavy, barbell-style press.
less_suitable_when: The fixed rail's path doesn't match a user's natural press arc, which can shift stress onto the shoulder joint rather than the chest.
mirror_effect: Same upper-chest shelf effect as a free-weight incline press, from the same incline angle.
limitations: The fixed rail path doesn't match every lifter's natural press arc, and a mismatch can load the shoulder joint rather than the chest.
Setting the bench angle and rack height correctly takes more fiddling than a standard incline bench, adding real setup time.
technique_cues: Set an incline bench under the bar so the bar comes down to the upper chest, and lie back with the shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it by rotating it off the hooks.
Lower the bar under control to the upper chest, with the elbows angled slightly below shoulder height.
Press back up until the arms are nearly straight, and set the safety stops just above the chest before starting.
common_mistakes: Bench positioned so the bar lands on the neck or mid-chest: the press line misses the upper chest and can strain the shoulders.
Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees: raises shoulder stress at the bottom of the press.
Bouncing the bar off the chest: the rebound skips the stretched part of the rep.
complements: A fly variation or a free-weight press with a distinct role.
evidence_notes: Same upper-chest evidence as incline-dumbbell-press (Chaves et al., 2020, PMC7449336; Rodríguez-Ridao et al., 2020, PMC7579505) — the incline angle is what the evidence is about, not the fixed rail.
video_title: Incline Smith Machine Bench Press - Exercise Tutorial

name: Smith Machine Romanian Deadlift
summary: Fixing the bar to a vertical rail keeps it automatically close to the body, easing the technical cue beginners struggle with most in a free-bar RDL.
why_this_exists: Fixing the bar to a vertical rail keeps it automatically close to the body through the hinge, which is the technical cue beginners most often struggle to hold with a free bar; this makes the pattern easier to groove before adding a free bar. Unlike a row, an RDL's correct bar path is already close to vertical, so the fixed rail helps rather than fights it.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical rail path; free-weight-like load curve.
best_used_when: The RDL's stretch-mediated stimulus is wanted while still learning to control the hinge, since the fixed rail removes the bar-path variable that most often breaks technique down under load.
less_suitable_when: Hip-to-torso proportions need more depth than the fixed rail allows, or the bar needs to accommodate individual leverages the way a free bar can.
mirror_effect: Same visible direction as the free-bar Romanian deadlift — combined hamstring and glute fullness viewed from behind — since the fixed rail changes how the movement is learned, not which muscles end up carrying the load.
limitations: The fixed rail path doesn't match every lifter's natural hip-hinge arc, which can force compensations at the knees or hips instead of removing them.
Once the bar-path-control training wheels are no longer needed, there's little further benefit over the free-bar version, so it's mainly useful as a stepping stone rather than a long-term staple.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet about hip width apart under the bar, holding it just outside the thighs with an overhand grip.
Unrack the bar and set a slight bend in the knees that stays the same throughout.
Push the hips back, letting the bar slide down the thighs on the rail, until a strong hamstring stretch is felt with a flat back.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, then rack the bar at the end of the set.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back to get the bar lower: depth should stop where a flat back stops.
Bending the knees more on the way down: turns it into a squat and the stretch on the hamstrings and glutes shrinks.
Standing too far in front of or behind the rail: the fixed path drags the bar away from the body or into the shins.
complements: hip-thrust
overlaps_with: romanian-deadlift (hamstrings module) — distinguish by how much the setup controls the bar path.
evidence_notes: Same evidence as the free-bar romanian-deadlift (hamstrings module) — see that record's evidence_notes for the general stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature. The fixed rail changes bar-path control, not the hip position the stretch claim is actually about.
video_title: How To Do A SMITH MACHINE ROMANIAN DEADLIFT | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Smith Machine Shoulder Press
summary: A barbell on a fixed vertical rail, removing most of the balance and bracing demand of a standing or seated overhead press.
why_this_exists: A barbell constrained to a fixed vertical or near-vertical rail, which removes most of the balance and bracing demand of a standing or seated barbell overhead press while still allowing a fixed-bar loading path.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical/near-vertical rail path; free-weight-like load curve.
best_used_when: A front-delt set is wanted pushed closer to true failure than could safely be handled unspotted with a free barbell.
less_suitable_when: The fixed rail's path doesn't match a user's natural press arc, which can shift stress onto the joint rather than the muscle.
mirror_effect: Same visible direction as the free-weight overhead press — front-delt roundness and mass — since the fixed rail changes stability demand, not which muscle ends up carrying the load.
limitations: The fixed rail path doesn't match every lifter's natural press arc, and pressing straight up rather than slightly forward can load the shoulder joint uncomfortably for some.
It removes the stabilizer training that a free-weight press provides, so strength built here transfers only partially back to an unassisted press.
technique_cues: Set a bench with an upright back under the bar so it comes down just in front of the face, and sit with the back flat against the pad.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it by rotating it off the hooks.
Lower the bar under control to about chin or upper-chest height.
Press back up until the arms are nearly straight, with the safety stops set just above the shoulders.
common_mistakes: Bench placed so the bar comes down onto the head or behind it: the fixed path forces the shoulders into an awkward position.
Arching the lower back off the pad to finish reps: turns it into an incline press.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the top: the upper traps take over the end of the press.
complements: Side- and rear-delt work.
video_title: Smith Machine Shoulder Press | Proper Form Tutorial for Shoulder Strength

name: Smith Machine Squat
summary: A fixed vertical bar path removing balance and bracing demand, well suited to training closer to failure without a spotter.
why_this_exists: A fixed vertical bar path that removes the balance and bracing demand of a free barbell squat, letting a user train closer to failure without a spotter.
resistance_profile: Fixed vertical rail path; free-weight-like load curve.
best_used_when: A quad-and-glute set is wanted pushed closer to true failure than could safely be handled unspotted with a free barbell.
less_suitable_when: The fixed vertical path doesn't match a user's natural squat path, which can shift stress onto the knees or lower back rather than the target muscles.
mirror_effect: Same visible direction as the free-weight back squat — overall front-of-thigh and glute mass — since the fixed rail changes balance demand, not which muscles carry the load.
limitations: The fixed vertical path doesn't match every lifter's natural squat arc, and a mismatch can shift stress onto the knees or lower back instead of the target muscles.
Removing the balance and bracing demand also removes the stabilizer training a free-weight squat provides, so strength here transfers only partially back to an unassisted squat.
technique_cues: Set the bar on the upper back and place the feet slightly in front of the bar, about shoulder width apart.
Unrack by rotating the bar off the hooks, and brace the trunk before each rep.
Squat down until the thighs are about parallel to the floor or as deep as the back stays flat, keeping the knees in line with the toes.
Drive up through the whole foot to standing, and rotate the bar back onto the hooks at the end of the set.
common_mistakes: Feet directly under the bar: the fixed path pushes the knees far forward and the heels may lift.
Knees caving inward on the way up: shifts the load away from the quads and stresses the knee.
Not setting the safety stops: the fixed path still needs stops set just below the bottom position in case a rep fails.
complements: A single-joint knee-extension movement.
video_title: Exercise Tutorial: Smith Machine Squat

name: Split-Squat Jump
summary: An explosive jump from a split stance, switching legs in the air and landing softly in the opposite split.
why_this_exists: Badminton lunges and push-offs happen from a split stance. Jumping from that position trains fast, powerful leg drive and a controlled landing with only bodyweight.
movement_patterns: split stance, switching legs in the air
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the landing absorbs more force than the jump produces, so landing control sets the limit.
best_used_when: Explosive leg drive from a split stance is wanted with no equipment, early in a session while fresh.
less_suitable_when: Knees or ankles are sore, or a soft, balanced landing is not yet reliable; split squats and lunges build the base first.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds explosive leg drive and landing control rather than muscle size.
limitations: Landing force is high, so knee or ankle discomfort, or a hard floor, limits how many quality reps are possible.
Balance on landing usually fails before power does when learning it.
technique_cues: Start in a split stance with the front knee bent, back knee just off the floor, and torso upright.
Drive hard through both feet and swing the arms up to jump straight up.
Switch legs in the air so the opposite leg lands in front.
Land softly on the balls of the feet into the same split depth, then pause or go straight into the next rep.
common_mistakes: Landing stiff-legged: the knees and ankles take the impact instead of the muscles absorbing it.
Front knee collapsing inward on landing: loads the knee awkwardly and is the main injury risk of the drill.
Rushing reps once tired: jumps get lower and landings sloppier, which turns power work into conditioning.
programming_notes: Learn it with a pause in the split after every landing before moving to continuous reps.
complements: A heavy single-leg strength exercise such as a split squat.
video_title: How to Do the Split Squat Jump

name: Standing Cable Hip Flexion
summary: Trains hip flexion under load, which most lower-body routines leave entirely to stretching.
why_this_exists: Trains hip flexion under load, which most lower-body routines leave entirely to stretching.
resistance_profile: Cable stack.
best_used_when: Hip-flexor strength and size are wanted for running, kicking, or knee-raise work — a specific, secondary role rather than a routine staple.
less_suitable_when: Session priorities haven't yet covered the larger movements that deliver most of a lower-body routine's growth stimulus.
mirror_effect: Minor and specific — the hip flexors are small, so any visible effect shows up as slightly more definition at the front of the hip and top of the thigh rather than a noticeable size change; this is more a functional than an aesthetic addition.
limitations: The hip flexors are a small muscle group relative to most compound lower-body work, so this movement adds only a minor growth stimulus on its own.
Anterior hip or lower-back symptoms can flare with hip-flexor-dominant work in general, making this one to reduce or drop rather than push through if that occurs.
technique_cues: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, stand facing away from the stack, and hold a support for balance.
Stand tall on the non-working leg with the working leg straight or slightly bent behind the body.
Drive the working knee up and forward until the thigh is about level with the hip, keeping the torso upright.
Lower the leg back under control to the start, then finish all reps before switching sides.
common_mistakes: Leaning the torso back to lift the knee higher: the lower back arches and takes over from the hip flexors.
Swinging the leg up with momentum: the hip flexors miss the controlled lift the exercise is for.
Letting the cable pull the leg back fast: the stretched end is uncontrolled, where the front of the hip is most exposed.
complements: Hip-extension work and trunk anti-extension work.
video_title: How To: Standing Cable Hip Flexion

name: Standing Calf Raise
summary: The straight-knee position lets the gastrocnemius contribute, the raise most responsible for calf width and shape.
why_this_exists: The straight-knee position lets the gastrocnemius contribute, which a seated raise limits — this is the raise most responsible for calf width and the diamond shape the muscle makes when flexed.
resistance_profile: A dedicated machine or a barbell in a Smith machine both give a fixed path; holding dumbbells while standing on a block or plate is the free-weight equivalent and needs no machine at all.
best_used_when: A heavier, mechanical-tension-driven stimulus for the gastrocnemius is wanted, with a full stretch at the bottom and a hard, paused contraction at the top. Turning the toes slightly out or in shifts a little more emphasis to the inner or outer head respectively.
less_suitable_when: The bottom stretch gets cut short by bouncing onto the toes quickly, trading away most of the growth stimulus for rep count.
mirror_effect: Consistent training here tends to show up as the diamond-shaped bulge and overall width of the calf, most visible from behind or the side when the muscle is flexed with the foot pointed — this is the raise most people mean when they picture a bigger calf. It doesn't change the lower leg's outline from the front the way a shin-focused movement does; it's specifically the back-of-leg shape.
limitations: Calf size is notoriously slow to respond even with consistent, well- executed training — genetics set a large part of the ceiling here more than with most muscle groups.
The range of motion quietly shrinks under fatigue or heavy load, since bouncing off the bottom stretch is an easy way to move more weight without feeling like technique broke down.
The dumbbell/block version caps load at what can be held and balanced on, which limits the mechanical-tension ceiling well below what a loaded machine allows.
technique_cues: Stand with the balls of your feet on the platform edge and the knees straight but not locked.
Lower the heels as far as possible and pause briefly in the stretch.
Rise as high as you can onto your toes and pause at the top.
Keep the knees straight throughout so the gastrocnemius stays involved.
common_mistakes: Bouncing out of the bottom: the Achilles tendon does the work and the range shrinks.
Bending the knees to help lift the load: shifts work to the legs and away from the calf.
Letting the range shrink as the set goes on under heavy load: the last reps skip the stretch and the top squeeze, where most of the calf work happens.
programming_notes: The toe-angle inner/outer head-bias cue now has real hypertrophy evidence behind it — see evidence_notes — though it was only tested with a machine calf raise, not this record's free-standing version.

Donkey variation: the same straight-knee raise done hinged forward at the hips with the hands on a support and the load over the hips, on a donkey calf machine or with a hip belt. It trains the same movement and is an option when load on the shoulders is uncomfortable.
complements: A bent-knee raise, which covers the soleus.
evidence_notes: Direct hypertrophy trial evidence, stronger than a coaching cue: Nunes et al. (2020, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 34(8): 2347-2351) trained 22 men for 9 weeks on a seated horizontal leg-press calf raise with the foot pointed outward, inward, or forward. Foot-pointed-outward produced significantly more medial (inner) gastrocnemius growth (+8.4% vs. +3.8% for foot-pointed-inward); foot-pointed-inward produced significantly more lateral (outer) growth (+9.1% vs. +5.5% for foot-pointed- outward). This matches this record's toes-out-to-inner, toes-in-to-outer framing. Caveats: it's one trial, in a leg-press calf raise rather than the standing free-weight/machine version this record describes, and the difference between conditions was modest relative to the overall growth every condition produced — the toe angle shifts emphasis, it doesn't isolate a head to the exclusion of the other. Evidence quality: moderate-to-strong — a real hypertrophy trial, the same tier as the triceps overhead- extension claim in the arms module, though from a single study rather than a replicated body of work.
video_title: How To: Standing Calf (BM)

name: Standing Quad Stretch
summary: Standing on one leg and holding the other foot behind the body to stretch the front of the thigh.
why_this_exists: The quads work hard in every lunge and landing. This is a quick quad stretch that needs nothing but a wall to hold for balance.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; tucking the pelvis deepens the stretch.
best_used_when: A quick quad stretch is wanted after play or training.
less_suitable_when: Bending the knee fully is painful; the couch stretch with padding or a lower range may suit better.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds quad range.
limitations: Balance can limit it, so holding a wall helps.
It is gentler on the hip flexors than the couch stretch.
technique_cues: Stand tall next to a wall and hold it with one hand.
Bend one knee and hold that foot or ankle behind the body.
Keep the knees close together and gently tuck the pelvis under until the front of the thigh stretches.
Stand tall and breathe slowly, then switch legs.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back: the stretch is lost.
Letting the bent knee drift forward or out to the side.
Pulling the heel hard into the buttock and straining the knee.
programming_notes: A strap around the foot helps if the foot is hard to reach.
complements: The couch stretch for a deeper hip-flexor stretch.
video_title: How To Do A STANDING QUAD STRETCH | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Static Lunge
summary: A fixed-stance, in-place lunge removing the stepping coordination of a walking or reverse lunge.
why_this_exists: A fixed stance lunge performed in place, without stepping, which removes the stepping coordination of a walking or reverse lunge and lets effort go directly into the working leg.
resistance_profile: A barbell on the back allows the heaviest load on a fixed path; dumbbells at the sides are a lighter, more accessible setup with independent arms; a shouldered sandbag adds a shifting, unstable load that raises the trunk-bracing demand beyond either. Bodyweight alone is the entry point and the no-equipment version.
best_used_when: A controlled, per-leg mechanical-tension stimulus is wanted without the extra coordination demand of moving between reps.
less_suitable_when: The higher-coordination, more athletic carryover a walking lunge provides is wanted instead.
mirror_effect: Same per-leg quad mass direction as a split squat, without the stepping coordination demand — the visible effect on the thigh is the same, just easier to load consistently.
limitations: The stationary stance still demands real hip and ankle mobility to keep the front knee tracking well, and poor mobility can push stress onto the knee joint.
Load options are somewhat limited compared to a bilateral squat — grip and trunk-bracing demand from a shouldered or side-held load cap how heavy this can go before those become the limiter.
technique_cues: Take a long split stance with the feet about hip width apart side to side and the back heel raised, holding the load: a barbell on the upper back, dumbbells at the sides, or hands on the hips.
Lower straight down by bending both knees until the back knee nearly touches the floor, keeping the torso upright.
Keep the front foot flat and the front knee tracking in line with the toes.
Drive up through the whole front foot, stay in the same stance for every rep, then switch legs.
common_mistakes: Feet in one line, as on a tightrope: balance fails and the hips twist, so the set ends before the legs are worked.
Pushing up mainly off the back leg: shifts the work away from the front leg's quads.
The front heel lifting at the bottom: the load moves onto the toes and the front of the knee.
programming_notes: Bodyweight version: the same split-stance squat with the hands on the hips or held in front. Once high reps are easy, slow the lowering or add a pause at the bottom before reaching for weights.
complements: A bilateral squat or press.
video_title: Stationary Lunge - HASfit Lunge Exercise Demonstration - Dumbbell Lunge - Barbell Lunge Workout

name: Step-Up
summary: A single-leg step onto a box or bench, driving through the front foot to stand on top, trainable with bodyweight or dumbbells.
why_this_exists: Most single-leg quad work in the library is a lunge or split squat. Stepping onto a bench or sturdy box loads one leg at a time with nothing but bodyweight, with little skill and little soreness, and dumbbells extend it when available.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, or dumbbells held at the sides once bodyweight is easy, hardest as the front leg starts to push from the bottom. A higher box increases the knee and hip bend at the start; a knee-height box suits most lifters.
best_used_when: Single-leg leg work is wanted with only a bench, step or sturdy chair.
A single-leg exercise with little skill and little soreness is wanted alongside squats or leg presses.
less_suitable_when: Heavy loading is the goal — balance on one leg limits the load well before the legs do.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time and alongside other leg work, as fuller quads and glutes — a supporting stimulus at bodyweight loads.
limitations: Pushing off the back foot is easy to do without noticing, and it takes much of the work away from the front leg.
Each side is trained separately, which doubles the time per set.
It needs a stable box or bench of a suitable height.
technique_cues: Stand facing a knee-height bench or box and place the whole working foot on top.
Lean the torso slightly forward and drive through the front heel to stand up on the box.
Bring the back foot up lightly beside the front one without pushing off the floor with it.
Lower slowly under control on the same leg, touching the trailing foot to the floor before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Pushing off the back foot: the trailing leg does the work and the front leg's quads barely get loaded.
Dropping down off the box: skips the controlled lowering, which is half of each rep's leg work.
Front knee caving inward on the way up: shifts the load away from the quads and stresses the knee.
programming_notes: Work the weaker leg first and match its reps on the stronger side. Progress from bodyweight to dumbbells at the sides, then to a slightly higher box.
complements: A hip-hinge movement such as a Romanian deadlift.
video_title: How to Do Bench Step Ups for Quads & Glutes

name: Stiff-Leg Deadlift
summary: Keeping the knees much straighter than an RDL pushes nearly all the stretch and tension onto the hamstrings specifically.
why_this_exists: Keeping the knees much straighter than an RDL removes most of the knee's contribution to the hinge, which pushes nearly all of the stretch and tension onto the hamstrings specifically, at the cost of the load capacity and lower-back sparing the RDL's knee bend provides.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, minimal knee bend.
best_used_when: The most hamstring-isolated stretch-mediated stimulus this movement family offers is specifically wanted, and the added lower-back demand the straighter legs bring can be tolerated.
less_suitable_when: Lower-back fatigue or hamstring flexibility limits how straight the legs can safely stay, or the RDL's higher load capacity and more balanced glute-hamstring stimulus is wanted instead.
mirror_effect: Where an RDL adds hamstring and glute mass together, this tends to show up as hamstring fullness specifically — the back of the thigh filling out on its own, with less glute involvement than an RDL gives, since the straighter knee shifts more of the work there.
limitations: The near-straight knee removes most of the lower back's usual mechanical advantage in a hinge, so lower-back load per pound lifted is higher than an RDL's.

Load capacity is meaningfully lower than an RDL's, since hamstring and lower-back tolerance for the straighter-leg stretch position becomes the limiting factor before the hamstrings' full strength does.
Poor hamstring flexibility can force the back to round to reach depth, which defeats the point of the exercise and adds spinal risk instead of hamstring stimulus.
technique_cues: Stand with the feet about hip width apart, holding the bar or dumbbells in front of the thighs with the knees almost straight but not locked.
Keep the knees in that nearly straight position for the whole rep.
Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back, letting the weight travel down close to the legs, as far as the hamstrings allow without the back rounding.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, keeping the back flat throughout.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back to reach lower: the spine takes the load the hamstrings are meant to take, the main injury risk.
Letting the knees bend more as the set goes on: it turns into a Romanian deadlift and the hamstring stretch shrinks.
Letting the weight drift away from the legs: the lower back takes more load at the bottom.
complements: A knee-flexion-dominant leg curl or a shortened-position movement such as the hip thrust.
evidence_notes: Same general stretch-mediated hypertrophy grounding as romanian-deadlift above — see that record's evidence_notes. No study specific to the stiff-leg deadlift was located.
video_title: How To: Barbell Stiff-Leg Deadlift

name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
summary: A lat-focused, cable-based option with the elbow mostly fixed, a stretch-mediated stimulus independent of grip or biceps endurance.
why_this_exists: A lat-focused option with the elbow mostly fixed, which may be useful when elbow flexors fatigue before the lats in pulldowns and rows.
resistance_profile: Constant cable tension. A band anchored overhead (for example looped over a pull-up bar) stretches further as the hands approach the thighs, so it gets heavier through the pull and is hardest at the end, in the shortened position, unlike the even tension of a cable.
best_used_when: A stretch-mediated, lat-isolated stimulus that doesn't depend on grip or biceps endurance is wanted, often as a pre-exhaust warm-up or a finisher after heavier pulling.
less_suitable_when: Back growth is currently limited by total heavy-pulling volume rather than needing more lat isolation — a compound pull delivers more overall stimulus per set.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fullness along the lower, outer edge of the lat — the "sweep" that flares out near the sides of the torso — since that's the stretched position this movement isolates, distinct from the more general width a vertical pull builds.
limitations: Load ceiling is inherently modest — the fixed-elbow, straight-arm path is a mechanically weaker position than a bent-arm pull, so this can't substitute for a heavy compound pull's overall stimulus.
It's easy for the shoulders to hike up or the movement to turn into a shrug-like motion under fatigue, which shifts the stimulus away from the lats.
technique_cues: Face a high pulley, hinge slightly forward at the hips, and hold a bar or rope with nearly straight arms.
Pull the bar down in an arc to your thighs, keeping a slight, fixed bend in the elbows.
Keep the shoulders down, away from the ears.
Let the arms rise back up until the lats stretch, without the torso moving.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows to push the bar down: it turns into a triceps pushdown.
Shrugging the shoulders up: shifts the stimulus away from the lats.
Rocking the torso to move the weight: the hips and body sway start the movement instead of the lats.
programming_notes: Band version: loop a band over a pull-up bar or a high door anchor, step back and pull the ends down to the thighs with straight arms. Stepping further back adds resistance.
complements: A vertical or horizontal pull.
evidence_notes: No study specific to the straight-arm pulldown or lat length was located. The "stretch-mediated" framing draws on the broader stretch-mediated hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld & Grgic (2020, SAGE Open Medicine) found full/longer-ROM training tends to match or beat partial-ROM training that avoids the stretch, and Wolf et al. (2023, International Journal of Strength and Conditioning, meta-analysis) found full and partial ROM produced broadly similar hypertrophy, with a possible but inconclusive advantage for partials at long muscle lengths. A later trial (Wolf et al., 2025, PubMed 39959841) found lengthened partials produced hypertrophy similar to, not clearly greater than, full ROM — so this is a well-supported general direction, not a settled, exercise-specific magnitude claim.
video_title: Cable Straight Arm Pulldown - Proper Form & Technique [4K]

name: Lying Strap Hamstring Stretch
summary: Lying on the back and raising one straight leg with a strap or towel around the foot to stretch the back of the thigh.
why_this_exists: Lunging for low shots needs comfortable hamstring range. Lying down keeps the back supported so the stretch stays in the hamstrings.
movement_patterns: lying straight-leg raise with a strap
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the strap sets how far the leg is drawn up.
best_used_when: Hamstring range is wanted after training or on a rest day, with the back fully supported.
less_suitable_when: The stretch causes tingling down the leg or pain behind the knee; ease off or stop.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds hamstring range.
limitations: Pulling the leg too high bends the knee or lifts the hips, which ends the stretch rather than deepening it.
It needs a strap, towel or band.
technique_cues: Lie on the back with one leg straight on the floor and the strap looped around the other foot.
Raise the strapped leg with the knee straight until a stretch is felt behind the thigh.
Keep the other leg flat and the hips level on the floor.
Relax the leg into the strap and breathe slowly; draw it a little higher only as the stretch eases.
common_mistakes: Bending the knee to get the leg higher: the hamstring stretch is reduced.
