Lifting the hips or the other leg off the floor.
Yanking the strap instead of easing into the stretch.
programming_notes: A slight knee bend is fine if the back of the knee feels strained.
complements: The figure-four glute stretch in the same lying position.
video_title: Hamstring Stretch with a Strap, Supine - Ask Doctor Jo

name: Suitcase Carry
summary: Loads one side at a time so the trunk resists lateral pull, while also training grip — a stability-and-durability tool.
why_this_exists: Loads one side at a time so the trunk resists being pulled sideways, while also training grip.
resistance_profile: Free-weight, whole-body fatigue cost.
best_used_when: Standing trunk-control work that carries over to real-world single-side loading is the goal — a stability-and-durability role more than a primary hypertrophy driver.
less_suitable_when: Grip fails long before the trunk does, ending the set before the intended stimulus is really reached.
mirror_effect: Worth a direct caveat: heavy oblique and lateral-trunk work like this can visibly thicken the waist if loaded heavy and often, which is the opposite of what many physique goals actually want — if a narrower-looking waist is the goal, this is one to keep light and controlled rather than a movement to progressively overload hard.
limitations: Grip commonly fails well before the trunk musculature does, especially without prior grip training, which can end the set before the intended stimulus is reached.
The whole-body fatigue cost is high relative to the trunk-specific stimulus delivered, making it an inefficient choice if trunk growth alone is the goal.
technique_cues: Pick up one dumbbell or kettlebell with a neutral grip and stand tall, the free arm relaxed at the side or held out slightly for balance.
Brace the trunk so the shoulders stay level and the torso leans neither toward nor away from the weight.
Walk with short, controlled steps, keeping the weight hanging still at the side without bumping the leg.
At the end of the distance or time, set the weight down with a flat back, switch hands and repeat on the other side.
common_mistakes: Leaning toward the weight: the trunk gives in to the sideways pull the exercise is meant to resist.
Leaning away from the weight to counterbalance it: the trunk side-bends under load in the other direction instead of staying upright.
Shrugging the loaded shoulder toward the ear: the traps take over and the shoulders stop being level.
complements: Anti-rotation and trunk-flexion work.
video_title: How To Perform The Suitcase Carry

name: Sumo Deadlift
summary: A wide-stance floor pull with real quad and adductor involvement and less lower-back range than a conventional deadlift.
why_this_exists: A wide stance with the toes turned out and the hands gripping inside the knees shortens the range of motion and keeps the torso more upright than a conventional deadlift, shifting the demand away from the lower back and toward the quads and adductors — enough that it's recorded here rather than with the conventional deadlift in the back module.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, floor start, wide stance, shorter range of motion than a conventional deadlift.
best_used_when: A maximal-load pull is wanted with real quad and adductor involvement and less lower-back range than a conventional deadlift, or torso or arm length makes the conventional stance's range awkward.
less_suitable_when: Hip external-rotation mobility is limiting, which can push stress onto the knees or hips instead of the intended muscles, or the fuller hip-hinge range and greater spinal-erector demand the conventional deadlift provides is wanted instead.
mirror_effect: Similar visible direction to the sumo squat — quad and inner-thigh mass together — with less contribution to lower-back erector thickness than a conventional deadlift, since the shorter range and more upright torso ask less of the lower back.
limitations: Hip mobility requirements are real and specific — a lifter without adequate external rotation can't set up the stance properly no matter how much they load the bar.
The technical demand is high, and the wide stance plus close grip inside the knees takes real practice to coordinate safely under heavy load.
technique_cues: Stand with a wide stance, toes turned out, and the shins close to the bar, then grip the bar with the hands inside the knees.
Push the knees out over the toes, drop the hips, and set a flat back with the chest up.
Push the floor apart with the feet and stand up, keeping the bar close to the legs until the hips and knees lock out together.
Lower the bar under control by pushing the hips back and bending the knees, keeping the back flat.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward as the bar leaves the floor: the hips lose their position and the knees take strain.
Hips shooting up first so the back does the lift: turns it into a stiff-legged pull and loads the lower back.
Rounding the lower back to reach the bar: the main injury risk of any heavy floor pull.
complements: A single-joint hamstring or glute movement.
video_title: How To Do A BARBELL SUMO DEADLIFT | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Sumo Squat
summary: A wide stance changes joint angles enough to bring the adductors in as a real mechanical-tension target, not just a stabilizer.
why_this_exists: A wide stance with the toes turned out changes the joint angles at the hip and knee, bringing the adductors into the squat as a real mechanical-tension target rather than just a stabilizer, and often allows a more upright torso than a shoulder-width stance.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, wide stance.
best_used_when: A squat variation is wanted that trains the adductors directly, or torso length or hip mobility makes a more upright squat more comfortable than a shoulder-width stance.
less_suitable_when: Hip external-rotation mobility is limiting, which can push stress onto the knees or lower back instead of the intended muscles.
mirror_effect: Tends to add inner-thigh (adductor) fullness alongside the usual quad mass, changing the leg's profile from the front more than a shoulder-width squat does — a fuller look through the inner thigh, not just the front.
limitations: Hip external-rotation mobility genuinely limits how wide and how deep the stance can go, and forcing it without that mobility can push stress onto the knees.
The wide stance is a real technical departure from a standard squat, so it takes its own practice rather than transferring automatically from shoulder-width squatting experience.
technique_cues: Set the bar on the upper back and stand with a wide stance, the toes turned out.
Brace the trunk and keep the chest up before each rep.
Squat down by pushing the knees out in line with the toes, as deep as the hips allow with a flat back.
Drive up through the whole foot, keeping the knees pushed out until standing.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward: the wide stance loses its point and the knees take strain.
Forcing a stance wider than the hips allow: the knees are pushed out of line with the toes.
Leaning the torso far forward: turns it into a good-morning and loads the lower back.
complements: A hip-hinge movement such as a Romanian deadlift.
video_title: How To Do A BARBELL SUMO SQUAT | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: T-Bar Row
summary: A free-standing row with a fixed, close, mostly neutral grip and a heavy, mechanical-tension-driven stimulus.
why_this_exists: A free-standing row with a fixed, close, mostly neutral grip, which changes the pull's path and torso demand from a barbell row.
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile, fixed handle position.
best_used_when: A heavy, mechanical-tension-driven row with a fixed bar path is wanted, which can make it easier to push close to failure than a barbell row's grip-width and balance demands allow.
less_suitable_when: The deepest possible range of motion is the priority, since the fixed handle position can shorten the pull compared to a barbell or dumbbell row.
mirror_effect: Same thickness-building visible direction as a barbell row — mid-back mass and density — at a heavier loadable ceiling than most machine row options.
limitations: The fixed handle position means grip width and hand angle can't be adjusted mid-set the way a barbell or dumbbell allows, which doesn't suit every lifter's shoulder mechanics.
Requires a dedicated T-bar station or a landmine attachment, which isn't available in every gym the way a barbell is.
technique_cues: Straddle the bar (or stand on the T-bar platform), grip the handle, and hinge at the hips with soft knees until the torso is well inclined with a flat back.
Let the weight hang at arm's length, then brace the trunk before each rep.
Pull the handle toward the lower chest by driving the elbows back.
Lower under control to straight arms while keeping the torso angle fixed.
common_mistakes: The torso rising with each rep: the row turns into a lean-back, and the back muscles move less of the weight.
Rounding the lower back under load: the main injury risk on any bent-over row.
Jerking the weight up with the hips: momentum moves the weight instead of the back muscles.
complements: A supported row or vertical pull.
video_title: How To: T-Bar Row

name: Thoracic Open Book
summary: Lying on one side with the knees bent and the arms together, opening the top arm across the body to rotate the upper back.
why_this_exists: Overhead clears and smashes need the upper back to rotate freely. The open book trains that rotation lying down, with the hips held still so the movement comes from the upper back.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; range is limited by upper-back rotation, not by load.
best_used_when: Upper-back rotation for overhead strokes is wanted, as part of a warm-up or a mobility session.
less_suitable_when: Lying on the side is uncomfortable for the shoulder underneath; thread the needle trains similar rotation on hands and knees.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds upper-back rotation.
limitations: If the knees drift apart, the lower back twists instead of the upper back, so the hips need to stay stacked.
It trains range, not strength, at the end of the rotation.
technique_cues: Lie on one side with the hips and knees bent to about 90 degrees and the arms straight out in front, palms together.
Keep the knees pressed together, or hold them down with the bottom hand.
Open the top arm up and across, following the hand with the eyes, until the chest faces the ceiling as far as is comfortable.
Breathe out at the end of the range, then return slowly and repeat.
common_mistakes: Knees lifting or sliding apart: the rotation moves to the lower back.
Forcing the arm to the floor: the shoulder gets stretched instead of the upper back rotating.
Rushing the reps: the drill works by easing a little further each time.
programming_notes: Do both sides; if one side is clearly stiffer, give it a few extra reps.
complements: Thread the needle, which trains the same rotation from hands and knees.
video_title: Thoracic Rotation Open Book

name: Thread the Needle
summary: From hands and knees, reaching one arm under the body and then up toward the ceiling, rotating the upper back each way.
why_this_exists: It trains upper-back rotation in both directions from a stable position on hands and knees, useful for the twisting involved in overhead and backhand strokes.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; range is limited by upper-back rotation.
best_used_when: Upper-back rotation is wanted as a warm-up or between sets, with no equipment.
less_suitable_when: Kneeling or weight on one hand is uncomfortable; the open book trains similar rotation lying on the side.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds upper-back rotation.
limitations: The hips tend to shift sideways to fake extra range, so it needs a deliberate, slow tempo.
Kneeling on a hard floor can be uncomfortable without a mat.
technique_cues: Start on hands and knees with the hands under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Slide one arm under the body, palm up, letting the shoulder and side of the head lower toward the floor.
Reverse the movement and reach the same arm up toward the ceiling, following the hand with the eyes.
Keep the hips level over the knees throughout.
common_mistakes: Hips swaying sideways: the movement comes from the hips instead of the upper back.
Collapsing onto the supporting arm: the shoulder sags and the rotation shrinks.
Bouncing at the end of the range: controlled reps work better than momentum.
programming_notes: A pause of a breath or two at the bottom turns it into a gentle held stretch.
complements: The thoracic open book for the same rotation lying down.
video_title: Thoracic rotation in quadruped - thread the needle

name: Tibialis Raise
summary: Directly trains the front of the shin, which no common lower-body lift loads, rounding out lower-leg development.
why_this_exists: Directly trains the front of the shin, which no common lower-body lift loads, rounding out lower-leg development rather than leaving the front of the leg entirely untrained.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight, band, or dedicated device.
best_used_when: Even lower-leg development and shin resilience are wanted alongside calf size, rather than treating "calves" as only the muscles on the back of the lower leg.
less_suitable_when: Calf size specifically is the goal — this movement does not load the gastrocnemius or soleus and will not move that goal.
mirror_effect: This changes the front of the lower leg, not the calf itself — consistent training tends to show up as more fullness on the shin, which frames the calf from the front and side rather than adding to the back-of-leg mass most people associate with "bigger calves."
limitations: Loading options are limited without a dedicated device — bodyweight, band, and wall variations all cap out at a fairly light stimulus for a trained lifter.
It's a narrow, single-joint movement with no meaningful carryover to overall lower-body strength or size beyond the shin itself.
technique_cues: Stand with the back and hips against a wall and the heels about a foot's length in front of it (or sit with a band looped over the top of the foot).
Keep the legs straight and the weight on the heels.
Pull the toes and the front of the feet up toward the shins as far as possible.
Lower the feet slowly until they almost touch the floor, without resting between reps.
common_mistakes: Rocking the hips off the wall to lift the toes: the body leans forward and the shins do less of the work.
Dropping the feet quickly on the way down: skips the controlled lowering, which is half of each rep's shin work.
Feet too close to the wall: the range is so small that the shins barely work; step the heels further out as it gets easier.
complements: Plantarflexion work.
video_title: Bodyweight Tibialis Raise | Fix Shin Splits

name: Triceps Kickback
summary: Holds the upper arm still and extends only the forearm, a light, low-fatigue mind-muscle-connection finisher.
why_this_exists: Holds the upper arm still and extends only the forearm against resistance, isolating the triceps at the end of the range where pressing and pushdowns are already easiest.
primary_targets: triceps (all three heads — no evidence of a differential lateral/medial bias; see evidence_notes)
resistance_profile: Free weight or cable, light load.
best_used_when: A light, low-fatigue, mind-muscle-connection finisher is wanted rather than a movement meant to add real mechanical tension.
less_suitable_when: The upper arm drops during the set, which turns the movement into a shoulder exercise and loses the isolated triceps stimulus that's the point of the kickback.
mirror_effect: A minor, finishing-touch contribution to triceps shape at best — the light loading this movement uses isn't enough on its own to be a primary driver of visible arm size.
limitations: The load ceiling is very low by design — this is not a movement that will ever feel heavy, and using more than light weight usually means the upper arm is dropping to help.
Keeping the upper arm genuinely still takes real attention, and it's an easy cue to lose without noticing once the light weight starts to feel like real effort.
technique_cues: Brace one hand and knee on a bench with a flat back, holding the dumbbell in the other hand (or stand bent over at a low cable).
Lift the working upper arm until it's alongside the torso, roughly parallel to the floor, with the elbow bent to about 90 degrees.
Straighten the elbow to push the weight back until the arm is fully straight, keeping the upper arm still.
Bend the elbow back to about 90 degrees under control before the next rep.
common_mistakes: The upper arm dropping toward the floor as the set gets hard: the shoulder swings the weight and the triceps do less of the work.
Swinging the weight back with momentum: the rep skips the controlled straightening that makes the exercise worthwhile.
Stopping short of a straight arm: misses the end of the range, the part this exercise exists to train.
complements: A pressing movement or a pushdown.
evidence_notes: Same correction as close-grip-bench-press: no evidence found for a differential lateral/medial-head bias here — see that record's evidence_notes for the full reasoning. The shoulder stays extended and roughly still through a kickback, so this movement doesn't put the long head through the stretched, shoulder-flexed position the overhead-extension evidence is actually about either.
video_title: How To: Tricep Kickback (Dumbbell)

name: Upright Row (Wide Grip)
summary: A wide-grip pull from the thighs to about chest height, training the side delts through abduction with the elbows leading, from a bar, dumbbells, cable or a band.
why_this_exists: The lateral raises are the side delts' main isolation work, but all need a dumbbell, cable or machine. The wide-grip upright row trains the same abduction as a multi-joint pull that also works from a band, so side delts can be trained with minimal kit.
resistance_profile: Hardest toward the top as the elbows rise out to the sides. A cable keeps tension at the bottom; a band gets heavier the higher it is pulled, which matches the top-loaded shape of the movement.
best_used_when: Side delts need direct work and only a band or a bar is available.
A heavier, multi-joint side-delt movement is wanted alongside lateral raises.
less_suitable_when: Pulling the elbows up toward shoulder height is uncomfortable for the shoulders — a lateral raise trains the same muscle with less internal rotation.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up, over time, as wider-looking shoulders from the front — the same side-delt contribution as lateral raises, from a movement that also loads the upper traps.
limitations: The elbows rise with the upper arm turned inward, which some shoulders tolerate poorly, especially with a narrow grip or when pulling above chest height.
The upper traps share the work, so it is a less isolated side-delt stimulus than a lateral raise.
technique_cues: Hold the bar or handles with a grip clearly wider than shoulder width, arms hanging straight in front of the thighs.
Lead with the elbows, pulling them up and out to the sides while the hands stay close to the body.
Stop when the upper arms are about parallel to the floor, with the elbows level with or just above the hands.
Lower slowly back to straight arms, keeping the torso still throughout.
common_mistakes: Narrow grip and pulling to the chin: turns the shoulder further inward at the top and makes it the uncomfortable version of the exercise.
Leaning back and heaving the weight: momentum and the lower back move the load instead of the side delts.
Hands rising above the elbows: the biceps and forearms take over and the elbows stop leading the abduction.
programming_notes: With a band, stand on the middle with the feet about hip width; a wider stance or a shorter grip on the band adds resistance.
complements: Rear-delt work such as reverse flyes or face pulls.
video_title: Wide Grip Barbell Upright Row

name: Walking Lunge
summary: Continuous forward stepping adds a coordination and conditioning demand on top of the per-leg quad stimulus.
why_this_exists: Stepping forward continuously and alternating legs removes the reset between reps a static or reverse lunge has, adding a coordination and conditioning demand on top of the per-leg quad stimulus.
resistance_profile: A barbell on the back allows a fixed path but adds the most balance demand of the three loading options; dumbbells at the sides are the easier entry point; a shouldered sandbag adds a shifting, unstable load on top of a movement that's already balance-demanding. Bodyweight alone is the no-equipment version and the way to learn the stepping pattern.
best_used_when: A higher-rep, pump-and-conditioning-oriented per-leg stimulus with athletic carryover is wanted, rather than a controlled mechanical-tension set.
less_suitable_when: Balance and coordination limit the load before the legs are meaningfully fatigued, capping how much of the intended stimulus the set can deliver — a static or reverse lunge reduces that limiter.
mirror_effect: Same per-leg quad direction as other lunges. It is usually trained for higher reps as a conditioning-style set, so it tends to support quad development rather than be the heaviest quad loading in a programme.
limitations: The continuous, alternating-leg demand makes balance and coordination the limiting factor for many lifters well before the quads are meaningfully fatigued.
Space requirements (a clear walking lane) make it harder to fit into a typical gym session than a stationary lunge or squat variation.
technique_cues: Stand tall holding the load (dumbbells at the sides, a barbell on the upper back, a sandbag on one shoulder, or hands on the hips), with a clear lane ahead.
Take a long step forward and lower straight down until the back knee nearly touches the floor, keeping the torso upright.
Push through the whole front foot to rise, bringing the back foot through into the next step.
Keep the feet about hip width apart side to side on every step, alternating legs through the set.
common_mistakes: Steps too short: the knees end up cramped and the torso tips forward to stay balanced.
Stepping along one narrow line, as on a tightrope: balance fails and the hips twist, ending the set before the legs are worked.
Rushing the steps to stay balanced: momentum carries the body forward and the controlled lowering gets skipped, cutting the quad work in each rep.
programming_notes: Bodyweight version: walk the lunges with the hands on the hips. It needs only floor space for several steps; add weight once the stepping pattern is steady.
complements: A bilateral squat or press.
video_title: The Walking Lunge

name: Wall Calf Stretch (Straight and Bent Knee)
summary: Leaning into a wall with one leg back, first with the back knee straight and then bent, to stretch both layers of the calf.
why_this_exists: Constant jumping, lunging and split-stepping load the calves and Achilles. Stretching with a straight and then a bent knee covers both the upper and lower calf muscles.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; leaning further forward deepens the stretch.
best_used_when: The calves feel tight after play, or ankle range for deep lunges is wanted.
less_suitable_when: The Achilles is painful or swollen; that needs assessing rather than stretching.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds calf and ankle range.
limitations: The back heel tends to lift or the foot turns out, which reduces the stretch.
It stretches the calf but does not build the calf strength that also protects it; calf raises do that.
technique_cues: Stand facing a wall with the hands on it and one foot well behind the other, both feet pointing forward.
Straight knee: keep the back leg straight and the heel down, and lean forward until the upper calf stretches.
Bent knee: bring the back foot in a little, bend the back knee, and keep the heel down to feel the lower calf.
Hold each version and breathe slowly, then switch legs.
common_mistakes: Back heel lifting: the stretch is lost.
Back foot turning outward: the stretch moves off the calf.
Bouncing into the wall instead of holding.
programming_notes: Hold each version separately; the bent-knee version is often the one that feels tighter after court sessions.
complements: Single-leg calf raise for calf strength.
Knee-to-wall ankle mobility for ankle range.
video_title: Standing Calf Stretch - Straight and Bent Knee

name: World's Greatest Stretch
summary: A deep lunge with the hand down, dropping the elbow toward the instep and then rotating the arm to the ceiling, linking hip, hamstring and upper-back mobility.
why_this_exists: It moves the hips, hamstrings and upper back in one flowing drill, which makes it an efficient warm-up before court sessions.
movement_patterns: lunge with elbow drop and rotation
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the depth of the lunge and rotation sets the range.
best_used_when: A single, efficient whole-body warm-up drill is wanted before playing or training.
less_suitable_when: A deep lunge is uncomfortable on the knees or hips; do the parts separately at a smaller range.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it warms up hip and upper-back range together.
limitations: It has several steps, so rushing it shortens every part of the range.
The back knee can be uncomfortable on a hard floor if it touches down.
technique_cues: Step one foot forward into a long lunge and place the opposite hand on the floor.
Drop the same-side elbow down toward the inside of the front foot.
Rotate that arm up toward the ceiling, following the hand with the eyes.
Return the hand to the floor, then step back and repeat on the other side.
common_mistakes: A short lunge: the hip-flexor stretch on the back leg is lost.
Rotating from the lower back instead of the upper back.
Rushing through the steps.
programming_notes: Some versions add a hamstring stretch by straightening the front leg before stepping back.
complements: Leg swings earlier in the warm-up.
video_title: How To Do The World's Greatest Stretch | Full Body Mobility | Emily Jones

name: Wrist Curl
summary: Direct loading for the wrist flexors, which larger lifts train only indirectly through gripping.
why_this_exists: Direct loading for the wrist flexors, which larger lifts train only indirectly through gripping.
resistance_profile: Barbell allows the heaviest fixed-path load; dumbbells let each wrist move independently; a cable keeps tension through the whole range at the cost of a less natural wrist path. A band anchored under the foot is lightest at the bottom and heaviest as the wrist curls up.
best_used_when: A direct mechanical-tension stimulus for forearm size is wanted, or wrist strength that doesn't depend on grip endurance running out first.
less_suitable_when: The wrists are already loaded by heavy pressing and pulling in the same session, adding fatigue without much additional growth stimulus.
mirror_effect: Tends to show up as fullness on the palm-side of the forearm, most noticeable near the elbow with the palm facing up — this thickens the inner forearm rather than changing its outline from the back of the hand side.
limitations: The wrist's small range of motion caps how much mechanical work each rep can do, so this exercise is inherently a slow-growth, high-volume tool rather than a heavy-load one.
Elbow-region tendons can take on real strain if load increases faster than the tendons adapt, since the forearm musculature is small relative to the loads gripping and pulling exercises expose it to.
technique_cues: Sit with your forearms on your thighs or a bench, palms up and wrists just past the edge.
Let the bar roll down toward your fingertips, then curl the fingers and wrist up as high as possible.
Move only the wrists and fingers; keep the forearms down.
common_mistakes: Lifting the forearms off the support: the elbows and shoulders help move the weight.
Raising load faster than the forearm tendons adapt: elbow pain is the usual result.
Short, fast reps that skip the full wrist range: the forearm flexors miss the stretched and fully curled positions, which are most of what the exercise trains.
programming_notes: Band version: sit with the forearm on the thigh, palm up, and the band anchored under the foot. Shorten the band to add resistance.
complements: Wrist extension work, which balances the other side of the forearm.
video_title: How To Do A STANDING BARBELL WRIST CURL | Exercise Demonstration Video and Guide

name: Wrist Flexor and Extensor Stretch
summary: Holding one straight arm out and gently bending the wrist back, then forward, with the other hand to stretch both sides of the forearm.
why_this_exists: Gripping a racket and snapping the wrist load the forearm muscles on both sides. These two stretches cover the front and back of the forearm.
resistance_profile: Bodyweight; the other hand sets the depth of each stretch.
best_used_when: The forearms feel tight after play, especially on the racket arm.
less_suitable_when: There is numbness, tingling or sharp pain in the wrist or elbow; that needs assessing rather than stretching.
mirror_effect: Not a physique exercise; it builds wrist and forearm range.
limitations: It stretches the forearm but does not build the grip and forearm strength that also matter for racket sports.
Bending the elbow takes most of the stretch away.
technique_cues: Hold the arm straight out in front at shoulder height.
For the front of the forearm: palm up, use the other hand to gently bend the fingers and wrist down toward the floor.
For the back of the forearm: palm down, gently bend the wrist down so the fingers point at the floor.
Keep the elbow straight and hold each stretch, then switch arms.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbow: most of the stretch is lost.
Pulling hard on the fingers: forearm stretches should be gentle.
Only stretching one side of the forearm.
programming_notes: Hold each direction for the full time; give the racket arm the most attention.
Wrist curls and reverse wrist curls build the forearm strength this stretch does not.
complements: Wrist curl and reverse wrist curl for forearm strength.
video_title: How to do the Wrist Flexor and Extensor Stretch- Oakville Physiotherapy

name: Zottman Curl
summary: Curls up supinated like a standard curl, then rotates pronated and lowers like a reverse curl — one movement for biceps and forearm.
why_this_exists: Curls up with a supinated grip like a standard curl, then rotates to a pronated grip at the top and lowers like a reverse curl, so one movement trains the biceps on the way up and the forearm extensors and brachioradialis on the way down.
movement_patterns: grip rotation from supinated to pronated
resistance_profile: Free-weight profile with a mid-rep grip rotation.
best_used_when: A combined biceps-and-forearm growth stimulus is wanted in one movement, with the slow eccentric half adding real tension the concentric-only lift of a standard curl skips.
less_suitable_when: The rotation at the top breaks down under heavier load, capping how much weight can be used for either half of the stimulus.
mirror_effect: Contributes to biceps mass on the way up and forearm/brachioradialis width on the way down — a combined effect across two visible areas from one movement, though each half is milder than a dedicated exercise for either.
limitations: The grip rotation at the top is a coordination demand that breaks down under heavier load, which caps how much weight can be used for either half of the movement.
Because load is limited by the rotation, neither the concentric biceps stimulus nor the eccentric forearm stimulus reaches the intensity a dedicated single-purpose exercise could deliver.
technique_cues: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, palms facing forward.
Curl the dumbbells up with the palms facing up, keeping the elbows at the sides.
At the top, rotate the wrists so the palms face down.
Lower slowly with the palms facing down, then rotate back to palms-up at the bottom before the next rep.
common_mistakes: Rotating the grip partway through the lowering instead of at the top: the reverse-curl half of the rep is cut short.
Dropping the dumbbells quickly on the way down: skips the slow palms-down lowering that is the point of the exercise.
Swinging the body to start the curl: momentum moves the weight instead of the biceps.
complements: A standard curl or a reverse curl programmed on their own for more focused volume.
overlaps_with: reverse-curl (forearms module) — the eccentric half of this movement.
video_title: How to Perform Zottman Curls | Bicep / Forearms Exercise Tutorial
